## 4. Measuring User Proficiency, Error Reduction, and Time-to-Competency

### 4.1 The core problem with the most common metric

The most common adoption metric — training course completion rate — is a weak predictor of operational success. The SysGenPro ERP benchmarking literature [sysgenpro.com/distribution-erp-implementation-metrics] notes: "Many manufacturing programs still rely on completion rates for training courses as a proxy for readiness. That approach is insufficient in cloud ERP migration and modernization programs where role changes, process harmonization, and control redesign are significant. A planner may complete training, for example, yet still be unable to manage exception messages, reschedule supply, or interpret planning outputs in the new system."

**Prosci's measurement-quality finding** is the sharpest quantitative result on this question [prosci.com/blog/measuring-what-actually-predicts-erp-success]:
- Organizations with **strong metrics were 2.5× more likely** to exceed expectations for their ERP transformations.
- Organizations with **poor metrics succeeded only 7% of the time, versus 26% for organizations with no formal metrics at all.**
- Conclusion stated by Prosci: "measuring the wrong things can do more harm than not measuring at all."

**Prosci's three human-factors ROI metrics for ERP:**
1. **Speed of adoption** — how quickly people begin working effectively in the new environment.
2. **Ultimate utilization** — whether intended users use the new system and processes.
3. **Proficiency** — how well people perform their work after adoption.

Activity metrics (training completion, communications sent, milestones, support tickets) "help teams manage delivery but provide little insight into whether people can use the new system effectively."

### 4.2 Stronger metric set

From SysGenPro and the LMS-ERP integration case study at Upscend [upscend.com/blogs/lms-erp-case-study-cutting-skill-gaps-43-in-manufacturing; sysgenpro.com/manufacturing-erp-adoption-metrics-that-reveal-readiness-gaps-before-go-live; sysgenpro.com/distribution-erp-implementation-metrics-that-help-leaders-track-rollout-performance; sysgenpro.com/distribution-erp-training-strategy-for-reducing-errors-in-order-inventory-and-warehouse-processes; sysgenpro.com/manufacturing-erp-dashboards-that-improve-shop-floor-and-executive-visibility; sysgenpro.com/manufacturing-erp-migration-best-practices-for-operational-continuity-during-cutover]:

| Domain | Stronger metric | Operational interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Proficiency | Role-based proficiency pass rate (transaction-based) | Can the user actually complete the transaction? |
| Proficiency | First-30-day transaction accuracy by role | Are they doing it correctly? |
| Operational | Exception-handling readiness | Can they recover from nonstandard events? |
| Operational | Mean Time to Competency (MTC) | How long from go-live to standard performance? |
| Operational | Process adherence rate | Are they using the standardized workflow? |
| Operational | Manual adjustment / rework volume | Are they creating reconciliation work? |
| Operational | Support tickets by user group | Where is friction? |
| Operational | Super-user engagement rate | Are peer coaches being used? |

### 4.3 Documented time-to-competency outcomes

**Upscend automotive parts plant (mid-sized)** [upscend.com/blogs/lms-erp-case-study-cutting-skill-gaps-43-in-manufacturing]: An LMS–ERP integration cut **mean time to competence by 43%** (42 days → 24 days; arithmetic: (42 − 24)/42 = 0.4286 → 42.9%), improved first-pass yield by 10 points (78% → 88%), and halved operator-related errors over a six-month pilot (process error rate per 1,000 ops from 160 to 88; (160 − 88)/160 = 0.45 → 45%). Training hours per operator/month dropped from 18 to 12 (−33%). Output per operator rose 7%. The mechanism: event-driven microlearning triggered by ERP work orders, so that a technician assigned a new routing automatically receives the right training content in the ERP UI rather than in a separate LMS.

**Epicor beverage packaging plant case** [epicor.com/en/blog/technology-and-data/manufacturing-case-study/]: Reduced new-hire training time from 18 months (538 days) to 4 months (125 days), a 77% reduction (arithmetic: (538 − 125)/538 = 0.7676 → 76.8%), by converting tribal knowledge and paper SOPs into structured, on-the-floor digital job aids with tracked task lists and proficiency quizzes.

**TruPeer transition analysis** [trupeer.ai/blog/reduce-time-to-proficiency-in-transitions]: Defines Time to Proficiency (TTP) as the period from knowledge-transfer start to the point where the receiving team consistently meets agreed quality and productivity targets without extra support. Recommends measuring TTP rather than KT-session count, because TTP is what actually drives service levels, error rates, and backlog after go-live.

### 4.4 Documented error-reduction outcomes

- **Adaptive Fiori manufacturing case (Harvey 2026, SSRN)** [papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7488856]: Material-movement posting errors −47%, production-order confirmation time −31%, cognitive load −34%, SUS 58→78.
- **Intelligent Process Automation in SAP S&MM (WJARR 2022)** [wjarr.com/sites/default/files/fulltext_pdf/WJARR-2022-0212.pdf]: User productivity +35%, process completion times −42%, error rates −68% across 12 organizations over 18 months. Caveat: this paper is a single-author study of unclear peer-review status.
- **LMS–ERP case (Upscend)**: Halved operator-related errors; 16% baseline torque-sequence error rate on the chassis line was the specific driver. First-pass yield shortfall of 22% across two assembly lines was the catalyst.
- **LIDD food manufacturer (NetSuite)**: Reduced manual inventory adjustments, improved pick confirmation accuracy, shortened order release delays within first quarter post go-live (specific percentages not reported).
- **CYB Software NetSuite dashboard redesign**: Mid-sized electronics manufacturer's planners dashboard did not show supplier lead times or component shortages; after redesign to include late POs by vendor, work orders missing components, and a supplier-reliability trend, **late shipments dropped 18% in two months** [cybsoftware.com/how-to-customize-netsuite-dashboards-for-every-role-in-your-manufacturing-business/].

### 4.5 Training-time outcomes

- **SAP Fiori vs. SAP GUI (JENRS synthesis)**: 25–40% faster learning curve.
- **SAP Screen Personas with persona-based customization (WJARR 2022)**: up to 60% training-time reduction; specific to S&MM module.
- **Fiori-specific Sygeon vendor data**: "Fiori's intuitive design typically reduces training requirements by up to 50% compared to traditional SAP interfaces" [sygeon.com].
- **In-app microlearning (Epicor case)**: 77% reduction in new-hire time to full proficiency for a beverage packaging plant.

---

## 5. Role-Based Views vs. Comprehensive Dashboards

### 5.1 The case for role-based

The role-based view is not just a UI preference; it is the dominant pattern in documented manufacturing implementations.

NN/g's enterprise portal research (B2B Website Usability report, 79 participants) found that **"role-based personalization usually works better than individual personalization"** [nngroup.com/reports/intranet-portals-experiences-real-life-projects/].

The Role-Based Dashboard design literature (ifactoryapp.com, connect981.com, eposly.io) converges on three role tiers in manufacturing [ifactoryapp.com/blog/role-based-dashboard-operator-supervisor-director; connect981.com/glossary/role-based-dashboard; eposly.io/blog/role-based-dashboards-for-manufacturing-faster-shop-floor-decisions; cybsoftware.com/how-to-customize-netsuite-dashboards-for-every-role-in-your-manufacturing-business/; peoplesenseerp.com/what-is-role-based-erp-for-manufacturers-and-why-does-it-matter/; onramp-solutions.com/blog/erp-for-manufacturers-built-for-every-user-on-your-floor/]:

| Role | Time horizon | Primary decisions | Critical metrics | Aggregation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Operator | Seconds–minutes | Whether to stop the line | OEE, scrap, downtime cause | Real-time, single line |
| Supervisor | Minutes–hours | Resequence jobs, escalate, reassign labor | Schedule adherence, WIP aging, downtime, scrap, labor variance | Shift-rolled, line-rolled |
| Plant manager / director | Days–months | Capacity, cost, capital | Trended cost, throughput, on-time delivery | Plant-rolled, week/month |

The ifactoryapp.com article makes the most explicit case: "Give an operator a director's dashboard and they'll ignore it within a week. Give a director an operator's dashboard and they'll drown in cycle-time noise that tells them nothing about the resourcing decision they actually need to make." It also identifies the implementation pitfall: building three separate reporting pipelines for three roles guarantees that the numbers drift apart within a year. **The solution is a single source of truth at the machine level, aggregated differently per role.**

For the 45–60 production supervisor specifically, the operator view is too narrow and the plant-manager view is too aggregated. The right default is a supervisor-specific view that aggregates across the lines and shifts they manage, with clear drill-downs to the operator view and clear roll-ups to the plant view. The Cyb Software manufacturing guide puts it as: "A production planner doesn't need to see EBITDA trends. A finance lead doesn't need to see machine uptime" [cybsoftware.com].

A Polish UEQ study of ERP operation-registration screens in manufacturing environments is useful for *what production users value*: **pragmatic dimensions (perspicuity, efficiency, dependability) rated favorably; hedonic dimensions (stimulation, novelty) rated neutral to negative** [ph.pollub.pl/index.php/acs/article/view/7625]. Your supervisors want clarity, speed, and reliability — not novelty. A "delightful" comprehensive dashboard directly contradicts this.

### 5.2 The case for occasional access to advanced functions

The production supervisor does occasionally need advanced functions: routing a nonstandard work order, investigating a variance, running an ad-hoc inventory query. The empirical evidence (Bentley follow-up study; ACM 2025 study) shows that progressive disclosure works only if the second-layer trigger is easy to find. In practice:

- **SAP Fiori** implements this through the "Adapt Filters" and "Settings" menus on each app, plus the App Finder (a search-indexed catalog of all apps the user is entitled to). The role-based launchpad shows only the role's apps by default, with the App Finder one click away.
- **Dynamics 365 Business Central** implements it through the "Tell Me" search feature (Alt+Q), Role Explorer, and Views that allow per-user filtering and sorting.
- **Oracle NetSuite** provides the Advanced Manufacturing tablet UI with collapsible headers and a Quick Search field; custom dashboards

# The Anthropology of Gift Economies: A Comprehensive Literature Review from Malinowski to the Blockchain

## I. Introduction

The anthropological study of gift economies has produced, over more than a century, a layered corpus of theory, ethnography, and critique. What began as an attempt to explain why Melanesian islanders risked their lives "to give away what appear to be worthless trinkets" (Malinowski, https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55822/pg55822-images.html) became the analytical scaffolding for thinking about exchange, personhood, power, and—in its most recent extensions—the political economy of open-source code, attention metrics, and decentralized ledgers. This review traces that arc comparatively through (1) the classical foundations (Malinowski, Mauss, Sahlins, with Lévi-Strauss and Gregory as immediate interlocutors), (2) feminist anthropological critiques (Gayle Rubin, Annette Weiner, Marilyn Strathern, and Pierre Bourdieu), and (3) three contemporary sites of application: free/open-source software, social-media "attention economies," and cryptocurrency governance. The central question animating all of these literatures is whether the gift/commodity binary retains analytical purchase in conditions that no longer map onto the pre-capitalist or archaic societies in which the categories were forged.

## II. The Classical Foundations

### A. Malinowski and the Kula (1922)

Bronisław Malinowski's *Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (1922) established the kula as the paradigmatic case of non-market exchange. Ethnographic fieldwork among the Trobriand Islanders produced the now-canonical description of a vast inter-island circuit in which two classes of valuables—red shell-disc necklaces (*soulava*) traveling clockwise and white shell armbands (*mwali*) traveling counterclockwise—circulated among partners arranged in permanent, dyadic relationships (*karayta'u*) (https://anth1001.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/malinowski_excerpts.pdf; https://paas.org.pl/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Malinowski_Argonauts_of_the_Western_Pacific.pdf). The Wikipedia entry on the kula confirms the system "spans 18 island communities of the Massim archipelago, including the Trobriand Islands, and involves thousands of individuals" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kula_ring).

Crucially, the kula valuables were "of high value, but of no real use" (https://acdigitalpedagogy.org/mpelzel/kula-ocr.pdf), and "no man ever keeps any of the articles for any length of time in his possession." Malinowski developed a dense taxonomy distinguishing the kula from subsidiary trade: pure gifts, opening gifts (*vaga*), return gifts (*yotile*), solicitary gifts (*pokala*), and the clinching gift (*kudu*) (https://www.berose.fr/IMG/pdf/malinowski_1922-argonauts.pdf). Ownership was "in order to acquire prestige and rank" (Britannica, https://www.britannica.com/topic/kula-trade), and the system was "clearly linked to political authority" (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kula_ring). Malinowski's contribution was to ground the method of participant observation that would define modern anthropology—by living in Omarakana, learning the language, and watching daily life, he showed that exchanges dismissed as irrational were in fact part of a coherent system linking economy, magic, myth, and political authority (https://escholarship.org/content/qt4rg9t7wv/qt4rg9t7wv.pdf).

A crucial structural point is that the kula ring "has neither been intentionally created by the individual actors nor designed by a central authority. It is the unintended by-product of so many doings"—an emergent order without a designer (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S037887330700072X). The kula has accumulated a measurable scholarly footprint: Macintyre's (1983a) bibliography lists 625 publications on the phenomenon (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S037887330700072X). Subsequent game-theoretic interpretations have modeled the kula as a signaling system for peaceful inter-community relationships, "with inbuilt checks against cheating" (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/25a4/2c81cff90795d0fe620590fcbe113663182c.pdf).

### B. Mauss and the Hau (1925)

Marcel Mauss's *Essai sur le don: forme et raison de l'échange dans les sociétés archaïques* was published in 1925 in *L'Année Sociologique*, the first issue after World War I had killed twelve of Mauss's colleagues, including his uncle Émile Durkheim (Wikipedia entry on the essay, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gift_(essay)). The 2016 expanded English edition, translated by Jane Guyer with a foreword by Bill Maurer, situates the essay back within its original framing materials (HAU Books, https://haubooks.org/the-gift/; full text at https://haubooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Marcel-Mauss-The-Gift-Expanded-Edition-Selected-Annotated-and-Translated-by-Jane-Guyer.pdf).

Mauss argued that in "archaic societies" exchange is organized by what he called "total prestation"—not individuals but collectivities transact, and what circulates includes "ceremonies, feasts, rites, military services, women, children, dances, celebrations, fairs" (https://web.stanford.edu/class/ihum54/odyssey/mauss_gift.htm). The gift, for Mauss, is a *"total social fact" (fait social total)*—simultaneously religious, juridical, moral, political, familial, and economic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gift_(essay)). His central conceptual move was the introduction of the Maori *hau*, "the spirit of the gift," drawn from the text of Tamati Ranapiri recorded by Elsdon Best: "Suppose you have some particular object, taonga, and you give it to me... Now this taonga I received from him is the spirit (hau) of the taonga I received from you and which I passed on to him" (https://web.mit.edu/allanmc/www/mauss1.pdf). On Mauss's reading, "to present something to someone is to present something of oneself"—a thing given retains a spiritual claim on the recipient, and the counter-gift is compelled by this mystic residue (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.14318/hau6.2.017).

Mauss decomposed the gift cycle into three obligations: "to give in the first place, and the obligation to receive" and, "most importantly, to repay" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gift_(essay)). Mauss explicitly extended his framework to the potlatch of the American Northwest (Chinook jargon *potlatch*, "to feed"), where "honor and credit" replace mere utility as the medium of value, and to the vindicating logic of gift-equals-gift as a "total social phenomenon" (Monoskop 1990 translation, https://monoskop.org/images/b/b9/Mauss_Marcel_The_Gift._The_Form_and_Reason_for_Exchange_in_Archaic_Societies_1990.pdf).

Three reception points complicate the standard reading. First, Lévi-Strauss's introduction attacked the *hau* as a mystical non-explanation, insisting reciprocity itself was the universal basis of social relations (https://archive.org/stream/StoneAgeEconomics_201611/StoneAgeEconomics-MarshallSahlins_djvu.txt). Second, Bill Maurer (2016, *HAU*) argues the *hau* "does not use… explanatory work" in Mauss at all: the "force in the thing" derives from Mauss's construction of the Roman legal institution of *nexum*—debt-bondage—not from Polynesia (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.14318/hau6.2.017). Third, Jane Guyer's expanded translation (2016) revealed the essay's political aim: that "the clan, the tribe, and the peoples have learned—as tomorrow… classes and nations and individuals too will have to learn—how to confront one another without massacring each other" (https://haubooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Marcel-Mauss-The-Gift-Expanded-Edition-Selected-Annotated-and-Translated-by-Jane-Guyer.pdf). The *Essai* was, from birth, a mixed-economy manifesto, not a gift-economy utopia—a point David Graeber stresses against reductive readings (https://davidgraeber.org/wp-content/uploads/What-is-Debt-%E2%80%93-An-Interview-with-Economic-Anthropologist-David-Graeber.pdf). Sahlins later called the essay "Mauss's famous *Essay on the Gift* becomes his own gift to the ages … a source of an unending ponderation for the anthropologist *du métier*, compelled as if by the *hau* of the thing to come back to it again and again" (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf).

### C. Sahlins and the Dialectic of Distance (1972)

Marshall Sahlins's *Stone Age Economics* (1972) built on and criticized both Mauss and Lévi-Strauss. Sahlins synthesized the formalist-substantivist debate into a refusal to apply "the ready-made models of orthodox Economics…to the primitive societies" and instead located the economy "as a category of culture rather than behaviour, in a class with politics and religion rather than rationality or prudence" (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf; book details at https://www.routledge.com/Stone-Age-Economics/Sahlins/p/book/9781138702615).

Sahlins's "On the Sociology of Primitive Exchange" (1965; collected in *Stone Age Economics*, 1972) synthesized Polanyi's tripartite scheme (reciprocity/redistribution/market) with Lévi-Strauss's (exchange of goods, women, words) (https://archive.org/stream/StoneAgeEconomics_201611/StoneAgeEconomics-MarshallSahlins_djvu.txt). The most enduring analytic contribution of the volume is a classification of reciprocity along a continuum indexed by social distance:

1. **Generalized reciprocity** — "basically, what Mauss called 'communism'" — solidary, diffuse transfers among close kin where return is not stipulated or timed (https://hraf.yale.edu/teach-ehraf/reciprocity-exchange-the-kula-ring/index.html).
2. **Balanced reciprocity** — a "middle zone… governed by fairness," obligating return within a specified time of roughly equal value (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(cultural_anthropology)).
3. **Negative reciprocity** — "the attempt to get something for nothing," the sphere of haggling, theft, and barter.

David Graeber, in his foreword to the Routledge Classics edition, called this tripartite scheme one of the most consequential theoretical devices in modern social theory, "adopted by archaeologists, historians, classicists, literary theorists, political theorists, psychologists, art historians, sociologists, philosophers, and students of religion," while lamenting that "the only discipline that has never made significant use of the theoretical tools provided in this collection is economics itself" (https://davidgraeber.org/articles/foreword-to-the-routledge-classics-edition-stone-age-economics-marshall-sahlins/).

The master variable is kinship distance: the moral tone of a transaction is "a function of social distance," with reciprocity "inverse to kinship distance"—a continuum rather than discrete types (https://www.thetedkarchive.com/library/marshall-sahlins-stone-age-economics). Two of Sahlins's formulations travel exceptionally well into digital contexts: "If friends make gifts, gifts make friends"—material flow underwrites social relations (https://redefineschool.com/stone-age-econ/)—and his scope caveat that the typology "applies only insofar as the economy and social relations have not been modified by the historic penetration of states" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(cultural_anthropology)). Paul Sillitoe later extended it by sphere of production: subsistence goods circulate under generalized reciprocity; "wealth objects—by their nature from outside—are competitively exchanged to acquire status" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(cultural_anthropology)).

Sahlins also devoted a sustained chapter, "The Spirit of the Gift," to a critical re-reading of Mauss's *hau*. Sahlins catalogues three authoritative attacks on Mauss's *hau* interpretation (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf): **Lévi-Strauss** argued that Mauss allowed himself to be "mystified by the native": the *hau* is only how a people *represents* an unconscious necessity (reciprocity); **Raymond Firth** charged that Mauss simply misunderstood the *hau*, conflating distinct senses of the term—the real sanctions are secular and social; **J. Prytz Johansen** preferred "a part of life … used ritually" and suggested Ranapiri's *hau* simply meant "countergift." Against these, Sahlins proposed that *hau* "really means something on the order of 'return on' or 'product of,'" and that the obligation is best understood secularly: "one man's gift should not be another man's capital, and therefore the fruits of a gift ought to be passed back to the original holder" (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf). Ranapiri was explaining a three-party transaction to show that "the gift has had issue"—a claim about the distinction between gift and capital that anticipates twenty-first-century debates about platform appropriation.

### D. Lévi-Strauss and the Universalization of Reciprocity

In *Les Structures élémentaires de la parenté* (1949), Claude Lévi-Strauss elevated reciprocity to the foundational operator of social life (Archive full text, https://archive.org/stream/TheElementaryStructuresOfKinshipLeviStrauss/The+Elementary+Structures+Of+Kinship+-+Levi+Strauss_djvu.txt). His programmatic claim was that "the gift binds both the giver and recipient in a continuing social relationship" (https://ebooks.inflibnet.ac.in/antp10/chapter/structuralism-levi-strauss-and-edmund-leach/). Marriage exchange, in his account, was the exemplary case in which the exchange of women institutes a structural and durable reciprocity between groups. As Sahlins noted, Lévi-Strauss criticized Mauss for failing to grasp exchange as "a unified and integral principle" rather than fragmented acts of giving, receiving, and repaying—the so-called "mystic cement" of *hau*—though Lévi-Strauss "does not presume to criticize Mauss on Maori ethnography" and instead stages a debate of principles (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf).

### E. Gregory and the Gift/Commodity Distinction (1982)

Christopher Gregory's *Gifts and Commodities* (1982) established the binary that became the field's reference typology for the next generation. Drawing on Karl Polanyi's substantivism, Gregory argued that gift exchange is premised on the alienable relationship between persons and things: in gift exchange, persons and things are "inseparably linked," while commodity exchange presupposes their alienation. Commodity exchange entails "reciprocal independence"—transactors are strangers; gift exchange entails "reciprocal dependence," measured by Sahlins's "kinship distance." In gift economies, "things and people… assume the social form of persons"; in commodity economies, of objects (http://haubooks.org/viewbook/gifts-and-commodities/10_ch03).

Gregory's crucial empirical point was that in colonial Papua New Guinea, gift and commodity economies expanded simultaneously—contrary to neoclassical assumptions that gifts would simply give way to markets (https://researchportal.helsinki.fi/en/publications/reprises-chris-gregorys-gifts-and-commodities-and-the-frontier/). He subsequently clarified that the book was "intended precisely as an affirmation of the coexistence of gifts and commodities" and of the "paradoxical efflorescence of gift exchange" under colonialism (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Gregory). The point that gifts and commodities coexist and convert into one another—capitalist commodity value is "everywhere created through tapping and transforming non-capitalist social relations" (https://journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.14318/hau3.1.003)—is the single most important bridge to the contemporary cases reviewed below. Subsequent work cited Gregory repeatedly to demarcate the analytical and moral stakes of digital exchange (e.g., Nardi and Harris, https://www.academia.edu/2074844/).

## III. Feminist Critiques

### A. Gayle Rubin and "the Traffic in Women"

Gayle Rubin's *The Traffic in Women* (1975) turned Lévi-Strauss's gift theory against itself. Reading *The Elementary Structures of Kinship* as "a radical gloss" on Mauss's *Essay*, Rubin argued that the **incest taboo** functions as "a rule obliging the mother, sister, or daughter to be given to others. It is the supreme rule of the gift" (https://glc.yale.edu/sites/default/files/pdf/rubin_the_traffic_in_women.pdf). Marriage, on this account, is "a most basic form of gift exchange, in which it is women who are the most precious of gifts." Rubin's intervention was to show that the classic theory of reciprocity **presupposes women as objects of exchange rather than as subjects**, and to name the resulting system a **"sex/gender system"** analytically distinct from capitalism—thereby founding gender studies as a field (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Traffic_in_Women:_Notes_on_the_Political_Economy_of_Sex).

### B. Annette Weiner and the "Forgotten Dimension"

Annette Weiner's *Women of Value, Men of Renown* (1976) directly challenged Malinowski's gendered account of the Trobriands by showing that women's labor in producing banana-leaf bundles and fiber skirts (*doba*) was central to mortuary distributions (*sagali*), the very exchanges Malinowski had described as if women were socially peripheral. On her first day of fieldwork in a village three-quarters of a mile from Malinowski's own site, Weiner saw a mortuary ceremony in which women distributed "up to 30,000 bundles in one day, each worth about one Australian cent" (https://www.academia.edu/35663879/Women_of_Value_Men_of_Renown). These bundles were *"women's wealth"*—made, exchanged, and controlled by women—and embodied "'womanness': sexuality, reproduction, and nurture," a "cosmic statement of regeneration of pure *dala* substance" (https://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/n2571/pdf/epilogue.pdf). The flow of yams between men was tied to the flow of women's wealth: a man gardens not for himself but to give to his sister and her husband, and husbands must help wives accumulate women's wealth for the *sagali* (https://pub-ucpec2-prd.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/view?anchor.id=bkd0e1262).

In *Inalienable Possessions* (1992), Weiner formalized the concept of "inalienable possessions"—objects that "must not be given or, if they are circulated, must return finally to the giver"—and argued that "the degree of control over the production and distribution of cloth wealth coincides with women's rank and the development of hierarchy in the community" (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/inalienable-possessions/paper). The "paradox of keeping-while-giving" reframed Mauss's reciprocity: rather than circulate away from the giver, inalienable wealth accumulates around him or her, anchoring rank and political authority (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inalienable_possessions). Weiner specifically re-examined the *hau*: "not all gifts must be returned. Only gifts that are 'immoveable property' can become inalienable gifts" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inalienable_possessions). She applied the framework not only to Oceania but signaled Western analogues, from heirlooms to national patrimony.

Weiner's chapter "Kula: the Paradox of Keeping-While-Giving" repositioned Malinowski's findings within feminist analytical frameworks (https://academic.oup.com/california-scholarship-online/book/22469/chapter/182762889). The framework was contested. Jonathan Friedman's review of *Inalienable Possessions* in *Pacific Studies* called the theoretical architecture "vague and often self-contradictory" and the supposed "newness" of the theory overstated, while praising Weiner's earlier articulation of women's reproductive power (https://digitalcollections.byuh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2256&context=pacific-studies-journal). A more pointed critique, "Inalienable ethnography: keeping-while-giving and the Trobriand case" (https://researchportalplus.anu.edu.au/en/publications/inalienable-ethnography-keeping-while-giving-and-the-trobriand-ca/), argued that "Weiner's ethnographic illustrations do not lend support to her theory of inalienable possessions; that her conceptual framework is at considerable variance with well-founded understandings of Melanesian sociality; and that the paradox of keeping-while-giving is more appropriately seen as deriving from Western presuppositions of individual boundedness, subjectivity, possession, ownership, and hierarchy."

### C. Marilyn Strathern and the *Dividual*

Marilyn Strathern's *The Gender of the Gift* (1988) extended the feminist critique beyond Weiner's focus on women-as-keepers to a wholesale rethinking of Melanesian personhood (UC Press, https://www.ucpress.edu/book/9780520072022/the-gender-of-the-gift; Oxford Academic, https://academic.oup.com/california-scholarship-online/book/21765). Rejecting the Euro-American model of the individual, Strathern proposed the "dividual"—"a new, non-unitary model of embodiment" in which persons are composed of the detachable substances and relationships that circulate in exchange. Strathern argued that "gender relations have been a particular casualty of unexamined assumptions held by Western anthropologists and feminist scholars alike" (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-gender-of-the-gift/pdf). Rather than importing Western categories of "exploitation," "oppression," "control," "labor," and "production," Strathern derived gender from Melanesian exchange practices themselves: among the Melpa, persons are defined as men or women not by fixed attributes but by **modes of action**—production of trade goods for women, transaction for men (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bxjg20p7m4b). Her engagement with Western anthropology contended that comparison itself depends on "a Western construction" and that Melanesian sociality "might look like if they were to appear in the form of those preoccupations" (https://digitalcollections.byuh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2056&context=pacific-studies-journal).

David Lipset's "The 'Dividual Androgyne' and Me" challenged the empirical adequacy of the concept, arguing that Strathern mistook "a virulently anti-female ideology—including a fantasy in which men may subsume or incorporate certain aspects of female anatomy—for benign accommodation between the sexes," and that the dividual "paradoxically affirms Lévi-Strauss' classic demonstration in the *Elementary Structures of Kinship* (1949) that 'the gender of the gift' is invariably female" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/dbsjqhp8dpm). A more recent critique, "Controlling Fictions," frames the dividual model as "ideological relativism that is fraught with dangerous political consequences for the disciplinary project of anthropology" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bf0jhkx301z).

### D. The Weiner–Strathern Disagreement

Strathern's strategy differed from Weiner's. Where Weiner sought to extend reciprocity theory by adding the "forgotten dimension" of keeping, Strathern questioned reciprocity theory itself, arguing that the categories of "woman," "exchange," and "the gift" imported by Western and feminist anthropology alike mis-described Melanesian social life. Jointly, however, they produced a feminist anthropology of exchange that displaced the Malinowskian image of women as marginal to male ceremonial rivalry. Margaret Jolly criticized Weiner for essentializing "an unchanging Trobriand order" and treating women's wealth as the expression of timeless female values, and Strathern's 1981 review is repeatedly cited as the origin of a continuing debate "that continues to haunt contemporary feminist anthropology" (https://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/n2571/pdf/epilogue.pdf).

### E. Bourdieu and the Symbolic Denegation

Pierre Bourdieu's intervention (*Le Sens pratique*, 1980; *La Misère du monde*, 1993) cut across the feminist debate by treating the gift as a structured misrecognition. Bourdieu summarized his position: "The objective truth of the gift is exchange; its subjective truth is disinterestedness" (cited in "What's wrong with Bourdieu's gift?", https://shs.cairn.info/article/E_RDM_052_0074/pdf?lang=en). Gift exchange is thus the transformation of economic capital into symbolic capital via a "denial of the economic in the sense in which we understand it"—a Freudian *Verneinung* (denegation) at the level of the social. Subsequent work has applied this framework to health-and-wellness entrepreneurship and other Western market contexts (Plymouth research, https://pearl.plymouth.ac.uk/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1421&context=pms-research).

### F. The Gender-Blindness of the Maussian Tradition

A large feminist literature now reads Mauss's *Essay* as "colonialist, gender-blind and gender-biased," and the same charge is extended to Lévi-Strauss's derivative account (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/0399/39b9a835cc40843eef452ce8878d2b3a8171.pdf). White, Bracken, Leacock, Strathern, and Weiner are cited as showing that male authors "uncritically projected onto gift-giving in general … some of the taken-for-granted gender biases of the societies they themselves are part of." Morny Joy's edited collection *Women and the Gift* argues that "gifting and the gift economy are … a feature of male power and dominance that excludes the possibility of feminine subjectivity," and notes the paradox that "women are deeply associated with the gift but only … as the given … or as the all-giving in the mode of self-abnegation occasioned by infinite care" (https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:813107/FULLTEXT01.pdf).

## IV. Contemporary Applications

### A. Open-Source Software as Gift Culture

**The "gift culture" thesis.** The conceptual genealogy is traceable to Eric Raymond. Raymond's *The Cathedral and the Bazaar* (1997; First Monday republication, https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/view/1472) first contrasted the centralized "cathedral" model of proprietary development with the open "bazaar" model of Linux, articulating Linus's Law: "given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cathedral_and_the_Bazaar). Raymond's sequel, *Homesteading the Noosphere* (1998), explicitly framed open-source production as "a 'gift culture' in which members compete for status by giving things away": "gift cultures are adaptations not to scarcity but to abundance … In gift cultures, social status is determined not by what you control but by what you give away. Thus the Kwakiutl chieftain's potlatch party … And thus the hacker's long hours of effort to produce high-quality open-source code" (https://catb.org/~esr/writings/cathedral-bazaar/magic-cauldron/ar01s02.html; http://www.catb.org/~esr/writings/cathedral-bazaar/homesteading/ar01s06.html). Raymond speculated it is "the globally optimal way to cooperate for generating (and checking!) high-quality creative work" (http://catb.org/~esr/writings/homesteading/homesteading/ar01s19.html).

**Anthropological refinements.** David Zeitlyn's response accepted that gift theory is useful but refined it: software engineers "may have subgroupings which parallel kinship groups such as lineages," and within such groups "gift giving is not necessarily or directly reciprocated"; instead members work according to the **"axiom of kinship amity,"** where "direct economic calculation is not appropriate within the group," and use **Bourdieu's "symbolic capital"** to enhance reputation (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2589753_Gift_economies_in_the_development_of_open_source_software_Anthropological_reflections_David_Zeitlyn). Zeitlyn also insisted on the Maussian point that "the giver and the object given cannot be completely separated" and that "being owed is better than owing" (https://sci-hub.st/storage/2024/1746/0d168596d46d06ac105718d7fac3fe2d/zeitlyn2003.pdf).

The most sustained ethnographic engagement is Christopher Kelty's *Two Bits: The Cultural Significance of Free Software* (Duke University Press, 2008; full text at https://twobits.net/pub/Kelty-TwoBits.pdf). Kelty introduces the analytic of the "recursive public"—"a public that is vitally concerned with the material and practical maintenance and modification of the technical, legal, practical, and conceptual means of its own existence as a public." Free Software is paradigmatic, with Creative Commons and Open Access as adjacent instances. Kelty's broader point is that the *question of how* the gift is constituted, regulated, and made legally durable (via the GPL and similar licenses) is precisely what ordinary anthropology of the gift missed: software is given by a reconfiguration of property rather than by suspending it. The conceptual genealogy is traceable to hackers themselves (Raymond as a self-described "hacker anthropologist") who imported Maussian vocabulary.

Bergquist and Ljungberg (*The power of gifts*, 2001) argued the gift economy is important "not only because it creates openness, but also because it organizes relationships between people in a certain way," and that "the giver gets power from giving away," a power used to guarantee code quality—explicitly paralleling gifts of scientific knowledge and peer review (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vj9gbz8t91z). Mathias Studer analyzed free software through the **M.A.U.S.S.** (Mouvement Anti-Utilitariste en Sciences Sociales) reading of Mauss, describing a "culture of gift exchange" among hackers (https://thecommoner.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Matthias-Studer-Gift-and-Free-Software.pdf). M. Kastrinou-Theodoropoulou's *The Gift of the Code* goes furthest: "Like a modern-day kula ring, the Linux code is analysed in terms of a gift: one cannot keep it for one's self, it contains obligations and a promise of future reciprocity" (https://bura.brunel.ac.uk/bitstream/2438/12328/1/Fulltext.pdf).

**The strongest challenge to the analogy.** Greger Petersen's *The gift of sharing* argues that FOSS is **not** a gift economy but a system of **social sharing**, because "where is the transaction between partners, or agreed-upon exchange between individuals?" In a true gift economy "the giving of a gift requires the receiver to reciprocate," which is absent when code is "left at a publicly accessible place for anyone to take" (https://fahrplan.events.ccc.de/congress/2006/Fahrplan/attachments/1171-GiftOfSharingGregersPetersen.pdf). The blog critique at 250bpm makes the same point: the gift is "given to 'the community' … not to a particular person or group," and "unlike with true gift cultures, the gift is not to a particular person or group"—so the three-party structure and the obligation to receive that Mauss insisted on are missing (http://250bpm.wikidot.com/blog:93). Dave Elder-Vass's moral-economy analysis likewise questions "the view that giving is a form of exchange," noting that many digital goods are made available "without any obligation to reciprocate" (https://eldervass.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Elder-Vass-2015d-Moral-Economy-of-Digital-Gifts-IJSQ-PPV.pdf).

**Commodification and capture.** A *First Monday* study of Blender's open-source animation filmmaking shows that "the wealth of open cultural production relies on combining multiple dimensions of gifting with fiscal and hidden forms of capital, producing a culture of secrecy in parallel to that of openness" (https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/download/6944/5627). And the GISWatch account of FLOSS documents **corporate co-optation**: "The free software movement has been co-opted by corporations, which now fund project activities; it is no longer something people did out of necessity on a non-profit basis, but has instead become a job" (https://giswatch.org/en/floss-freelibre-open-source-software-open-source-technology/what-if-f-floss-was-feminism).

**Gender in FLOSS — the quantitative picture.** The feminist critique of gift exchange has a direct empirical parallel here. A widely cited survey found **1.5% of F/LOSS participants were women**, compared with **28% of people in technical roles in firms relying on closed intellectual property** (https://https-sage-cnpereading-com-443.webvpn1.xju.edu.cn/doi/10.1177/1461444811422887; https://culturedigitally.org/2012/06/engendering-change-gender-advocacy-in-open-source/). That is, women are roughly nineteen times less represented in FLOSS than in comparable proprietary software roles. If women are ~50% of the population, then 1.5% represents just 3% of parity—a 97% shortfall. A 2022 systematic review of **51 articles (2000–2021)** found that "only about **5% of projects** were reported to have women as core developers," and "women authored less than 5% of pull-requests, but had similar or even higher rates of pull-request acceptances than men" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3510460). A 2025 study of **20 popular GitHub projects** found "the percentage of female developers that actively contribute to open-source software (OSS) projects is less than 10%," with negligible gender association in contribution counts—"except for the top 10%, where men are still over-represented" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-025-10653-x).

Dawn Nafus's "'Patches don't have gender'" argues that "'openness' is a complex construct" that "weaves together ideas about authorship, agency, and the circumstances under which knowledge and code can and cannot be exchanged," and that "notions of openness tie the social to the technical by separating persons from one another and relieving them of obligations that might be created in the course of other forms of gift exchange. In doing so, men monopolize code authorship and simultaneously de-legitimize the kinds of social ties necessary to build mechanisms for women's inclusion" (https://https-sage-cnpereading-com-443.webvpn1.xju.edu.cn/doi/10.1177/1461444811422887). This is a striking reproduction of the canonical feminist finding: as Weiner showed that Malinowski's kula-centric gaze rendered women's *doba* invisible, so the FLOSS "gift culture" renders relational, maintenance, and non-code labor—disproportionately performed by women—invisible. The **invisible labor** literature in CSCW formalizes the same point: OSS ecosystems involve "substantial invisible labor: undercompensated or uncompensated activities" that are "rendered invisible … because they take place out of sight, or because they lack physical form altogether" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3757417).

### B. Social Media and the "Like" Economy

**The gift as mutual recognition.** The article "The Economy of the Digital Gift: From Socialism to Sociality Online" argues that recent reterritorialization of the web means "the internet can no longer be considered a reply to capitalism"; the Like button and Twitter Mention are recoded as gifts of mutual recognition, "interference between gift exchange and market economy which is daily at work online" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0263276415619474). In anthropology and social philosophy "the term 'gift' has often been used improperly, and that gift exchange has nothing to do with goods exchange, but with **mutual recognition**." The claim that attention is exchanged as recognition, not as goods, is a direct Maussian move: the gift constitutes the social relation rather than transferring utility.

**"Accumulation by gift."** The most important critical intervention is *A Maussian bargain: Accumulation by gift in the digital economy* (2020). It notes that the "harvesting of data … is often described as a process of 'accumulation by dispossession,'" but argues this "does not square well with the fact that enrollment into digital systems is often experienced (and presented by companies) as a much more benign process: signing up for a 'free' service, responding to a 'friend's' invitation, or being encouraged to 'share' content." The paper proposes the regime of **"accumulation by gift"**: "The economic relation that develops as a result of a digital gift offering not only masks the structural asymmetry between giver and gifted but also permits the creation of the new commodity of personal data, obfuscates its true value, and naturalizes its private appropriation" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2053951719897092). This is almost exactly Sahlins's principle that "one man's gift should not be another man's capital"—now applied to platforms that convert users' give-to-get relations into data capital.

**Platform value creation as asymmetric gift exchange.** A companion paper in *Big Data & Society* by Oliver Nachtwey and Simon Schaupp, "The valorization of interactions: Gift exchange, power and value creation on digital platforms" (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/20539517241259639), combines Marxian and anthropological value theory, understanding "the interactions of platform users … as asymmetrical practices of gift exchange."
