# Career Transition from Berlin Backend Engineering to AI Safety Research: Realistic Pathways and Europe vs US Comparison

## Honest Baseline Assessment

Your profile — 28, several years of backend engineering, Berlin-based — sits in the realistic-but-not-easy band for AI safety research. Rubi Hudson's widely-cited "Path to a Job in AI Safety" cautions: "There are not many organizations hiring, few job openings at those organizations, and when openings are posted they tend to be extremely competitive. Depending on your starting position, finding full time employment as a technical AI safety researcher can be a multi-year process" (https://crossingtherubicon.substack.com/p/the-path-to-a-job-in-ai-safety).

That said, the field explicitly recruits your archetype. 80,000 Hours states plainly: "Are a strong software engineer, you could apply for empirical research contributor roles right now (even if you don't have a machine learning background, although that helps)" (https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-researcher/). The flagship MATS program's Empirical track weights "educational background and seniority… lightly" and looks for fellows "whose primary tool is ML engineering" (https://www.matsprogram.org/tracks/empirical). A LessWrong roadmap identifies one of two successful archetypes as "Engineers without research experience. They have several years of software development experience. They either already worked with transformers or quickly learn transformers" (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/muH6H9i8CtNAubcoo/roadmap-through-ai-safety-programs-for-early-career).

Ryan Carey's 2019 guidance, still cited in 2024 EA Forum posts, frames the realistic ceiling: "If you've already been a Google engineer for a couple of years, and have an interest in AI, you have a fair chance of getting a research engineer role at a top industry lab. If you have a couple of years of somewhat less-prestigious industry work, there's a fair chance of getting a valuable research engineer role at a top academic lab" (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/so3t8vPMtjMp6xPhJ/ryan-carey-on-how-to-transition-from-being-a-software).

The binding constraint is not your coding skill — it is proving research taste and clearing the talent pipeline. An EA Forum post notes the field is "mostly talent and mentoring constrained… we don't have enough mentoring to upskill new researchers" (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/kDyG6p6FqwJ4ioQt4/concerns-about-ai-safety-career-change).

## The Standard Transition Sequence

Multiple authoritative write-ups converge on a four-step pipeline:

**Step 1 — Build technical foundations.** ARENA's curriculum lists prerequisites: Python, PyTorch, deep learning basics, transformer internals, RL/RLAIF, LLM evals, and mechanistic interpretability (https://www.arena.education/curriculum). Your existing Python, Git, Docker, and distributed systems experience maps directly onto skills listed as preferable or essential at organizations like FAR.AI, which explicitly says: "We encourage applications from strong software engineers who are new to ML" (https://www.far.ai/careers/research-engineer).

**Step 2 — Replicate a paper.** Carey's prescription: "spend a month trying to replicate a paper from the NeurIPS safety workshop. It's normal to take 1-6 weeks full time to replicate a paper when starting out." Daniel Ziegler adds to that advice: rather than only fully replicating one paper, "read a variety of papers and at least roughly reimplementing a few of them (without trying to get the same performance as the paper)" (same source).

**Step 3 — Acquire the math.** "You need to be able to write code, and to understand linear algebra, statistics, and calculus at an undergraduate level" (Crossing the Rubicon, citing 80,000 Hours).

**Step 4 — Apply to fellowships and research-engineer roles in parallel.** The current pipeline recommendation, per the EA Forum post "How to be an AI safety research engineer," is to treat fellowships as the "first-class" option and university degree programs as a backup: "Fellowships are much more targeted at getting you good at AI safety than a degree. In my opinion, treat a degree as the second-class option. If you can get into a fellowship, start there" (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/G5qTbBu6mNxTAEnJS/how-to-be-an-ai-safety-research-engineer).

## Concrete Programs to Target

**Foundations (free, weeks 0–8):**
- **BlueDot Impact Technical AI Safety course** (~40h, free, remote) — written for people who have "shipped… and built large systems" and find "the field can feel academic and hard to break into from industry" (https://bluedot.org/courses/technical-ai-safety). BlueDot claims 10,000+ people trained since 2022 and "25% of our graduates land impactful roles within six months" (https://bluedot.org/).
- **ARENA self-study curriculum** at learn.arena.education (free) — full PyTorch, transformer internals, mech interp, RLHF coverage (https://www.arena.education/curriculum).

**Part-time / while-employed (months 2–8):**
- **Alignment Research Fellowship (ARF)** — 14-week, online, ARENA-based program run by AI Safety Hungary with the European Network for AI Safety (ENAIS) and AI Safety Global Society: 10 h/week, TA-guided, covering transformers from scratch, mech interp, and LLM evals (https://www.aishungary.com/activities/alignment-research-fellowship; https://www.aisglobalsociety.org/arf). Good option to do while keeping your Berlin job.
- **SAIGE Incubator (Germany)** — 10–20 h/week mentored projects across Technical AI Safety, AI Governance & Policy, Technical AI Governance, and Communications tracks (https://safeaigermany.org/incubator).
- **SPAR** (Supervised Program for Alignment Research) — virtual, part-time (5–20 h/week), 3-month mentored projects; Fall 2025 had 80+ projects and expected 200+ mentees, open to professionals (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/pGWoLWQJk3uGpifk/apply-to-spar-fall-2025-80-projects).
- **Apart Research** — remote, part-time 3–6 month fellowships plus an 8-week "Lab Studio" bridge; "particularly excels at supporting mid-career professionals from technical domains such as cybersecurity and software engineering" (https://apartresearch.com/news/apart-in-2024).

**Funded in-person bootcamps (months 3–9):**
- **ARENA bootcamp** (4–5 weeks, in-person at LISA in London; ARENA 9.0 runs Oct 5–Nov 6, 2026): free, with travel, visa expenses, accommodation, and meals covered — "we aim to ensure that finances do not present a barrier" (https://www.arena.education/). ARENA explicitly targets "strong coders (e.g., have a CS degree / work experience in SWE…)" and prepares people for "research engineering roles at dedicated AI safety organisations such as Apollo Research, FAR and METR, as well as on the safety teams of frontier labs such as Anthropic" (https://www.arena.education/faqs). This is the single most concrete first move available to a Berlin-based SWE because it removes relocation cost barriers entirely.

**Funded full-time fellowships (months 6–18):**
- **MATS** (ML Alignment & Theory Scholars) — 12-week in-person program at Berkeley, CA or London, UK, with an optional 6–12 month funded extension. Stipend figures vary by source and cohort: $1,250/week on the main page (https://www.matsprogram.org/), $1,600/week ($19,200 for 12 weeks) per the FAQ (https://www.matsprogram.org/faq), or $6,400/month per the Winter 2027 announcement (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/Cb8Py9osCsZeuCetn/mats-winter-2027-applications-are-now-open), plus travel, housing, office space, weekday meals, and $24–48k compute. Acceptance rate is "about 4–7% of applicants" (https://www.matsprogram.org/faq/getting-into-mats). MATS provides J-1 visa support for US placement, and explicitly states that if securing a US visa is difficult, "we are likely to be able to support participation from our London office" (https://www.matsprogram.org/faq) — a critical fallback for you.
- **LASR Labs** (London, 13 weeks, full-time, in person at LISA) — teams of 3–4 take a project to a submitted paper; recent cohorts published at NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML workshops; £15,000 stipend (Winter 2027; £11,000 in the Summer 2026 round) plus food, office space, and travel, with visa support under the UK Government Authorised Exchange route (https://www.lasrlabs.org/; https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/KBtLzLzrSxzZm4HZK/lasr-labs-summer-2026-applications-are-open). Participants without existing UK work rights "will be provided with support for visas under the Government Authorised Exchange programme" (https://www.arcadiaimpact.org/lasr).
- **Anthropic Fellows Program** (6 months, US-centric) — for "mid-career technical professionals" transitioning into AI safety; fellows receive funding plus ~$15k/month compute; since early 2025, 200+ fellows have participated, >65% published work from the fellowship, and >35% subsequently joined Anthropic full-time; applications are rolling (https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/anthropic-fellows-program-2026/).
- **Pivotal Research Fellowship** — 15 weeks at LISA, £6,000–£8,000 plus travel to London, £2,400 housing for non-Londoners, meals and compute (https://www.pivotal-research.org/fellowship). Pivotal reports 8 cohorts and 129+ alumni.
- **PIBBSS Fellowship** (~3 months, remote) — explicitly lists software engineering as a relevant background; past fellows went on to AI safety labs, UK AISI, and academia (https://princint.ai/programs/fellowship/).
- **Global AI Safety Fellowship** (Impact Academy, up to 6 months, fully funded) — placements with CHAI (UC Berkeley), Conjecture, FAR.AI, and UK AISI; 10–20 fellows per cohort (https://globalaisafetyfellowship.com/).
- **Cambridge AI Safety Hub Alignment Fellowship** (5 weeks, part-time, open to professionals, with career coaching and a hiring referral database) — a lighter-weight European entry point (https://caish.org/fellowship).

**Career transition grants:**
- **BlueDot Impact Career Transition Grants** (formerly administered by Coefficient Giving) — "Career Transition Grants generally start at $20,000, up to $200,000; Rapid Grants up to $20,000" (https://atomgrants.com/grant/career-development-and-transition-funding-coefficient-giving). Use cases explicitly include "6 months of independent research," "master's degree in ML to work on AI alignment," and "3-month career exploration period." The constraint: "Career Transition Grants require full-time commitment without another full- or part-time role" — so this is a substitute for your job, not a supplement to it. Rubi Hudson's qualification is important: "I would only recommend applying to people who already have some non-AI safety credentials, such as enrollment in a PhD program or a couple years experience as a software engineer" (https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/global-catastrophic-risks-opportunities/career-development-and-transition-funding/) — a Berlin SWE with several years of backend experience fits this bar.

**Direct applications as research engineer:**
- **Apollo Research** (London + SF): Research Engineer/Research Scientist salaries of £136,000–£258,000 in London ($204,000–$385,000 in SF); "We sponsor visas in both the UK and US" (https://jobs.lever.co/apolloresearch/24d016aa-5a19-4976-8936-af2fbf748000).
- **Conjecture** (London): 4 days/week in-person in central London, sponsors visas, offers relocation (https://www.conjecture.dev/career).
- **UK AI Security Institute (AISI)**: £65,000–£145,000 total (base + "technical talent allowance"), with an additional 28.97% employer pension contribution on base salary (https://job-boards.eu.greenhouse.io/aisi/jobs/4966360101). "Technical roles: we can hire almost all nationalities and sponsor visas."
- **FAR.AI** (Berkeley + remote): Sponsors visas for in-person US employees; "can also hire remotely in most countries" (https://www.far.ai/careers/research-engineer).
- **Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind** (US, SF-centric): US base salaries for safety-focused research engineers $220,000–$350,000 plus equity that can take total compensation to $400k–$700k+; senior+ research scientist roles push above $1M (https://llmhire.com/blog/ai-safety-researcher-salaries-2026-openai-anthropic). London frontier-lab bands now overlap US bands at the top end — Anthropic London research engineer roles at up to £630k (https://www.cityam.com/london-ai-jobs-boom-as-anthropic-salaries-hit-630k/).
- **Redwood Research, ARC, METR** (US nonprofit/Berkeley): Sponsor visas for hires.
- **Helsing** (Berlin): Hiring an AI Research Engineer for AI Safety in Berlin, "Fully remote C++ Python Rust… No German required" (https://pegel.berlin/jobs/ai-research-engineer-ai-safety-5680a888). This is a defense AI company rather than a frontier-model safety lab, but it represents on-the-ground Berlin options.

## Berlin-Specific Advantages

Berlin is a genuinely viable base, not a compromise:

- **AI Safety Berlin** (aisafety.berlin) runs regular talks, hackathons, an accountability group explicitly "for people moving into AI safety work," and daily coworking at the Æthos space in CIC Berlin; its members have collaborated with MATS, Redwood Research, BlueDot, METR, UK AISI, SAIGE, SPAR, ARENA, and CeSIA (https://aisafety.berlin/).
- **SAIGE (Safe AI Germany)** is a national field-building organization (started January 2026) with an incubator program and local hubs in Berlin, Munich, Tübingen, Saarland, Kaiserslautern, and Hamburg; it co-hosted the 2026 European Frontier AI Safety Day in Berlin, drawing 250 researchers, policymakers, and field-builders (https://safeaigermany.org/). It notes Germany has the EU's highest share of STEM Master's degrees (35% vs. a 25% EU average) but a shortage of people actually working in AI safety — i.e., a talent gap you'd be filling (https://safeaigermany.org/our-mission).
- **KIRA Center**, a Berlin-based think tank, works on EU AI Act code-of-practice safety chapters and compute infrastructure policy; its founder was a Lead Writer on the 2025 International AI Safety Report (https://kira.eu/).
- **Hertie AI Policy Initiative** anchors the governance side (https://www.hertieaipolicy.org/about).
- **ENAIS** (European Network for AI Safety) connects city-level hubs across Europe (https://www.enais.co/).

A small but real UK-funded German technical safety node exists ~4 hours from Berlin by train: ELLIS Institute Tübingen now hosts Maksym Andriushchenko's AI Safety and Alignment group (started 1 September 2025, focused on alignment of autonomous LLM agents and rigorous evaluations), Sahar Abdelnabi's COMPASS group on safe/steerable agents, and Jonas Geiping's safety- and efficiency-aligned learning group — all co-affiliated with the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and the Tübingen AI Center (https://institute-tue.ellis.eu/en/news/new-principal-investigators-join-the-ellis-institute-tubingen; https://is.mpg.de/aisa). Notably, UK DSIT is funding these three PIs for two years to work on "The Alignment Project," supporting five ELLIS researchers full-time (https://institute-tue.ellis.eu/en/news/ellis-institute-pis-supported-by-uk-government-to-research-ai-safety).

A correction worth noting: CeSIA, often conflated with German AI safety circles, is actually a Paris-based French nonprofit focused on policy research and education, funded by the European Commission, ENS, and UK AISI (https://cesia.org/en/about/).

Practical implication: use Berlin for community, accountability, and governance-adjacent work; expect to travel to London (ARENA, LASR, MATS-London, LISA ecosystem) for the core technical fellowship stage.

## Funding Landscape

The macro picture from Longterm Wiki and 80,000 Hours: global AI safety spending is ~$700M–$1.25B per year vs. AI capabilities investment >$100B/year, a ratio of approximately 100:1 to 150:1 (https://www.longtermwiki.com/wiki/E708; https://80000hours.org/2025/01/it-looks-like-there-are-some-good-funding-opportunities-in-ai-safety-right-now/). Estimated qualified safety researchers globally: ~1,000. The field is roughly 27–29% annualized growth in headcount over recent years based on a 2025 census of ~600 technical FTEs (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/7YDyziQxkWxbGmF3u/ai-safety-field-growth-analysis-2025).

Funding is unusually concentrated: Coefficient Giving accounts for roughly 60% of external philanthropic AI safety funding, with roughly $336M in cumulative AI safety grants and ~$50M in 2024. The Survival and Flourishing Fund (SFF), funded primarily by Jaan Tallinn, is the second-largest funder, having "allocated over $19m of grants" in a recent round compared to a $5M target. Coefficient Giving has tightened its categories — excluding "many Republican-leaning think tanks," "post-alignment" causes, and a number of non-US-aligned organizations — putting pressure on European organizations to find alternative funders (SFF, European philanthropies, government contracts).

For an individual transitioner, the practical effect is: a UK-based job will likely be funded through different channels than a US-based one, but the individual grants from Coefficient Giving / BlueDot / LTFF / SFF are still the same regardless of where you live.

## Visa Comparison

### Germany (no-relocation path)

If you're an EU/EEA citizen, you already have full rights. If not, the EU Blue Card is the standard route. 2026 thresholds: gross salary of at least €50,700/year (general) or €45,934.20/year for STEM and other shortage occupations. Software engineering is on the shortage occupation list, so the lower threshold applies (https://www.make-it-in-germany.com/en/visa-residence/types/eu-blue-card; https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/eu-immigration-portal/eu-blue-card/eu-blue-card-germany_en).

Crucially, the rules explicitly accommodate IT professionals without a formal university degree: "IT specialists without a formal qualification, but having worked in IT for at least three of the past seven years and with professional experience at university level may also qualify for an EU Blue Card" (https://www.make-it-in-germany.com/en/visa-residence/types/eu-blue-card). Settlement-permit conversion is generally possible after 21 months (or 27 months) on a Blue Card with B1 German — an attractive long-term path. For a Berlin-based applicant already in Germany, an internal move from a German tech company to a German AI safety org (e.g., Helsing) requires no visa work at all.

### UK

The UK has become comparatively AI-safety-friendly. UK AISI explicitly states: "Technical roles: we can hire almost all nationalities and sponsor visas." Apollo Research, Conjecture, MATS (London site), and ARENA also sponsor visas and finance relocation. The UK Skilled Worker visa general threshold rose to £41,700 on 22 July 2025 (new-entrant floor £33,400; degree-level skill requirement RQF6) — trivially cleared by AI safety salaries (https://www.davidsonmorris.com/increases-in-skilled-worker-visa-salary-thresholds-2025/).

The underrated route is the **UK Global Talent visa**. Beyond fast-track routes (academic appointment, individual fellowship, UKRI-endorsed funder grant), Route 4 peer review requires you to "work in an approved research discipline; be an active researcher — for example in a university, research institute or business; have a PhD or equivalent research experience, including industrial or clinical research." You apply as "exceptional promise" (potential leader, explicitly for people at an early stage of their career). You need a letter from an eminent UK-based person with internationally recognised expertise. No job offer is required. Decisions take ~2 weeks on the fast track, ~5 weeks via peer review (https://www.gov.uk/global-talent-researcher-academic). Read plainly: your engineering career can substitute for a PhD, and you do not need a sponsor. Fellowship logistics are handled for you: LASR supports Government Authorised Exchange visas; ARENA covers visa expenses.

### US

The H-1B route has become materially harder. Presidential Proclamation 10973 (Sept 19, 2025) imposes a $100,000 fee for new H-1B petitions filed on or after Sept 21, 2025 for beneficiaries outside the US without a valid H-1B visa; it does not apply to existing valid visas or to extensions/changes of status filed from within the US, runs 12 months unless extended, and allows national-interest exceptions at DHS discretion (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/text/2025/09/24/2025-18601.txt; https://www.dorsey.com/newsresources/publications/client-alerts/2025/10/h1b-proclamation-fee-guide; https://www.bakermckenzie.com/en/insight/publications/alerts/2025/10/north-america-uscis-issues-h-1b-payment-guidance). For you this means: a US lab would need to either pay $100k, qualify for an exception, or use another route.

Mitigation: MATS provides J-1 visa support (J-1 is an exchange category, not the H-1B), so a US fellowship is still reachable; a direct US hire as a first step is now materially harder.

**O-1A ("extraordinary ability")** is the realistic path for safety researchers with an existing record. It has no cap and no lottery, can be filed any time, and runs 3 years with unlimited 1-year extensions (https://www.f1jobs.io/resources/blog/o-1-visa-complete-guide-2026). You must meet 3 of 8 criteria — awards, selective memberships, published material about you, judging/peer review, original contributions of major significance, authorship of scholarly articles, critical role at a distinguished organisation, high salary. For an AI/ML researcher, the standard evidence pattern is publications with independent citation context, documented peer review, and contributions others build on (https://www.gojumpstart.com/blog/o-1-visa-researchers-papers). This is a two-to-three-year project from where you stand today, not a first move — but it is a coherent target: the same fellowships that get you a job also produce exactly this evidence.

**H-1B cap-exempt research organizations** are another option: "Universities, affiliated research hospitals, nonprofit research organizations, and government research entities are cap-exempt — they can file H-1B petitions year-round with no lottery" — covering university AI labs, national labs, and nonprofit AI research institutes (https://www.f1jobs.io/resources/blog/machine-learning-engineer-h1b-sponsorship).

A typical transitioner arrives on a Skilled Worker visa to a UK organization, builds a publication record at MATS or in an entry-level role, and only then becomes O-1A-eligible for the US.

## Compensation Comparison

| Role / org | Location | Base | Total comp | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anthropic Research Engineer (Safety) | SF | $220K–$350K | $370K–$750K+ | https://llmhire.com/blog/ai-safety-researcher-salaries-2026-openai-anthropic |
| Anthropic Research Engineer | SF | $315K–$560K base | $340K–$690K total | https://www.levels.fyi/companies/anthropic/salaries; https://www.businessinsider.com/top-ai-startup-companies-salaries-pay-data-openai-anthropic-perplexity-2025-7 |
| OpenAI Member of Technical Staff | SF | ~$310K median | ~$870K median | https://jobsbyculture.com/blog/ai-engineer-researcher-salary-2026 |
| OpenAI Research Scientist | SF | $245K–$440K base | $771K–$1.47M total | https://www.sundeepteki.org/advice/research-engineer-vs-research-scientist-at-frontier-ai-labs |
| Apollo Research Scientist | London | £100K–£200K (~$130K–$260K) | + equity | https://jobs.lever.co/apolloresearch/271eb45a-3aa9-42bb-8686-9cd1fc5e377e |
| Apollo Research Engineer | London | £136,000–£258,000 | — | https://jobs.lever.co/apolloresearch/24d016aa-5a19-4976-8936-af2fbf748000 |
| Anthropic London Research Engineer | London | £260k–£630k total | — | https://www.cityam.com/london-ai-jobs-boom-as-anthropic-salaries-hit-630k/ |
| Google DeepMind Research Scientist | London | £210K–£290K (~$265K–$365K) | — | https://ctaio.dev/en/salary/google-deepmind-salary/ |
| Google DeepMind Research Scientist | Mountain View | L5: $475K–$625K total | — | https://ctaio.dev/en/salary/google-deepmind-salary/ |
| UK AISI Research Engineer | London | £65K–£145K (base + tech allowance) | + 28.97% employer pension on base | https://job-boards.eu.greenhouse.io/aisi/jobs/4966360101 |
| FAR.AI Research Engineer | Berkeley or remote | $180K–$280K (est.) | — | Bay Area nonprofit band |
| Conjecture Research Engineer | London | not published | not published | Visa-sponsored, relocation supported |
| Helsing AI Research Engineer (AI Safety) | Berlin | not published | not published | "No German required," fully remote option |

The Google DeepMind comparison is the cleanest cross-Atlantic data point: London L5 research scientist typically lands at $265k–$365k total comp, vs. Mountain View L5 at $475k–$625k. The ratio check: $265k/$475k = 0.56; $365k/$625k = 0.58 → London ≈ 56–58% of Mountain View at the same level. US frontier-lab comp is roughly 1.7–1.8× the London equivalent at the same level, before tax and cost-of-living adjustments.

The key trade-off: SF roles at frontier labs pay roughly 3–4× a Berlin backend SWE salary for safety work, but UK and Berlin safety roles already pay meaningfully more than typical Berlin SWE comp, and have lower cost-of-living differentials than SF.

## Research Culture: US vs Europe

### Two-hub structure

80,000 Hours names "the California Bay Area and London" as the main concentrations, with Oxford, New York, Pittsburgh and Boston as secondary (https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-technical-research/). Nature (2026) reports on the UK government's AI Security Institute's outsized role: "When Mythos, an artificial-intelligence model from US firm Anthropic, launched to a limited group of companies earlier this year, rumours quickly circulated about the system's hacking capabilities and threats to cybersecurity. Real clarity about the model's power came only once the AI Security Institute (AISI) — a UK government-backed organization in London — had evaluated the model" (https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-01389-9).

The **LISA space** in Shoreditch co-locates Apollo Research, BlueDot Impact, IAPS, Pivotal, ARENA, LASR Labs, PIBBSS, MATS extension, and many independent researchers in one building (https://www.arena.education/faqs; https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/y795kpdRqC3uRmhtt/arena-9-0-call-for-applicants). LISA frames London's advantage as proximity — "policy-makers and researchers are all within 30 mins of one another" — plus UK government engagement and favourable immigration.

### US/Bay Area
- Strong concentration of frontier-lab internal safety teams (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind)
- Nonprofits clustered around Berkeley: MIRI, ARC, Redwood Research, METR, FAR.AI, CHAI
- Higher compensation, faster iteration on frontier models
- Stronger ties to the EA/rationalist community; MATS's anchor physical office is here
- Larger headcount at safety teams, but proportionally smaller share of total headcount — Anthropic grew from ~1,100 employees (2025) to ~4,585 (Feb 2026), with safety roles remaining only ~4% of AI/ML headcount (https://algeriatech.news/ai-safety-researcher-rolerise-frontier-models-demand-2026/)

### UK/London
- Host of Apollo Research, Conjecture, UK AISI, BlueDot, ARENA/MATS/LISA, ARC Evals, and several academic hubs (Oxford, Cambridge, DeepMind, UCL)
- Government-backed (AISI) safety institute with serious policy influence
- Tighter compensation band than the US but materially better than typical EU tech salaries
- Higher in-person density than the US: most London safety orgs require 4 days in office
- Stronger ties to governance/policy and "responsible scaling" framing

### Continental Europe (Berlin, Zurich, Paris, Vienna, Amsterdam)
- Helsing (Berlin) is the largest pure-AI-safety-adjacent employer
- EuroSafeAI and Geodesic Research operate from Switzerland
- LISA-style coworking hubs are sparse on the continent
- London is functionally treated as a "regional" hub by many continental applicants; many Berlin/Zurich safety researchers travel to London for events, MATS, and ARENA
- Zurich AI Safety explicitly markets itself as "#2 AI engineer density in Europe" and serves as a waypoint for many European safety researchers (https://zurich.aisafety.ch/)

### EU-level funding
EU-level funding is large but governance-shaped. Horizon Europe is running ELSA (European Lighthouse on Secure and Safe AI, closed August 2026, covering robustness/certification, privacy-preserving collaborative learning, human-in-the-loop oversight) (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101070617); ELLIOT (€25M, July 2025–June 2029, 30 organisations across 12 countries, including explicit work on AI safety and transparency) (https://ellisalicante.org/assets/press_release/PR_ELLIOT_en.pdf); ELLE (a Marie Skłodowska-Curie doctoral network funding 15 PhD positions, starting March 2027) (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101312622); and RAISE, a virtual European research institute pooling compute, data, talent and funding, launched from the October 2025 European Strategy for AI in Science (https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/strategy/strategy-research-and-innovation/our-digital-future/european-ai-science-strategy/raise-resource-ai-science-europe_en). The EU AI Office is building enforcement capability for general-purpose AI under the AI Act and has tendered for technical assistance across six lots that explicitly include loss of control risks and agentic evaluations (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/forthcoming-call-tenders-artificial-intelligence-act-technical-assistance-ai-safety).

### Insularity and a noted concern
Celia Ford's "The perils of AI safety's insularity" in Transformer (Dec 2025) flags a real tension: "Rather than being done in academia, the work of making AI models safe and secure is increasingly performed by AI companies themselves, or at non-profits that are better resourced, and can move faster, than universities." She further reports that the MATS program "has seen a roughly 20x increase in applications over the past three years" (https://www.transformernews.ai/p/the-perils-of-ai-safetys-insularity). The interview process at AI safety teams is described as having "its own hiring rubrics, partly because the work is technically distinct from general ML engineering, and partly because the team's culture self-selects for a specific kind of candidate. A generalist applying to an AI safety team without preparing for the specific dimensions tends to be filtered out fast — not for technical weakness, but for misalignment between candidate framing and team norms" (https://www.techinterview.org/post/3233474929/ai-safety-team-interview-process/).

## Recommended Path for Your Profile

A realistic 12–24-month sequence:

**Phase 0 (months 0–3, while still employed):**
- Complete AI Safety Fundamentals (BlueDot technical alignment course)
- Work through Chapter 0 of the ARENA curriculum (free, online at https://www.arena.education/)
- Read the Alignment Forum and 1–2 published safety papers
- Attempt to replicate a NeurIPS safety workshop paper (1–6 weeks full-time equivalent)
- Join AI Safety Berlin's accountability group and coworking (https://aisafety.berlin/)

**Phase 1 (months 3–9): Apply in parallel**
- Apply to ARENA (winter cohort deadline July; covers travel/visa/lodging in London)
- Apply for a BlueDot Career Transition Grant ($20K–$200K range) to fund 6–12 months of focused upskilling
- Do ARF online (10 h/week) or SAIGE's Incubator; apply to SPAR for a part-time mentored project
- Ship one public project (evals harness, interp reproduction, or a security-flavored AI control tool playing to your backend strengths)

**Phase 2 (months 9–18): Apply to fellowships**
- Apply to MATS Winter (Berkeley or London; ~4–7% acceptance) — the "gold standard" route per multiple sources
- Apply to LASR Labs (London, 13 weeks, £15k stipend)
- Pursue a PhD (backup option) at a safety-active group (Tübingen ELLIS PIs are an option)

**Phase 3 (months 18–30+): Direct employment**
- Apply to Apollo Research, Conjecture, UK AISI, FAR.AI, Redwood Research, ARC, METR
- Helsing (Berlin) as a geographically convenient option that allows staying in place
- Keep Anthropic Fellows (rolling applications) as the US option, entered with the J-1/Global Talent workarounds rather than a direct H-1B hire

Throughout: maintain visible research artifacts (blog posts, reproductions, open-source contributions on TransformerLens or Inspect).

## Three-Way Choice Summary

- **Choose US/Bay Area if** your priority is maximum frontier-lab exposure, large equity packages, and density of mentors — accept ~12+ months of relocation friction and visa complexity (current H-1B fee of $100k for new petitions outside the US, plus O-1A requires a prior publication record).
- **Choose UK/London if** you want smoother visa sponsorship (Apollo, Conjecture, AISI all explicitly sponsor), an in-person safety community (LISA), and lower cost-of-living than SF. This is the path with the least friction for a Berlin-based EU applicant who already speaks English and has a working background.
- **Choose to stay in Berlin if** Helsing or another Berlin-based safety role materializes as a fit, or if you keep your current employment as a financial floor while upskilling on the side (BlueDot courses, ARF, SAIGE Incubator, paper replications). Berlin's strength is community and governance; the technical fellowship stage will likely require a London stay of 3–12 months.

In all three cases, the common thread is that the credible transition for someone of your profile is to first produce legible AI safety research artifacts (papers, replications, ARENA/MATS completion) and then convert that legibility into a research-engineer role — using fellowships and transition grants as bridges.

## Key Caveats

1. **Acceptance rates are Harvard-tier.** MATS runs at ~4–7% acceptance; LASR Labs and Anthropic Fellows are highly competitive. The path is realistic but not guaranteed.
2. **The job market favors PhDs and people with prior safety research output.** Your competitive advantage is high-quality engineering execution, not theory.
3. **Funding concentration risk:** 60%+ of external AI safety philanthropic funding flows through one source (Coefficient Giving), which has recently tightened its categories. Organizations you depend on for a job may pivot.
4. **The "research engineer at top industry lab" path that Ryan Carey described in 2019 has tightened significantly since the post-ChatGPT hiring boom.** The current hedge is to apply to a wider set of organizations (Apollo, Conjecture, FAR.AI, Redwood, METR, UK AISI, ARC, MATS, LASR Labs) rather than defaulting to the big-three frontier labs.
5. **Program figures drift.** MATS' own pages show $1,250/week (main page), $1,600/week (FAQ), and $6,400/month (Winter 2027 post); LASR's stipend moved from £11,000 (Summer 2026) to £15,000 (Winter 2027). Verify at application time.
6. **Acceptance rates are not published for MATS, ARENA, or Anthropic Fellows; all sources describe them as highly competitive.** BlueDot's "25% of graduates land roles within six months" is self-reported and selection-biased.
7. **Berlin's technical research org density is genuinely thin** — the city's strength is community and governance; the technical fellowship stage will likely require a London stay of 3–12 months.
8. **Nationality matters for visa analysis.** If you hold EU/EEA citizenship, Germany and the EU are effectively visa-free for you, while the UK and US remain the relevant friction points. If not, Germany is still very accessible via the Blue Card IT-specialist route.
9. **Some sources cited reflect 2025–2026 labor market dynamics and forward projections.** Specific organizational details (e.g., MATS cohorts, ARENA versions) should be verified against current program calendars before applying, as cohort timelines move annually.

# Evolution of Lithium Extraction Methods and Environmental Footprints: Chile (Atacama), Australia (Hard Rock), and China (Salt Lakes), 2015–2024

## Production context

Between 2015 and 2024, global lithium production grew from roughly 35,000 tonnes of contained lithium to about 240,000 tonnes per year. By 2024, Australia accounted for ~37% of that supply (88,000 t), Chile ~21% (49,000 t), China ~17% (41,000 t), Argentina ~9% (22,000 t), and other producers ~8% (https://www.iisd.org/system/files/2026-06/commodity-profile-lithium.pdf). The three jurisdictions in scope follow divergent regulatory, technological, and environmental trajectories, all converging on battery-grade lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃) and lithium hydroxide (LiOH·H₂O) as the primary feedstock for NMC and LFP cathode supply chains.

---

## 1. Evolution of extraction methods, 2015–2024

### 1.1 Chile: solar evaporation at the Salar de Atacama

Throughout the window, Chilean lithium extraction relied almost exclusively on solar evaporation ponds, which concentrate lithium-bearing brine (initially ~1,500–1,800 ppm Li in Salar de Atacama) over a 12- to 18-month cascade of ponds before precipitation with Na₂CO₃ to produce battery-grade lithium carbonate (https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9276/14/2/33). SQM's production capacity rose from approximately 48,000 t/y in 2011 to 210,000 t LCE in 2024, including both lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide at its Salar del Carmen / La Negra complex (https://minedocs.com/29/SQM-AR-2024.pdf). Albemarle operates a parallel concession on the same salar; together, both companies pumped brine at a combined rate of nearly 2,000 liters per second in 2024 — over 63 billion liters of brine per year — through approximately 308 wells spread across the southwest sector of the 1,700 km² salt flat (https://news.mongabay.com/2024/12/as-lithium-mining-bleeds-atacama-salt-flat-dry-indigenous-communities-hit-back/).

### 1.2 Australia: hard-rock spodumene concentrate

Australia's lithium industry expanded from a single producer (Greenbushes) in 2015 to seven significant operations by 2024, all based on open-pit mining of spodumene ore (typically 1.5–2.5% Li₂O) followed by crushing, dense-medium separation, and flotation to 5.5–6.0% Li₂O concentrate ("SC6") (https://www.oretrade.com/guides/lithium/). Greenbushes alone is 3.5 km long and 455 m deep, processing 16 million bank cubic meters of raw material annually to produce 9.5 Mtpa spodumene concentrate at full capacity (https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wat2.1748). Pilbara Minerals commissioned its P680 expansion at Pilgangoora in 2024 (680,000 tpa spodumene) and was advancing P1000 toward >1 Mtpa (https://1pls.irmau.com/site/pdf/a6148fec-a633-4aa7-ab4f-a251fddb8507/2024-Annual-Report-incorporating-Appendix-4E.pdf). Ganfeng and Mineral Resources operate Mt Marion as a 50/50 JV producing spodumene concentrate (https://mining.com.au/the-worlds-10-largest-lithium-mines/).

### 1.3 China: salt-lake brines in Qinghai and Tibet

China's brine resource base is concentrated on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, where high Mg/Li ratios (≥2,000:1 at Qarhan) have historically posed technical challenges (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-86425-w; https://zgmining.com/sustainability/esgnews/esgsoc/1967936844238684161.html). Three principal methods have been deployed at industrial scale:

1. **Solar evaporation / salinity-gradient solar ponds (SGSP):** used at Zabuye (Tibet) for lithium carbonate production, constrained by low Li⁺ concentration in the brine (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-86425-w).
2. **Adsorption (Li/Al layered double hydroxides, manganese-oxide ion sieves):** the dominant Chinese DLE technology, deployed at Qinghai salt lakes (e.g., the Qarhan/Chaerhan basin) by producers including Qinghai Salt Lake Lanke, CITIC Guoan, and 5M Salt Lake (https://bishtref.com/articles/10.1016/j.desal.2024.117659).
3. **Membrane separation / electrodialysis:** pioneered by the Qinghai Institute of Salt Lakes (CAS) for high-Mg/Li-ratio brines (http://english.isl.cas.cn/Re/rg/etrc/202411/t20241115_694342.html).

At Qinghai CITIC Guoan, solar-pond lithium recovery was raised from under 50% (industry norm) to over 78%, and overall plant recovery from 75.38% to 90.41%, using a desalinated-brine adsorption process (https://news.metal.com/en/newscontent/103749155-SMM-Analysis-Qinghai-Salt-Lake-Lithium-Extraction-Achieves-Major-Breakthrough-Overall-Plant-Recovery-Rate-Exceeds-90). Zangge Mining's "One-Step" process converts Qarhan's ultra-low-grade brine to battery-grade carbonate in five hours, eliminating lengthy evaporation pond evaporation (https://zgmining.com/sustainability/esgnews/esgsoc/1967936844238684161.html). In 2025, the China Petroleum and Chemical Industry Federation issued T/CPCIF 0416-2025, a national green-clean technical specification for adsorption-based lithium extraction from salt-lake brine (https://www.ndls.org.cn/standard/detail/f2a7f37dd87150c1b38338912e68bca3).

## 2. Water consumption per tonne LCE

### 2.1 The accounting-methodology dispute

Quantitative work consistently shows water intensity varies dramatically by extraction route, but a single methodological choice produces 1–2 orders of magnitude difference in reported "water use per tonne": some studies count evaporated brine water as freshwater consumption; others exclude it because it is not potable or irrigation-grade. One recent review found that of eleven water-footprint studies, three treated brine as equivalent to freshwater, seven did not, and one hedged both ways (https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/17/11/1670). Additionally, vendor-funded LCAs exist — SQM's widely cited 15.5–32.8 m³/t life-cycle figure came from an Argonne National Laboratory study funded by SQM (https://www.euractiv.com/section/energy-environment/news/facing-water-stress-chiles-lithium-industry-under-scrutiny-in-atacama-desert/). This single methodological choice produces differences of 1–2 orders of magnitude in reported "water use per tonne."

### 2.2 Salar de Atacama: brine-as-freshwater attribution

A 2024 cradle-to-gate LCA by TU Berlin covering SQM's 2022–2023 operations estimated a total water footprint of 442 m³ world-equivalents per tonne of lithium product (87% Li₂CO₃ / 13% LiOH) using the AWARE characterisation, of which 326 m³ came from brine concentration in evaporation ponds. All indicators improved 9%–42% versus 2020–2021, attributed to higher brine recovery rates and lower energy use (https://depositonce.tu-berlin.de/items/dd0600ff-39c3-45d2-84be-f07309158895/full). Schomberg et al. (2021) report total water in brine per tonne Li₂CO₃ at ~298 m³ (https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/537785/1/1-s2.0-S0921344924001496-main.pdf).

Independent literature gives a wider range: 500,000–1,000,000 L per tonne Li₂CO₃ (Marconi et al. 2022); 100–800 m³ water in brine per tonne Li₂CO₃ (Vera et al. 2023); 2,000 m³ evaporated per tonne of lithium (Garcés, Universidad de Antofagasta, 2020, https://www.albemarle.com/cl/en/diario-financiero-direct-extraction-chiles-advances-most-sustainable-technology-lithium-industry); 3,822 L/t Li₂CO₃ primary fresh water extracted from the salt flat (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024001288).

SQM's environmental permit caps freshwater pumping at 240 L/s, with actual withdrawal near 180 L/s. The arithmetic of that flow over a year:

```
180 L/s × 31,536,000 s/yr = 5.68 million m³/yr
5.68 Mm³ ÷ 205,000 t LCE (SQM 2024 sales) = 27.7 m³/t LCE
```

That 27.7 m³/t figure is 4–9× higher than SQM's quoted 2.95–7.30 m³/t — because the 180 L/s serves all SQM Salar products (nearly 2 Mt of potassium salts, 270,000 t lithium chloride solution, plus magnesium salts), not lithium alone (https://sqm.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/SQM_-_Sustainable_Lithium_-_English.pdf). Which numerator is accepted determines whether SQM looks like a 3 m³/t or a 28 m³/t freshwater user.

The SQM-CORFO lease permits extraction rates up to 1,500 L/s in MOP wells, with annual brine extraction of 47–59 million m³ (https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/531362/2/Supplementary%20Information.pdf). Kelly et al. (2021) report 23.4 million m³/yr of brine abstracted for lithium (60% of total) at Atacama, with 17 million m³ (81.93%) evaporated (https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/537785/1/1-s2.0-S0921344924001496-main.pdf). Mongabay's higher figure of 63 billion liters/yr (~63 Mm³) is ~2.7× Kelly's 23.4 Mm³ because the larger figure includes potash-destined brine (https://es.mongabay.com/2024/11/comunidades-indigenas-interponen-denuncia-por-hundimiento-de-salar-de-atacama-por-litio-chile/). As intensity metrics:

```
63 Mm³/yr ÷ ~250 kt LCE (combined, est.) ≈ 252 m³ brine/t LCE
23.4 Mm³/yr ÷ 205 kt LCE (SQM alone) ≈ 114 m³ brine/t LCE
```

SQM's extraction is contractually shrinking: planned brine extraction declines from 1,159 L/s in 2024 to 822 L/s by 2030 (https://minedocs.com/26/Salar-de-Atacama-TR-04052024.pdf).

### 2.3 Argentina (Olaroz, Fénix — useful comparators)

A 2025 study based on Environmental Impact Reports found total water footprints of 51.0 m³/t Li₂CO₃ at Olaroz and 135.5 m³/t Li₂CO₃ at Fénix. Blue-water consumption at Olaroz was equivalent to the domestic water use of ~32,238 people in nearby Susques; at Fénix, ~141,047 people (https://exa.ai/library/publication/n4zfds3mdyt).

### 2.4 Australia (hard rock)

Greenbushes does not rely on local groundwater because basement permeability is very low (https://www.epa.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/Referral_Documentation/Appendix%20H%20-%20Onshore%20GDV%20Report.pdf). Greenbushes fresh water abstraction from Mining Data Online:

| Year | Fresh water (ML) |
|---|---|
| 2022 | 1,999 |
| 2023 | 1,560 |
| 2024 | 3,457 |

The published life-cycle inventories for Greenbushes spodumene concentrate (SC6) show 3 m³ water per tonne of concentrate in modern inventories (Kelly et al. 2021; Chordia et al. 2022), versus 2,140 m³/t in the older Stamp et al. 2012 inventory — a boundary and vintage artifact, not a 700× improvement (https://minerva-access.unimelb.edu.au/server/api/core/bitstreams/0f8fcff0-3e0d-40dc-acdd-fe8d15c636f9/content). Pilbara Minerals reported 4.2 GL of water consumed for FY24 on 725,329 dmt of spodumene production — 5.79 m³/t concentrate; 94% of this is recycled or saline water in most Australian operations, which the aggregate figure does not separate (https://www.sustainabilityreports.com/pilbara-minerals/2024/annual-report).

Combining the 3 m³/t SC6 inventory with 7.5–8 t SC6 per tonne Li₂CO₃ conversion ratio (https://www.indexbox.io/search/battery-grade-lithium-carbonate-price/):

```
3 m³/t SC6 × 7.5–8.0 t = 22.5–24.0 m³/t Li₂CO₃   (mining-and-concentration only)
```

Water stress, not water volume, is the operative differentiator for Australian operations, and Pilbara's expansion explicitly depends on securing new borefield water approvals (https://announcements.asx.com.au/asxpdf/20240621/pdf/064snjgd3c8grt.pdf).

### 2.5 China (Qaidam salt lakes)

The most directly comparable cross-regional dataset is an LCA of eleven brine operations in *ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering* (https://pubs.acs.org/ascecg/article/13/38/15828/3762690/Environmental-Impacts-of-Lithium-Brines-Across-the):

| Region | GWP (t CO₂-eq/t LCE) | WCP (m³/t LCE) |
|---|---|---|
| Chile (Atacama) | 3.30 | **58.04** |
| China (Qaidam) | 11.11 | **163.55** |
| United States | n/r | **496.53** (highest, low-grade brines) |

By technology in the same study, natural evaporation has the lowest GWP (solar-driven, low energy), electrolysis the highest GWP (14.93 t CO₂-eq/t LCE), and adsorption–membrane coupling the highest WCP at 617.1 m³/t LCE. This is a critical and often-missed finding: DLE is not automatically a water win. The Qarhan Mg/Li ratio of ≥2,000:1, vs Atacama's lower ratio, explains much of the WCP gap independent of technology (https://zgmining.com/sustainability/esgnews/esgsoc/1967936844238684161.html).

### 2.6 Summary table — water intensity midpoint values

| Route / Site | Total water (m³/t Li₂CO₃) | Methodology / source |
|---|---|---|
| Salar de Atacama, EP | ~298–442 (AWARE) | TU Berlin 2024; Schomberg 2021 |
| Salar de Atacama, brine-only | 58.04 (WCP, ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. 2024) | https://pubs.acs.org/ascecg/article/13/38/15828/3762690/Environmental-Impacts-of-Lithium-Brines-Across-the |
| Olaroz, Argentina, EP | 51 | https://exa.ai/library/publication/n4zfds3mdyt |
| Fénix, Argentina, EP | 135.5 | https://exa.ai/library/publication/n4zfds3mdyt |
| Qarhan/Qinghai, EP | 163.55 (WCP) | https://pubs.acs.org/ascecg/article/13/38/15828/3762690/Environmental-Impacts-of-Lithium-Brines-Across-the |
| DLE adsorption–membrane coupling | 617.1 (highest WCP in study) | Same ACS study |
| DLE various | 500–2,000 | Vera et al. 2023 cited in https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/537785/1/1-s2.0-S0921344924001496-main.pdf |
| Australia hard rock (concentrate) | 2,140 m³/t concentrate (Stamp 2012) → ~3 m³/t concentrate (modern LCI) | https://minerva-access.unimelb.edu.au/server/api/core/bitstreams/0f8fcff0-3e0d-40dc-acdd-fe8d15c636f9/content |
| Australia hard rock (Li₂CO₃ equivalent) | ~22–24 m³/t (mining + concentration only) | Derived from 3 m³/t SC6 × 7.5–8 t/t Li₂CO₃ |

The apparent "favorability" of brine operations in simple m³ terms is partly an accounting artefact — pumping brine with ~170 g/L total dissolved solids is not equivalent to consuming fresh water of comparable volume, which is why some Chilean producers dispute blue-water-intensity framings (https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9276/14/2/33).

## 3. Evaporation pond acreage vs. DLE adoption

### 3.1 Pond acreage

Brine evaporation operations occupy multi-square-kilometre footprints. SQM's lease covers 1,400 km² with brine extraction permission over 820 km², of which the "light blue zone" ponds visible in SQM's 2024 Technical Report Summary cover a substantial portion of the nucleus (https://minedocs.com/26/Salar-de-Atacama-TR-04052024.pdf). Lithium mining at Salar de Atacama quadrupled its surface area from 20.54 km² (1997) to 80.53 km² (2017) — roughly 19,900 acres (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214790X22000053). This is total operational surface, not pond area alone, and is not normalized per tonne.

Deloitte's 2023 GreenSpace analysis concluded that DLE can shrink land use by nearly 95% compared with evaporation ponds (https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-zone4/br/pt/docs/about/2024/Deloitte-2023-GT-direct-lithium-extraction.pdf). IBAT's commercial modular DLE plant in Utah sits on about one acre and produces at a rate of nearly 5,000 t/yr (https://me.smenet.org/in-lithium-industry-first-ibat-commercializes-new-extraction-technology/; https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/international-battery-metals-ibat-commences-operations-of-worlds-first-commercial-modular-direct-lithium-extraction-dle-plant-and-first-commercial-dle-plant-in-north-america-302194337.html). Scaled to SQM's 205,000 t LCE:

```
1 acre ÷ 5,000 t/yr × 205,000 t ≈ 41 acres
```

That figure is illustrative, not engineering-grade — it ignores brine-gathering infrastructure, pipelines, and well fields, which dominate the real footprint. But as a directional comparison against ~19,900 acres of disturbed surface at Atacama, it is the most concrete contrast available. A rigorous peer-reviewed acres-per-tonne-LCE figure for evaporation ponds was not retrievable from the literature surveyed.

### 3.2 DLE adoption rates, 2015–2024

According to Wood Mackenzie, DLE produced approximately 83.7 kt LCE in 2023, with output concentrated in Argentina and China, and is projected to reach 301 kt LCE by 2028 (a ~2.6× increase) (https://www.woodmac.com/news/opinion/direct-lithium-extraction-is-the-hype-justified-by-the-reality/). Against global demand of ~1.2 Mt LCE in 2024, that is:

```
83.7 kt ÷ ~1,200 kt ≈ 7% of the market
```

ILiA's 2024 DLE brochure indicated approximately 60% of global lithium came from hard rock (mostly Australia), 30% from evaporation ponds, and 10% from DLE in 2022 (https://lithium.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ILiA-DLE-Brochure-Full-Version-July-2024.pdf). The same source notes only 30% of DLE technologies reported 2017–2022 were tested with real brine, the rest with synthetic solutions — a serious commercial-maturity caveat.

Benchmark Mineral Intelligence counted 13 operating DLE projects in 2024 forecast to produce ~124,000 t LCE, with DLE expected to contribute 14% (~470 kt) of total lithium supply by 2035. Nearly three-quarters of new brine projects globally are expected to use some form of DLE (https://source.benchmarkminerals.com/article/rise-of-dle-will-open-up-new-sources-of-lithium-supply-this-decade).

**Commercial milestones within the window:** IBAT commissioned the world's first commercial modular DLE plant (Utah, July 2024) at ~5,000 t/yr; Eramet/Tsingshan commissioned Centenario-Ratones in Argentina with 24,000 t/yr battery-grade Li₂CO₃ capacity, first production targeted November 2024 (https://www.reuters.com/markets/commodities/global-lithium-sector-eyes-argentinas-salt-flats-tech-test-run-2024-07-10/; https://source.benchmarkminerals.com/article/eramet-and-tsingshan-open-direct-lithium-extraction-plant-in-argentina); Arcadium (Livent, now part of Rio Tinto after 2024) already used DLE at Hombre Muerto, with expansions targeting 100 ktpa LCE; SLB launched a commercial DLE system in September 2024 after Nevada testing, targeting client production by 2027 and ~90%+ recovery (https://www.reuters.com/markets/commodities/slb-launches-lithium-filtration-system-after-nevada-tests-2024-09-10/).

### 3.3 Commercial deployment by jurisdiction

- **China:** Adsorption-based DLE is widely deployed at Qinghai salt lakes; the 2025 T/CPCIF 0416-2025 standard formalized best-practice specifications (https://www.ndls.org.cn/standard/detail/f2a7f37dd87150c1b38338912e68bca3).
- **Argentina:** Arcadium (Rio Tinto post-2024) uses DLE at Hombre Muerto; Ganfeng/Lithium Argentina announced a 5,000 tpa solvent-extraction DLE demonstration plant at Cauchari-Olaroz to be commissioned in 2025, and a Stage 2 expansion of 45,000 tpa (initial 10,000 tpa) using adsorption DLE targeted for 2028 (https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/30/3372374/0/en/lithium-argentina-announces-cauchari-olaroz-stage-2-scoping-study-results-and-acceleration-of-initial-phase-of-10-000-tpa.html).
- **Chile:** Chile's 2023 National Lithium Strategy explicitly pushes new projects to implement DLE for water/environmental reasons, with implementation expected 2025–2030 (https://cdn-blob.investsmart.com.au/articles/images/alankohler/LITHIUM%20technology_20230428_0906.pdf). Albemarle has piloted DLE at Salar de Atacama; SQM and Codelco's joint "Salar Futuro" program commits to "producing more lithium with less brine and no use of continental water" (https://grist.org/energy/chile-lithium-mining-salt-flat-water/).

**Critical environmental counter-evidence on DLE:** Wood Mackenzie notes that at Salar del Hombre Muerto in Argentina, overall freshwater consumption is roughly 200% higher than at Salar de Atacama (https://www.woodmac.com/news/opinion/direct-lithium-extraction-is-the-hype-justified-by-the-reality/). The ACS LCA found adsorption–membrane coupling — a leading DLE configuration — has the highest WCP of any technology studied at 617.1 m³/t LCE (https://pubs.acs.org/ascecg/article/13/38/15828/3762690/Environmental-Impacts-of-Lithium-Brines-Across-the). DLE also has a higher carbon footprint than evaporation ponds (though lower than hard rock). DLE's advantage is speed (hours-to-days vs. 12–18 months), recovery rate (40–60% → 70–90%), and land area, not necessarily water consumption.

## 4. Aquifer impacts and indigenous water rights disputes

### 4.1 Salar de Atacama aquifer decline

Recent satellite-InSAR studies detected land subsidence of up to ~2 cm (0.8 inches) per year in the mining-concentrated core of the Atacama salt flat during 2020–2022, when lithium-carbonate extraction roughly doubled. Researchers attribute it to brine extraction beginning with the 2015 lithium boom and intensifying 2020–2022. Scientists warn the main consequence could be loss of the aquifer's storage capacity, and because the salt flat sits on a tectonic fault, subsidence could propagate to two protected areas (https://news.mongabay.com/2024/12/as-lithium-mining-bleeds-atacama-salt-flat-dry-indigenous-communities-hit-back/; https://es.mongabay.com/2024/11/comunidades-indigenas-interponen-denuncia-por-hundimiento-de-salar-de-atacama-por-litio-chile/).

Christian Herrera of the Catholic University of the North estimated that mining in northern Chile uses water volumes comparable to the entire flow of the Loa River, the region's main waterway (https://grist.org/energy/chile-lithium-mining-salt-flat-water/). Groundwater levels around Toconao, San Pedro de Atacama, and Peine have measurably declined; households in Peine face nightly water shutoffs to refill communal tanks (https://grist.org/energy/chile-lithium-mining-salt-flat-water/). Basin-level water use exceeded supply by 15 m³/s in 2016 (CEPAL-OCDE, cited in https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214790X22000053), and the Fifth International Rights of Nature Tribunal recorded that six times more water is extracted from the basin than it can naturally regenerate (https://www.rightsofnaturetribunal.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/final-veredict-chile-tribunal.pdf).

A 2022 study by the Catholic University of the North, conducted with the Council of Atacameño Peoples' environmental unit, established that the La Brava lagoon on the salt flat's edge is fed partly by Atacama brine, making it directly vulnerable to mining drawdown. The Chilean State Defense Council (Consejo de Defensa del Estado) subsequently filed suit against Albemarle, Zaldívar (copper), and Minera Escondida (copper) for irreparable damage to the Monturaqui-Negrillar-Tilopozo aquifer, the principal recharge source for these lagoons; in December 2024 the First Environmental Court of Antofagasta approved a settlement requiring the companies to restore the aquifer and compensate Peine residents (https://news.mongabay.com/2024/10/chilean-indigenous-association-participates-in-key-study-for-lawsuit-against-mining/; https://grist.org/energy/chile-lithium-mining-salt-flat-water/).

### 4.2 Historical SQM water-rights ruling

In December 2019, the First Environmental Court of Antofagasta upheld an indigenous complaint against SQM, ruling that SQM's compliance plan in response to regulator SMA findings of brine over-extraction was "insufficient." The court invoked the precautionary principle because of the ecosystem's "particular fragility" and "high level of scientific uncertainty," jeopardizing SQM's USD 400 million lithium-carbonate expansion plan at the time (https://www.business-humanrights.org/en/latest-news/chile-court-upholds-complaint-from-indigenous-communities-against-sqm-over-water-usage-rights-linked-to-lithium-mining/).

### 4.3 Atacameño (Lickanantay) position

In October/November 2024, the Council of Atacameño Peoples (CPA) — representing 18 Lickanantay communities — filed an environmental damage complaint with the Superintendency of the Environment (SMA) over the subsidence findings; the complaint was admitted for processing. The CPA's argument is that the findings "could lead to a review of their environmental permits by virtue of aspects that the environmental assessment failed to observe or take into consideration" (https://news.mongabay.com/2024/12/as-lithium-mining-bleeds-atacama-salt-flat-dry-indigenous-communities-hit-back/). The CPA has formally resolved "not to be partners or part of lithium production, to promote territorial unity, and to occupy every decision-making space concerning lithium." However, some communities have signed compensation agreements: Albemarle committed 3.5% of annual sales to Atacameño communities in a cooperation, sustainability, and mutual benefit agreement signed a decade ago (https://grist.org/energy/chile-lithium-mining-salt-flat-water/). The CPA's environmental unit, formed in 2017 and formalized in 2019, has trained Atacameño hydrogeologists to conduct independent monitoring — a model that Mongabay characterizes as "unique for Latin America" (https://news.mongabay.com/2024/10/chilean-indigenous-association-participates-in-key-study-for-lawsuit-against-mining/).

### 4.4 Australia: indigenous heritage concerns

In Western Australia, Indigenous Noongar communities have raised concerns over tailings facilities and pit-lake rehabilitation near Greenbushes (https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wat2.1748). The 2020 destruction of the 46,000-year-old Juukan Gorge rock shelters in the Pilbara region by Rio Tinto prompted a federal inquiry and tighter heritage-protection legislation that has since affected all major mining approvals, including lithium project expansions. WA's Aboriginal Heritage Act 1972 (amended 2020 in response to Juukan Gorge) and the Commonwealth Native Title Act 1993 require consultation with Traditional Owners.

### 4.5 China: dry-up evidence

The 2023 central environmental inspection found that, due to long-term water extraction, West Taijinar Lake and East Taijinar Lake have essentially dried up, and West Dabuxun Lake's water volume fell from 10.1 million m³ in 2003 to 460,000 m³ in 2018 (https://big5.mee.gov.cn/gate/big5/www.mee.gov.cn/ywgz/zysthjbhdc/dcjl/202312/t20231201_1057812.shtml; https://www.nbd.com.cn/articles/2023-12-01/3143049.html).
