final.content:
# The State of Deepfake Detection Research Since 2022

## 1. Framing

Between 2022 and 2025, deepfake detection research shifted on four axes: (1) generation moved from GAN-dominated face-swapping toward diffusion models, talking-head/lip-sync systems, and commercial voice cloning (e.g., ElevenLabs); (2) the dominant research question moved from in-dataset accuracy to cross-dataset and cross-generator generalization; (3) the field bifurcated into image/video, audio (anti-spoofing), and multimodal audio-visual tracks, each with its own benchmark ecosystem; and (4) detection became a regulatory object as the EU AI Act, U.S. state and federal laws, and China's labeling regime imposed marking and disclosure duties that detection technology is expected to help satisfy (Chandra et al., 2025; https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02857v4). A 2025 systematic review found that only 46.3% of surveyed publications claim techniques generalize to various forgery types (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2543925125000075).

---

## 2. Video Detection: Architectures and Methods

### 2.1 CNN-to-Transformer Shift

Detection backbones shifted from pure CNNs (Xception, EfficientNet, ResNet) to Vision Transformer (ViT)-based and hybrid designs. A 2024 systematic review on FaceForensics++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF reported that transformer-based architectures suffer about 11.33% cross-dataset performance decline versus more than 15% for CNN-based approaches, at 3–5× higher computational cost (https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/7/2/68).

Representative transformer-based detectors cited in "A Timely Survey on Vision Transformer for Deepfake Detection" (Khan et al., 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2405.08463):

- **UIA-ViT (2022)**: AUC 99.33 on FF++ (HQ); cross-dataset AUC 94.68 (DFD), 82.41 (Celeb-DF-v2), 86.59 (Celeb-DF-v1), 75.80 (DFDC).
- **ISTVT (2023)**: 99.0% accuracy on FF++ (HQ), 96.15% on FF++ (LQ), 99.8% on Celeb-DF, 92.1% on DFDC.
- **M2TR (2022)**: AUC 99.51 (FF++ HQ), 99.92 (FF++ RAW), 95.5 (Celeb-DF), 86.7 (SR-DF).
- **FA-ViT** (Forgery-aware Adaptive ViT, arXiv:2309.11092): 93.83% AUC on Celeb-DF and 78.32% AUC on DFDC in cross-dataset evaluation (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.11092).
- **DeepFake-Adapter** (arXiv:2306.00863): first parameter-efficient tuning approach for deepfake detection, inserting globally- and locally-aware adapters into a frozen ViT.
- **FakeFormer** (arXiv:2410.21964): injects learning-based local attention (L2-Att) with artifact-vulnerable patch identification; generalizes to FF++, Celeb-DF, WildDeepfake, DFD, DFDCP, and DFDC.
- **Self-Supervised Graph Transformer** (arXiv:2307.15019): contrastive pretrained ViT features + graph Transformer for explainable detection.

The "SoK: Systematization and Benchmarking of Deepfake Detectors" study (https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04364v4) reviewed 51 detectors published 2019–2023, identified 18 critical factors, and built the first white-box deepfake dataset to evaluate 16 SOTA detectors under black-box, gray-box, and white-box conditions.

### 2.2 Diffusion-Generated Image Detection

Detection of diffusion outputs has become a distinct sub-field. Ricker et al. (2024; https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2024/124220/124220.pdf) showed that SOTA GAN detectors fail to reliably detect diffusion-generated images, but re-training them on diffusion images yields near-perfect detection that generalizes back to GANs; the difficulty reflects the absence of grid-like frequency artifacts typical of GANs.

Universal detectors include:

- **ZED** (Zero-shot Entropy-based Detector; https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15875): 3%+ average accuracy improvement over prior SOTA without needing AI-generated training data.
- **TSG** (Time Step Generating; https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11016v2): varies timestep t in a pre-trained diffusion network as a feature extractor; significant improvements on GenImage.
- **APN** (Artifact Purification Network; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.cviu.2024.104078): 5.6–16.4% higher accuracy on GenImage and 1.7–50.1% on DiffusionForensics for cross-generator detection.
- **LoL** (Learning on Less; https://arxiv.org/html/2412.00665): with only 1% of training data, achieves 13.6% average accuracy improvement across 8 diffusion models.
- **Community Forensics** (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04125v1): 2.7 million images from 4,803 different generators; detector generalization improves with both quantity and diversity of training generators.
- **Wavelet-CLIP** (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.18301v3): average AUC of 0.749 (cross-data) and 0.893 (unseen deepfake robustness).
- **D³ Discrepancy Deepfake Detector** (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.04584v1): 5.3% accuracy improvement in out-of-domain testing on UFD/GenImage while maintaining in-domain performance.

---

## 3. Audio Deepfake Detection

### 3.1 Architectures

RawNet2 and AASIST dominated end-to-end architectures. RawNet2 ingests raw waveforms and applies SincNet filters; AASIST combines a RawNet2-based encoder with heterogeneous stacking graph attention layers and a "max graph operation" (https://mm.kaist.ac.kr/pubs/pdfs/jung22c.pdf).

Improvements since 2022:

- **ARawNet2** (Li et al., Interspeech 2023; https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2023/li23h_interspeech.pdf): adds an attention-based channel masking block; EER 4.61% on ASVspoof 2019 LA, 8.36% on ASVspoof 2021 LA, 19.03% on ASVspoof 2021 DF — relative EER reductions of 12.00% and 14.97% over the RawNet2 baseline.
- **AASIST2** (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08279): replaces residual blocks with Res2Net blocks, applies Dynamic Chunk Size (DCS) and Adaptive Large Margin Fine-Tuning (ALMFT).
- **AASIST3 with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks** (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/borodin24_asvspoof.pdf): minDCF 0.5357 (closed) and 0.1414 (open) on ASVspoof 5, with 22.67% EER (closed) and 4.89% EER (open) — a more than two-fold improvement over baseline.
- **TO-RawNet** (https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2023/wang23w_interspeech.pdf): orthogonal regularization on Sinc-conv filters plus TCN; 66.09% relative EER reduction on ASVspoof 2019 LA vs. RawNet.
- **Whisper+AASIST** (https://faculty.cs.gwu.edu/xiaodongqu/papers/HCII_2024_572_Whisper_Qian.pdf): competitive on ASVspoof 2021 DF and surpasses baselines on in-the-wild audio.
- **wav2vec 2.0 + AASIST** (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17127): examines layer selection and fine-tuning strategies; SOTA on ASVspoof 2019 LA. A pretrained-on-bona-fide-data variant achieved a 90% relative EER improvement versus baseline (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2202.12233).
- **Frozen SSL + logistic regression** (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.05384v2): fewer than 2k learned parameters reduced EER from 30.9% (RawNet2) to 8.8% across eight deepfake datasets — a 71.5% relative EER reduction.

### 3.2 ASVspoof 5 Challenge Results (2024)

ASVspoof 5 (Wang et al., 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08739v1) introduced crowdsourced data with greater acoustic variation, neural codecs, and adversarial attacks. New primary metric is minDCF, with two tracks: standalone CM (Track 1) and spoofing-robust ASV (Track 2).

- Fraunhofer SIT: minDCF 0.589 (closed) / 0.174 (open, SSL) on the evaluation set (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/schafer24_asvspoof.pdf).
- ParallelChain Lab ensemble: minDCF 0.2660 on Track 1 closed (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/tran24_asvspoof.pdf).
- USTC-KXDIGIT: 0.3948 minDCF / 14.33% EER (Track 1 closed); 0.0750 minDCF / 2.59% EER (Track 1 open) (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/chen24_asvspoof.pdf).
- SHADOW team FwSE-ResNet34 with codec augmentation: minDCF 0.44 Track 1 Eval (47% improvement over baseline); a-DCF 0.397 Track 2 (42% improvement) (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/villalba24_asvspoof.pdf).

The ASVspoof 5 summary concluded that performance degrades under adversarial attacks and the application of neural encoding/compression schemes.

### 3.3 Cross-Domain Audio

The SOTA EER trajectory on ASVspoof 2021 DF went from 15.64% (system T23) to 2.85% using AASIST with wav2vec 2.0 features — an 81.8% relative reduction — yet the same methods performed far worse on In-the-Wild data: 24.73% EER for ASSERT+LPS and 34.81% for AASIST (https://faculty.cs.gwu.edu/xiaodongqu/papers/HCII_2024_572_Whisper_Qian.pdf).

CD-ADD (EMNLP 2024; https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.286.pdf) provides 300+ hours generated by five zero-shot TTS models with nine attack types. With attack-augmented training, Wav2Vec2-large reached 4.1% EER and Whisper-medium 6.5% EER; one minute of target-domain data yielded strong few-shot results. The authors warn that "neural codec compressors greatly affect the detection accuracy."

### 3.4 Interpretable Audio Detection

**SLIM** (Style-Linguistics Mismatch; https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/7d6930fd71740eae21224a5ffb70cb8c-Paper-Conference.pdf) uses self-supervised pretraining on real samples to learn style-linguistics dependencies and provides interpretable mismatch scores. **TADA** (Targeted Augmented Data; https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07598) applies adversarial training-time augmentation for RawNet2 and AASIST.

---

## 4. Cross-Dataset and Cross-Generator Generalization

Cross-dataset generalization is the field's central open problem. The 2024 systematic review (https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/7/2/68) found a 10–15% average performance drop across methodological classes, with strong evidence that models learn "dataset-specific compression artifacts rather than deepfake characteristics that are generalizable."

The XceptionNet reference baseline (Nadimpalli et al., CVPRW 2022; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022W/WMF/papers/Nadimpalli_On_Improving_Cross-Dataset_Generalization_of_Deepfake_Detectors_CVPRW_2022_paper.pdf): AUC 0.997 trained and tested on FF++, but **0.482 when transferred to Celeb-DF** — a 52% relative degradation.

Kamat et al. (ICCVW 2023; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023W/DFAD/papers/Kamat_Revisiting_Generalizability_in_Deepfake_Detection_Improving_Metrics_and_Stabilizing_Transfer_ICCVW_2023_paper.pdf) found methods fail differently depending on artifact mode: on diffusion fakes, spatial-, temporal-, and lip-reading-based methods scored 96%, 75%, and 51% AUC respectively; on talking-head fakes, the same methods scored 80%, 99%, and 92%. Leading detectors generalize best when they abandon certain detection modes, because "when artifacts get sparse, overly relying on hand-picked cues has its costs."

DF40 (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks; https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13495) is the most consequential benchmark shift: 40 distinct deepfake techniques, 10× the diversity of FF++, with four evaluation protocols. Its central claim is that the **dataset, not the algorithm, is the primary culprit** for generalization failure, since FF++ forgery techniques are four-plus years out of date.

DeepfakeBench (NeurIPS 2023; https://neurips.cc/virtual/2023/poster/73502) provided unified preprocessing and metrics for 15 SOTA methods across 9 datasets — motivated by the observation that inconsistent protocols produce "unfair performance comparisons and potentially misleading results."

---

## 5. Foundation Model Integration

CLIP-based adaptation became a major research direction:

- **CLIPping the Deception** (Khan & Dang-Nguyen, ICMR 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12927): prompt tuning on CLIP with 200k images outperforms prior SOTA by 5.01% mAP and 6.61% accuracy while using less than one-third of the training data (a 72.2% reduction); evaluated on 21 datasets including GAN, diffusion, and commercial tools.
- **C2P-CLIP** (https://arxiv.org/html/2408.09647v2): category-common prompts; 12.41% accuracy improvement over vanilla CLIP, no extra inference parameters.
- **Forensics Adapter** (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.19715v3): only 5.7M trainable parameters; ~7% average improvement across five datasets.
- **CLIPMoLE** (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.04883): fine-tunes only 0.08% of parameters via mixture-of-LoRAs; +3.64% mAP and +12.72% accuracy across unseen diffusion and autoregressive models.
- **"Standing on the Shoulders of Giants"** (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.02664v4): model reprogramming with learnable visual perturbations and face-embedding-based adaptive text prompts; >88% AUC cross-dataset (FF++ → WildDeepfake).
- **GenD** (arXiv:2508.06248v4): fine-tunes only Layer Normalization parameters — 0.03% of the total — on CLIP, Perception Encoder, or DINO backbones, enforcing a hyperspherical feature manifold; SOTA average cross-dataset AUROC across 14 benchmarks; finds that detection difficulty on academic datasets has not strictly increased over time.
- **UCF-Net**: cascades CLIP's language-aligned semantic priors with DINO's self-supervised visual-structure priors via uncertainty-aware fusion; best in-domain mean AUC 95.33 and best cross-domain mean AUC 92.15 on a ~4M-image unified benchmark (https://xavierjiezou.github.io/UCF-Net/).

The community-forensics / GenImage / CLIP-MoLE line of work consistently shows that training-data diversity drives generalization more than architecture, and that parameter-efficient fine-tuning of CLIP largely preserves the foundation model's zero-shot transfer properties.

---

## 6. Multimodal Audio-Visual Detection

Single-modality detection is increasingly insufficient:

- **AVA-CL** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3625100): joint audio-visual attention with contrastive learning; uses MARLIN as a face representation model.
- **AVFF** (Oorloff et al., CVPR 2024; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Oorloff_AVFF_Audio-Visual_Feature_Fusion_for_Video_Deepfake_Detection_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf): two-stage cross-modal learning via self-supervision on real videos; **98.6% accuracy and 99.1% AUC on FakeAVCeleb — 14.9% and 9.9% gains over prior SOTA**.
- **ART-AVDF** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1016/j.cviu.2024.104133): articulatory representation learning; tested on DFDC, FakeAVCeleb, and DefakeAVMiT.
- **AV-LGNN** (ACM MM 2024; https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3664647.3688985): Audio-Visual Local-Global Interaction Module; submitted to the Video-Level Deepfake Detection challenge at ACM Multimedia 2024.
- **MFMS** (ACM MM 2024; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3664647.3688984): top performance in the AV-Deepfake1M competition.
- **SpeechForensics** (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/9c7900fac04a701cbed83256b76dbaa3-Paper-Conference.pdf): self-supervised masked-prediction on real videos for audio-visual speech representations; outperforms SOTA on cross-dataset generalization and robustness **without using any fake video in training**.
- **Zero-Shot Fake Video Detection by Audio-Visual Consistency** (Interspeech 2024; https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2024/li24ta_interspeech.pdf): uses pretrained ASR and VSR models; computes edit distance between recognized audio and video content sequences; strong cross-technique generalization.
- **MSOC** (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.14176): Multi-Stream Fusion with One-Class Learning; extends OCL to audio-visual; re-splits FakeAVCeleb into RAFV, FAFV, FARV, Unsynced.
- **AV-Deepfake1M** (Cai et al., ACM MM 2024, Best Award; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3664647.3680795): 1M+ videos across 2,000+ subjects targeting temporal localization of small manipulated segments; baseline AP@0.5 values were extremely low (e.g., Meso4 9.86, PyAnnote 0.03).

---

## 7. Privacy-Preserving Detection

- **FedForgery** (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.09563): variational autoencoder for residual feature maps plus a generalized federated learning strategy.
- **Dynamic-Aware Federated Learning for Face Forgery Video Detection** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3501814): first FL framework for face forgery with Inconsistency-Capture for global/local inter-frame inconsistencies.
- **Blockchain-based FL** (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12559-024-10255-7): SegCaps + CNN feature extraction with blockchain-based FL aggregation; 6.6% accuracy and 5.1% AUC improvements over six baselines.
- **FLADD** (https://eurekamag.com/research/110/713/110713846.php): dual-branch Res2Net + Rawformer with Multi-Factor Adaptive Weighting; EER 0.285% on ASVspoof 2019 LA and 2.045% on ASVspoof 2021 LA eval.
- **FedMaxAdapt** (https://researchonline.gcu.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/113968862/113434712.pdf): adaptive sparsity via gradient-guided per-layer pruning; reduces bandwidth by 43.1% (video) and 40.3% (audio) at 50% sparsity; 90.1% video and 91.0% audio accuracy.
- **Robust Detection of Deepfake Images in Blockchain Systems Using DP and Secure MPC** (https://exa.ai/library/publication/0l8tfgks3zx): 98.4% accuracy on DFDC dataset; PSNR 46.2 dB for privacy-preserving image quality.
- **Cognitive-Inspired Multimodal Framework** (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12559-026-10640-4): 98.32% accuracy on FoR (audio), 99.43% on SDFVD (video), 99.87% on TweepFake (text).
- **FMM-MMF** (https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10791-026-10073-5.pdf): federated micro-expression mining and multi-modal metadata fusion for V-KYC fraud; 96.74% accuracy and 0.987 F1 under non-IID conditions.

Two structural weaknesses are widely flagged: (1) the inferential privacy guarantee is often asserted rather than proven with formal DP budgets; (2) federated detection creates an attack surface — work on disruption-induced data poisoning shows that proactive "disruption" perturbations can poison downstream detector training (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/978-981-99-8024-6_14).

---

## 8. Proactive Defenses, Watermarking, and Provenance

- **AdvMark** (IJCAI 2024; https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0673.pdf): fine-tunes robust watermarks into adversarial watermarks to enhance downstream detector accuracy.
- **LampMark** (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.17209v1): training-free landmark perceptual watermarks using facial landmarks; superior cross-dataset and cross-manipulation performance.
- **ProMark** (CVPR 2024; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Asnani_ProMark_Proactive_Diffusion_Watermarking_for_Causal_Attribution_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf): embeds up to 2^16 unique watermarks for causal attribution.
- **ZoDiac** (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/43d33182360378d5c8e69dd706c24f2f-Paper-Conference.pdf): uses a pretrained Stable Diffusion latent space; >98% watermark detection rate and <6.4% false-positive rate under attacks.
- **RAW** (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/ee62ab636066cf45a27246acca9545b7-Paper-Conference.pdf): learnable watermarks with provable false-positive guarantees via conformal prediction.
- **C2PA Content Provenance** (https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/1.3/specs/C2PA_Specification.html): Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity standard using cryptographically signed manifests; backed by major media and tech companies.

---

## 9. Benchmark vs. Real-World Deployment

The single most important empirical result of 2024–2025 is the magnitude of the benchmark-to-deployment gap. The literature converges on roughly two orders of magnitude: 90–99% accuracy on academic benchmarks translates to 40–60% accuracy on real-world content, with even the best commercial systems hovering around 80%.

### 9.1 Deepfake-Eval-2024 (Chandra et al.)

A multi-modal in-the-wild benchmark with 45 hours of video, 56.5 hours of audio, and 1,975 images from 88 different websites in 52 languages (https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02857v4). Head-to-head AUC comparison:

| Modality | Model | Original AUC | DF-Eval-2024 AUC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Video | GenConViT | 0.96 | 0.63 |
| Video | FTCN | 0.87 | 0.50 |
| Video | Styleflow | 0.95 | 0.51 |
| Audio | AASIST | 1.00 | 0.43 |
| Audio | RawNet2 | 0.99 | 0.53 |
| Audio | P3 | 1.00 | 0.58 |
| Image | UFD | 0.94 | 0.56 |
| Image | DistilDIRE | 0.99 | 0.52 |
| Image | NPR | 0.98 | 0.53 |

The authors report aggregate AUC drops of approximately 50% for video, 48% for audio, and 45% for image. AASIST is the extreme case: AUC 1.00 → 0.43, a 57% relative collapse. Fine-tuning on Deepfake-Eval-2024 yields open-source accuracies of 61–69%, and the best commercial detector reaches 82% accuracy — still below expert forensic analysts. Human labelers showed 6.6% disagreement for video, 7.9% for audio, and 9% for images, leading the authors to argue models "should be able to achieve at least 90% accuracy" on the benchmark.

### 9.2 Independent Corroboration

- **Evaluating Deepfake Detectors in the Wild** (SumSubstance; https://arxiv.org/html/2507.21905): on >500,000 high-quality deepfake images, fewer than half of detectors achieved AUC > 60%, with JPEG compression and image enhancement causing additional large drops.
- **Revisiting Simple Baselines** (https://arxiv.org/html/2509.04150): a better-tuned Ojha-style CLIP baseline reaches 81% accuracy on DF-Eval-2024, +18 over the original report and matching commercial systems, showing part of the open-source shortfall is training-protocol variance.
- **Analyzing Commercial Deepfake Detectors on Real-World Cases** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3803629.3803675): commercial detectors achieve stronger out-of-domain generalization than academic baselines but are influenced by aggregation strategies, mosaic artifacts, and reliance on face detection.
- **Temporal decay** (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.07009v1): a two-stage detector reached AUROC > 99.8% on contemporary deepfakes, but **suffered >30% recall drop on deepfakes generated just six months later**. The authors conclude predictive power comes primarily from static, frame-level artifacts, not temporal inconsistencies.
- **Out-of-the-box performance** (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07814): a 37-percentage-point gap separates the best detector (75.0% mean accuracy) from the worst (37.5%); modern commercial generators (Flux Dev, Firefly v4, Midjourney v7) defeat most detectors, achieving only 18–30% average accuracy.
- **The Deployment Gap in AI Media Detection** (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/AIMS/papers/Budhkar_The_Deployment_Gap_in_AI_Media_Detection_Platform-Aware_and_Visually_CVPRW_2026_paper.pdf): detectors achieving AUC ≈ 0.99 in clean settings suffer substantial degradation under platform-aware attacks with pronounced calibration collapse.

---

## 10. Ethical Concerns

1. **Non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII)**: A 10-country survey of 16,000+ respondents found 2.2% personal victimization and 1.8% perpetration rates even in jurisdictions with specific legislation (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3613904.3642382). UK Online Safety Act analysis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0267364924000906) argues platform remedies are insufficient.

2. **Election and political misinformation**: Recorded Future identified 82 deepfakes impersonating public figures between July 2023 and July 2024 across 38 countries — 26.8% promoted financially motivated scams, 25.6% fabricated misleading statements, 15.8% were electioneering, 10.9% character assassination, 10.9% NCII (https://assets.recordedfuture.com/insikt-report-pdfs/2024/ta-2024-0924.pdf). Knight First Amendment Institute analysis of 78 election deepfakes found non-AI "cheap fakes" were used seven times more often than AI content, but AI deepfakes still pose disproportionate risks via the liar's dividend (https://knightcolumbia.org/blog/we-looked-at-78-election-deepfakes-political-misinformation-is-not-an-ai-problem).

3. **The liar's dividend**: Purdue's GRAIL lab (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/watch-out-for-false-claims-of-deepfakes-and-actual-deepfakes-this-election-year/) documents how politicians may falsely dismiss real evidence as AI-generated.

4. **Harms typology** (https://exa.ai/library/publication/h1jywj8cntt): analysis of 50 incidents found relational harm (64%) most common, with systemic, financial, and emotional harm also significant beyond NCII.

5. **Bias in detectors and training data**: A German survey (https://a-mcc.eu/backend/gpt/pdfs/deepfakes-in-the-context-of-ai-inequalities-analysing-disparities-in-knowledge-and-attitudes.pdf) found gender, age, and educational attainment predict deepfake knowledge, raising equity concerns.

6. **Detection ethics**: SOUPS 2024 research (https://www.usenix.org/conference/soups2024/presentation/brigham) documents public attitudes opposing creation and especially sharing of non-consensual synthetic intimate imagery, with significant variation by creator relationship and gender.

7. **Privacy in detection systems**: Federated-learning work explicitly addresses the centralized-detection-vs-user-privacy tension under GDPR and similar regimes.

---

## 11. Regulatory Frameworks

### 11.1 European Union — AI Act

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj) was adopted on **13 June 2024**. Deepfake-relevant provisions:

- **Article 50(4)**: Deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate image, audio, or video content constituting a "deep fake" must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Exceptions: content used for authorized law-enforcement purposes; or content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work, where disclosure is limited to indicating the existence of synthetic content in a manner that does not hamper the work.
- **Article 50(2)**: Providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated.
- **Article 50(5)**: Information must be provided "in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure."
- **Recital 134** (https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/recital-134): Disclosure obligation is "limited to disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work."

**Effective dates**: Article 50 applies from **2 August 2026** (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-transparency-obligations). The Commission has published Guidelines on Article 50 implementation and a voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content. Enforcement lies with national market surveillance authorities, the AI Office, and the European Data Protection Supervisor (for EU institutions).

### 11.2 United States

**Federal TAKE IT DOWN Act** (Pub. L. 119-12; https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/146). Sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX); passed Senate by unanimous consent on 13 February 2025 and the House 409-2 on 28 April 2025; signed by President Trump on **19 May 2025**.

- **Section 2**: Amends Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934 (47 U.S.C. 223) to add subsection (h) — criminal prohibition on intentional disclosure of non-consensual intimate visual depictions, including "digital forgeries" defined as any intimate visual depiction "created through the use of software, machine learning, artificial intelligence, or any other computer-generated or technological means."
- **Penalties**: Up to 2 years' imprisonment for offenses involving adults (3 years when the depiction involves a minor), plus fines and mandatory restitution. Threats to publish are similarly prohibited.
- **Section 3**: Requires "covered platforms" to establish a notice-and-removal process within one year (by 19 May 2026) and to remove flagged content within 48 hours of a valid notice. Failure to comply constitutes an unfair or deceptive act under FTC jurisdiction.

**State laws**: According to https://exa.ai/library/publication/dtbv24df4gm and https://www.joneswalker.com/en/insights/blogs/ai-law-blog/deepfakes-as-a-service-meets-state-laws-governing-synthetic-media-in-fragmente.html, 46 states have enacted deepfake legislation since 2022, with 169 laws total and 146 bills introduced in 2025 alone. Notable examples:

- **Texas Election Code § 255.004** (2019): Criminalizes creation of deepfake videos within 30 days of an election (some provisions constitutionally challenged).
- **Minnesota Statutes § 609.771**: Extends coverage to 90 days before a political convention; escalating felony penalties for repeat offenses.
- **Virginia Code § 18.2-386.2** (2019): First state criminal penalties for distribution of intimate imagery.
- **Tennessee ELVIS Act**: First state law explicitly protecting voice as a right of publicity in the AI context.

**Earlier federal action**: The 2022 Violence Against Women Act reauthorization established a federal civil right of action for NCII victims, with AI-generated imagery applicability unsettled. The FCC has also banned AI-generated voices in robocalls (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/watch-out-for-false-claims-of-deepfakes-and-actual-deepfakes-this-election-year/).

### 11.3 China

**Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis of Internet-based Information Services** (Order No. 12; https://www.cac.gov.cn/2022-12/11/c_1672221949318230.htm). Adopted by the Cyberspace Administration of China together with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Ministry of Public Security on 25 November 2022; effective **10 January 2023**.

- **Article 6**: Prohibits use of deep-synthesis services to produce or disseminate information prohibited by law or to fabricate false news.
- **Article 7**: Service providers must establish internal review, ethics, and security mechanisms.
- **Article 9**: Mandatory real-identity authentication of users (via mobile number, ID, or national network-identity authentication).
- **Article 10**: Content moderation via technical or manual review; establishment of illegal-content feature databases.
- **Article 11**: Mandatory rumor-refutation mechanism; reports to authorities on detection of fake news.
- **Articles 14–15**: Training-data management; safety assessments for tools generating biometric features (face, voice) or special non-biometric content.
- **Articles 16–17**: Mandatory visible marking for content produced by services that "may lead to public confusion or misidentification" (including smart dialogue, voice generation, face generation/replacement/manipulation, and immersive virtual scenes). Article 18 makes deletion, alteration, or concealment of these marks illegal.
- **Articles 19–20**: Mandatory algorithm filing for services with opinion-forming or social-mobilization capabilities; security assessments before launching new products.

**Companion regulation**: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (Order No. 15; effective 15 August 2023; https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2023/issue_10666/202308/content_6900864.html) applies to providers of generative AI services and explicitly cross-references the Deep Synthesis Provisions for content marking (Article 12).

### 11.4 United Kingdom and Other Jurisdictions

- **UK Online Safety Act 2023**: Contains offences related to sharing intimate images without consent, but research (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0267364924000906) argues its content-moderation approach is insufficient for non-consensual intimate deepfakes.
- **South Korea**: Amendments to the Information and Communications Network Act and the Telecommunications Business Act in 2024–2025 require explicit labeling of AI-generated content.
- **Japan**: Voluntary guidelines from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications; discussions toward binding rules.
- **Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI** (opened for signature in September 2024; not yet in force): addresses transparency and risk-management obligations intersecting with deepfake disclosure.

---

## 12. Quantitative Summary

| Task | Best in-dataset (academic) | Best real-world (in-the-wild) | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Image deepfake detection | AUC ~0.95–0.99 (UFD, NPR on academic datasets) | AUC ~0.52–0.56 on DF-Eval-2024; best commercial ~0.82 accuracy | ~40–50% AUC |
| Audio deepfake detection | EER ~0.5–2% (AASIST, RawNet2 on ASVspoof 2019 LA) | AUC 0.43–0.58 on DF-Eval-2024; ASVspoof 5 best minDCF 0.266 (closed) | ~50% AUC drop |
| Video deepfake detection | AUC 0.95–0.99 on FF++ (Xception, ViT variants) | AUC 0.50–0.63 on DF-Eval-2024; best commercial ~82% accuracy | ~30–50% AUC drop |

Cross-dataset gaps within academic benchmarks: ~11.33% AUC decline for transformer-based and >15% for CNN-based detectors.

---

## 13. Conclusion

Since 2022, deepfake detection research has matured significantly in architectural sophistication — transformer-based, CLIP-adapted, audio-visual, articulatory, and foundation-model approaches have collectively raised in-domain performance to saturation (>95% AUC on standard benchmarks). However, three persistent realities define the current state of the field:

1. **The deployment gap**: Models near-perfect on academic datasets perform near chance on real-world social-media content. Closing this gap requires broader and more current training corpora, modality-aware evaluation, and platform-aware adversarial robustness testing.
2. **The architectural plateau**: Empirical evidence suggests that within an architectural class, training-data diversity drives generalization more than model size or attention mechanism. Foundation-model adaptation (CLIP with PEFT) and federated / privacy-preserving training have emerged as the most promising directions.
3. **Regulatory momentum**: The EU AI Act, U.S. TAKE IT DOWN Act, and China's Deep Synthesis Provisions together establish a global baseline of disclosure-and-labeling obligations, with enforcement dates beginning in mid-2025 (U.S.) and 2026 (EU). These rules position detection and watermarking as compliance infrastructure rather than purely research problems.

Unresolved challenges include cross-generator generalization to unseen diffusion architectures, robustness to compression and platform transformations, multimodal consistency checking at video level, federated and on-device deployment under privacy constraints, harmonized provenance standards (C2PA), and detection in the presence of deliberate adversarial countermeasures. Researchers increasingly frame deepfake detection as a socio-technical system in which detection, provenance, regulation, and media literacy operate together.

# WISC-V versus NEPSY-II for ADHD in School-Age Children (8–12): A Systematic Literature Review on Working-Memory Sensitivity and Ecological Validity

## Bottom Line Up Front

**On working-memory (WM) sensitivity for ADHD diagnosis (8–12):** Neither test has adequate *diagnostic* sensitivity (cross-validated classification accuracy near chance; [PubMed 42501447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/)). In *group-discrimination* terms, the WISC-V Working Memory Index (WMI) is the only validated, normed WM composite and shows reliable medium-to-large ADHD-control effects (d ≈ 0.50–0.85). The NEPSY-II does **not** derive a WM composite—its domains are theoretically (not factor-analytically) constructed and the manual explicitly warns against composite use ([Pearson NEPSY-II Chapter 2](https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf)). The single head-to-head study (Newberry, 2025; unpublished PsyD dissertation) reports that NEPSY-II Animal Sorting and Response Set—but not WISC-V WMI—were significant independent predictors of ADHD diagnosis, but the dissertation is unreplicated, archival, and includes ages 8–16 ([AURA Newberry 2025](https://aura.antioch.edu/etds/1127/)). Standard Digit Span administration conventions further systematically under-detect WM deficits, biasing the WISC-V literature toward underestimation ([Wells et al., 2017, PMC5743590](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/)).

**On ecological validity:** No peer-reviewed head-to-head comparison of WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II ecological validity (EV) in pediatric ADHD exists. By expert consensus, the NEPSY-II's Inhibition, Animal Sorting, and Response Set subtests have **greater verisimilitude** (face similarity to real-world executive tasks) than the highly structured WISC-V WMI subtests, but predictive/criterion validity has been under-studied for both instruments (cf. [Cambridge JINS 2024 systematic review](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0)).

---

## 1. Disambiguating "Sensitivity": A Necessary Conceptual Step

The literature conflates three distinct psychometric senses of "sensitivity," which produce different verdicts:

| Sense | Definition | Verdict for WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) Statistical/group-discrimination sensitivity** | Between-group effect size for ADHD vs. controls | **WISC-V WMI has the edge.** d ≈ 0.50–0.85 across studies; NEPSY-II has no WM composite. |
| **(b) Diagnostic sensitivity** | Proportion of true ADHD cases correctly identified | **Neither is adequate.** Cognitive tests show "inadequate sensitivity and specificity" for ADHD ([*Clinical Neuropsychologist* 2020](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13854046.2019.1696409)). |
| **(c) Incremental sensitivity** | Predictive value *beyond* rating scales/interview | **Neither adds meaningful incremental validity** for ADHD diagnosis ([Sage *Assessment* 2023](https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/10731911231159933)). |

A claim that "X has better sensitivity than Y" must specify which sense is meant. The remainder of this review uses sense (a) as primary, with explicit qualifications for (b) and (c).

---

## 2. Search Strategy

A systematic search was conducted across Google Scholar, PubMed/PMC, PsycINFO-indexed outlets, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, MDPI, and journal-specific repositories (last updated for 2024–2026 publications). Search strings combined: ("WISC-V" OR "NEPSY-II" OR "WISC-IV") AND ("ADHD" OR "attention-deficit") AND ("working memory" OR "executive function" OR "Cognitive Proficiency Index") AND ("ecological validity" OR "sensitivity" OR "meta-analysis"). Priority was given to (i) meta-analyses and umbrella reviews, (ii) seminal theoretical papers, (iii) head-to-head comparative studies, and (iv) studies reporting diagnostic classification metrics. The single direct comparative pediatric ADHD study, Newberry (2025), is weighted as the most pertinent primary source for comparative claims.

---

## 3. Theoretical Frameworks

Four frameworks structure the literature:

**Barkley's Behavioral Inhibition Model (1997):** Deficient response inhibition produces secondary impairments in four executive functions—WM foremost. This model predicts performance deficits on tasks requiring online verbal/visuospatial manipulation ([Barkley 1997](https://dconducta.es/assets/barkley1997.pdf)). Barkley's broader critique also holds that "EF tests have very low or no ecological validity" ([Barkley BDEFS excerpt](https://www.guilford.com/excerpts/barkley20.pdf); [VA Psychological Association slide deck](https://www.vapsych.org/assets/docs/Theory%20of%20Executive%20Function%20%20Self%20Regulation%20-%20Barkley.pdf)).

**Rapport, Chung, Shore, and Isaacs's WM Model (2001):** WM deficits are central, with disinhibition as a downstream consequence; WM has been found to *mediate* (rather than moderate) the relationship between disinhibition and teacher-reported attention ([Sage 2001](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/082957350401900109)).

**Baddeley's Multi-Component Model:** Meta-analytic findings operationalize WM as phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive. The visuospatial and central-executive subcomponents show the largest ADHD effects ([Martinussen et al., 2005](https://www.kiphub.com/paper/61e505bbb5036434b3f63f42); [Kasper, Alderson, & Hudec, 2012](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979)).

**Luria's Functional-Systems Theory:** The NEPSY-II is grounded in Luria's model: "assessing a cognitive disorder requires separately assessing all the components that make up a functional system." Critically, NEPSY-II designers argue that factor analysis is *incompatible* with Lurian theory ([J Pediatr Neuropsychol 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8)). The two instruments are therefore evaluated against *incommensurable* evidentiary standards—a fact rarely disclosed in the comparative literature.

## 4. WISC-V: Architecture, Diagnostic Performance, and Working-Memory Evidence

### 4.1 Architecture
The WISC-V replaces the four-factor WISC-IV (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI) with five primary factors (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI) and ancillary indices (AWMI, Visual Working Memory Index, CPI = WMI + PSI). Pearson documentation frames the WMI as the principal clinical-utility advance in WM, with Picture Span allowing auditory–visual differentiation ([Pearson WISC-V FAQ](https://www.pearsonclinical.ca/content/dam/school/global/clinical/ca/assets/wisc-v-cdn/wisc-v-cdn-faqs.pdf)).

**Structural validity:** Dombrowski et al. (2021; N = 5,359 clinical sample, 47.6% ADHD) reported full scalar invariance across ADHD, anxiety, and encephalopathy groups ([Dombrowski et al., 2021](https://www.ux1.eiu.edu/~glcanivez/Adobe%20pdf/Publications-Papers/Dombrowski,%20Watkins,%20McGill,%20Canivez,%20et%20al.%20(2021)%20WISC-V%20Clinical%20Invariance.pdf)), supporting legitimate cross-group index-score comparison. However, factor structure is contested: a four-factor higher-order solution frequently shows superior fit ([BMC Psychology 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0)).

### 4.2 ADHD Diagnostic Performance: A Conflicting Evidence Base

**Pro-WMI studies** report large or medium-to-large effects:
- *Kindheit und Entwicklung* (2018, n = 103 ADHD vs. matched controls): Largest effects in WM, fluid reasoning, and FSIQ; WISC-V characterized as "valid and sensitive" ([Hogrefe 2018](https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/pdf/10.1026/0942-5403/a000256)).
- PubMed 42343738 (n = 188, ages 6–16): ADHD-Inattentive group showed lower WMI than ADHD-Combined; logistic regression: WMI (B = -0.067, p < .001), PSI (B = -0.043, p = .007), CPI (B = -0.091, p < .001) significantly predicted group membership ([PubMed 42343738](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42343738/)).
- MDPI *Sustainability* (2021, n = 159, ages 6–16): ADHD+SLD performed worse than controls on WMI, PSI, FSIQ, AWMI, CPI ([MDPI Sustainability 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948)).
- MDPI *Behavioral Sciences* (2025, n = 719, WISC-IV): VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI classified ADHD with Nagelkerke R² = 0.44; lower WMI and PSI increased ADHD likelihood ([MDPI BS 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/15/9/1279)).

**Anti-WMI-diagnostic-validity studies** report that discrepancies and even the WMI itself lack individual-level classification accuracy:
- *BMC Psychology* (2026, n = 241 ADHD, ages 6–17): Four-factor higher-order solution was best-fitting; WMI and PSI lower in ADHD, but the authors concluded that intra-individual discrepancies are "neither sensitive nor specific enough" as diagnostic markers ([BMC Psychology 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0)).
- PubMed 42501447 (n = 133, ages 6–16): Cross-validated multinomial classification accuracy = **.32** (barely above chance); neither GAI–CPI discrepancy nor profile configuration differentiated groups; the authors advocate a "shared-vulnerability framework" ([PubMed 42501447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/)).
- PubMed 38248904 (MGCFA, German WISC-V, n = 91 ADHD vs. 91 controls): Only partial scalar invariance; the ADHD group scored lower on four primary subtests, producing lower WMI, PSI, and FSIQ; authors caution that interpretation of WISC-V primary indexes is limited ([PubMed 38248904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/)).
- Iran J Psychiatry Behav Sci (2025, n = 250 ADHD vs. 250 controls, ages 7–9): Only Processing Speed subtests (Coding, Symbol Search, Random Cancellation, Structural Cancellation) exceeded diagnostic-validity thresholds (p < .001); **WM, verbal comprehension, visual-spatial, and fluid reasoning subtests failed to distinguish ADHD from controls** ([Brieflands IJPBS 2025](https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741.pdf)).
- Maherpub JNDD (2025, n = 240, WISC-V Extended): WM (Spatial Span Forward/Backward, Sentence Recall) and Processing Speed subtests exceeded critical values; "partial diagnostic validity" for ADHD ([Maherpub JNDD 2025](https://maherpub.com/index.php/jndd/article/view/514)).
- PubMed 36780371 (WISC-IV WMI, n = 865, population sample, ages 7–8): 22% of children had WM deficits, but **most did not have elevated behavioral regulation or hyperactivity/inattention problems**; only 4% had both. About one-third of those with combined WM + BR/HI problems met inattentive ADHD criteria—underscoring that low WMI is **neither necessary nor sufficient** for an ADHD diagnosis ([PubMed 36780371](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780371/)).

### 4.3 Quantitative Synthesis
Aggregating effect sizes from meta-analytic and primary studies:
- WISC WMI ADHD–control effects cluster at **d ≈ 0.50–0.85** in school-age children.
- Digit Span backward alone: Hedges' g = **0.56** (95% CI [0.49, 0.64]) across 49 studies (n = 4,956 ADHD vs. n = 3,249 controls), decreasing by 0.05 per additional year of age ([Ingenta Connect 2020](https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/clin/2020/00000034/00000005/art00002)).
- Kasper et al. (2012) report large between-group effects across both phonological and visuospatial WM domains, moderated by percent female, trial number, recall vs. recognition, and central-executive demands ([Kasper 2012](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979)).
- Pievsky & McGrath (2018) umbrella review of 37 meta-analyses identifies WM as the **second-largest ADHD-related neurocognitive deficit after reaction-time variability**, weighted mean SMD ≈ 0.54 ([Pievsky & McGrath 2018](https://exa.ai/library/publication/bkyymp4jqzv)).

### 4.4 Working-Memory Subcomponent Insights
**Martinussen, Hayden, Hogg-Johnson, & Tannock (2005), JAACAP 44(4):377–384** — the field-defining WM/ADHD meta-analysis (26 studies, 1997–2003):

| WM component | Effect size | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial storage | **0.85** | 0.62 – 1.08 |
| Spatial central executive | **1.06** | 0.72 – 1.39 |
| Verbal storage | 0.47 | 0.36 – 0.59 |
| Verbal central executive | 0.43 | 0.24 – 0.62 |

Deficits were "independent of comorbidity with language learning disorders and weaknesses in general intellectual ability" ([JAACAP](https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(09)61489-1/abstract); [PubMed 15782085](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15782085/)).

**Critical implication:** The WISC-V WMI's verbal span components (Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing) map most directly onto *verbal central executive / verbal storage* — the two **smallest** effect sizes in the field (0.43 and 0.47). The largest effects are spatial (0.85, 1.06), which the WISC-V WMI samples only partly via Picture Span.

**Kofler, Wells, and colleagues** demonstrated in 8–13-year-olds (n = 45 ADHD vs. 41 controls) that the standard WISC-IV Digit Span administration has weak construct validity for WM because of the discontinue rule; **alternate scoring (counting all digits rather than trials correct) raised correlations with WM reordering from non-significant to r = .58**, with academic achievement r = .49 ([PMC5743590](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/)). A Frontiers in Psychiatry (2024) report found that occupying WM capacity slowed RTs and reduced accuracy on inhibition tasks in ADHD vs. anxious children (d = 0.50–1.53), providing "strong evidence against" the claim that WM deficits are secondary to inhibition deficits ([Frontiers Psychiatry 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1277583/full)). "Good Holders, Bad Shufflers" analyses showed children with ADHD—especially ADHD-Inattentive—are poorer on backward (manipulation) than forward (maintenance) and on visual-spatial than auditory-verbal spans ([Cambridge JINS](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/abs/good-holders-bad-shufflers-an-examination-of-working-memory-processes-and-modalities)).

## 5. NEPSY-II: Architecture, Subtests, and Diagnostic Performance

### 5.1 Design Rationale
The NEPSY-II (Korkman, Kirk, & Kemp, 2007) revised the 1998 NEPSY from 27 subtests (ages 3–12) to **32 subtests** (ages 3–16) across six theoretical domains: Attention/Executive Functioning, Language, Sensorimotor, Visuospatial Processing, Memory and Learning, Social Perception. The revision targeted improved domain coverage, reduced ceiling/floor effects, simplified administration, and stronger sensitivity to clinical conditions including ADHD ([NEPSY-II manual excerpt](https://catalogimages.wiley.com/images/db/pdf/9780470436912.excerpt.pdf); [Sage J Psychoed Assess 2010](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282909346716)).

ADHD-relevant Attention/Executive subtests: **Animal Sorting** (concept formation/set-shifting), **Auditory Attention** (sustained auditory vigilance), **Response Set** (alternating set-shifting under inhibitory demands), **Inhibition** (Naming/Inhibition/Switching), **Word Generation** (fluency), **Clocks** (planning/organization). Memory and Learning: Memory for Designs, Word List Interference ([NEPSY-II manual](https://catalogimages.wiley.com/images/db/pdf/9780470436912.excerpt.pdf); [Wiley Essentials of NEPSY-II](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Essentials+of+NEPSY-II+Assessment-p-9780470634639)).

### 5.2 Three Decisive Architectural Facts
- "The domains are theoretically, not statistically, derived" ([Pearson manual](https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf)).
- "Domain scores are not derived in the NEPSY-II due to these psychometric issues and the clinical sensitivity and utility of the individual subtest scores" ([Pearson manual](https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf)).
- "Subtests within a domain may not correlate highly with one another" ([Pearson manual](https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf)).

**The net effect: NEPSY-II cannot produce a working-memory index. The WISC-V can.** This asymmetry alone makes head-to-head comparison methodologically problematic without constructing an ad hoc NEPSY-II composite, which the manual itself warns against.

### 5.3 Notable Revision History
The NEPSY-II revision removed three Attention/EF subtests (Knock and Tap, Tower, Visual Attention) and added three (Animal Sorting, Clocks, Inhibition); Auditory Attention/Response Set and Statue were retained with modifications; Design Fluency was unaltered ([Broz et al., Texas Woman's University](https://twu-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/cd5d9abc-ac46-4a2a-b0e9-e0689da46eb1/content)). **Notably, the revision removed Tower (a planning measure)**—the very domain for which Willcutt et al. (2005) reported among the strongest ADHD EF effects (planning d in the .46–.69 band; [*Biological Psychiatry* 2005](https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract))—representing a specific capacity reduction for ADHD-relevant EF.

### 5.4 Diagnostic Performance: NEPSY-II
- IRIS Sapienza (2024, n = 48, ages 8–15): No group differences emerged in cognitive performance, attention, or working memory among ADHD, anxiety-disorder (AD), and ADHD+AD groups; significant differences emerged only on inhibition, with AD children more efficient than ADHD or ADHD+AD. The authors recommend routine NEPSY-II Inhibition use in differential diagnosis ([IRIS 2024](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1741790)).
- MDPI *Children* (2024): NEPSY-II found no significant group differences in WM among ADHD, AD, and comorbid groups ([MDPI Children 12(6):798](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9067/12/6/798)).
- Cardinal Scholar (2015, n = clinical, WISC-IV + NEPSY-II): Canonical correlations were generally non-significant between WISC-IV composites and NEPSY-II Inhibition, suggesting clinically-referred children show weaker WMI/PSI–EF coupling than healthy children. However, WISC-IV WM and PS tasks were related to NEPSY-II Inhibition-Naming and Inhibition-Switching Combined scores ([Cardinal Scholar 2015](https://cardinalscholar.bsu.edu/items/1393f480-5723-49c0-b220-23237bd85e25)).
- Exploratory Factor Analysis of the NEPSY-II Conceptual Template (*J Pediatr Neuropsychol* 2024): For the 7–12-year-old group, a six-factor model best represented the data, broadly supporting conceptual domains. Variance partitioning indicated most subtests have adequate specificity, but Social Perception subtests in particular require cautious interpretation ([Springer 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8)).
- Matthews & Davis (2010); Davis & Matthews (2010), J Psychoeduc Assess (74 citations): Most influential independent NEPSY-II review; characterized NEPSY-II as comprehensive but cautious about subtest-level interpretation; flagged standardization-sample representation concerns ([Davis & Matthews 2010](https://exa.ai/library/publication/1fs8mqkt0rv); [Child Neuropsychol 2010](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297040903146966)).

## 6. The Only Direct Head-to-Head Study: Newberry (2025)

**Newberry, K. E. (2025).** *Pay Attention! A Comparative Analysis of Psychological Assessments and Neurological Mechanisms for ADHD Within a Pediatric Population.* Doctoral dissertation, Antioch University Seattle (PsyD in Clinical Psychology; April 2025). ([AURA](https://aura.antioch.edu/etds/1127/); [OhioLINK](https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=antioch1744236100254081&disposition=inline))

- **Sample:** 272 children aged 8–16 in archival data, grouped by ADHD subtype (Inattentive, Combined/Hyperactive, or no diagnosis).
- **Measures:** WISC-V (GAI, CPI, VSI, WMI, PSI), NEPSY-II (Animal Sorting, Auditory Attention, Response Set, Inhibition, Word Generation), Conners CPT-3, CATA.
- **Analyses:** Binary and multinomial logistic regressions controlling for gender.
- **Key findings:** (a) **Lower CPI** and lower NEPSY-II executive functioning scores (Animal Sorting, Response Set) significantly predicted any ADHD diagnosis versus no diagnosis; (b) **Higher CATA scores predicted lower likelihood of Inattentive and Combined/Hyperactive ADHD**; (c) The WISC-V WMI in isolation was not a robust predictor; (d) The NEPSY-II contributed incremental validity beyond the WISC-V.
- **Verbatim author conclusion:** "These results support using NEPSY-II, CATA, and CPT-3 for targeted, efficient ADHD assessments over traditional tools like the WISC-V. Streamlining batteries could improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce testing time, and enhance accessibility."

**Important caveats:** (i) The dissertation is a PsyD project, not a peer-reviewed journal article, and is not yet indexed in major bibliographic databases; (ii) The sample age range is 8–16, overlapping but extending beyond the requested 8–12 window; (iii) Archival, cross-sectional data limit causal inference; (iv) Replication has not occurred.

## 7. Working-Memory Sensitivity: WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II — Synthesis

The direct evidence favors the NEPSY-II's Animal Sorting, Response Set, and Inhibition subtests as **better independent predictors of ADHD diagnosis** than the WISC-V WMI in the only head-to-head study (Newberry, 2025). The WISC-V WMI is **strongly associated at the group level** with ADHD status (d ≈ 0.50–0.85), but the **WMI alone is neither sensitive nor specific as a diagnostic marker** ([BMC Psychology 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0); [PubMed 42501447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/); [Brieflands IJPBS 2025](https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741.pdf)), and low WMI is present in 22% of general-population 7–8-year-olds, most of whom do not have ADHD ([PubMed 36780371](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780371/)).

**Factors plausibly accounting for NEPSY-II's relative advantage on WM-related executive demands:**

1. **Modality coverage.** The NEPSY-II's Attention/Executive subtests include visual, auditory, and switching demands; the WISC-V WMI is heavily weighted toward auditory-verbal channels (Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing) with only one visual subtest (Picture Span, supplementary).
2. **Subcomponent granularity.** The NEPSY-II distinguishes maintenance (Auditory Attention), manipulation (Inhibition-Switching), set-shifting (Response Set), and concept formation (Animal Sorting)—closer to Baddeley's central executive, where ADHD–control effects are largest (spatial central executive d = 1.06; [Martinussen 2005](https://www.kiphub.com/paper/61e505bbb5036434b3f63f42)).
3. **Test impurity and ecological content.** NEPSY-II subtests include more game-like, multi-step procedures more sensitive to real-world executive breakdown.

The Kofler/Wells work on Digit Span Backward administration is instructive: **standard WISC-style discontinue rules systematically under-detect WM deficits**, and minor scoring changes (counting all digits correct) markedly improve sensitivity—an issue that applies to the WISC-V WMI ([PMC5743590](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/)).

**Verdict on WM sensitivity:** In the 8–12 range, the **NEPSY-II Attention/Executive subtests (Animal Sorting, Response Set, Inhibition) appear to provide stronger incremental validity for ADHD detection than the WISC-V WMI**, based on the single head-to-head study. However, the asymmetry of the comparison (no NEPSY-II WM composite exists; Newberry's findings are unpublished and based on a sample extending beyond the target age range) must be explicitly disclosed. The WISC-V WMI remains valuable for characterizing cognitive profile and excluding intellectual disability.

## 8. Ecological Validity

### 8.1 Conceptual Foundations
A 2024 *Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society* systematic review found that, of 90+ executive-function studies claiming EV, only 28% (28 studies) provided a formal definition; the term is used inconsistently, conflating **veridical/criterion validity** (prediction of real-world behavior) with **verisimilitude/face validity** (similarity to real-world tasks) and **sensitivity/specificity**. The authors call for replacement with concrete terminology (e.g., "criterion validity") ([Cambridge JINS 2024](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0)). A 2023 systematized review (Pinto, Dores, Peixoto, & Barbosa) operationalizes EV along two dimensions—**representativeness** (artificial↔natural, simple↔complex) and **generalization** (statistical prediction to everyday functioning)—and proposes a six-stage EV-checklist ([Pinto et al. 2023](https://exa.ai/library/publication/2xb6brjjgpy)). A 2012 review in *Applied Neuropsychology: Child* noted that EV research in pediatric neuropsychology is far less developed than in adult neuropsychology ([Tandfonline 2012](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330)).

### 8.2 Where WISC-V and NEPSY-II Sit on the EV Continuum
By the Pinto et al. framework:
- The **WISC-V WMI subtests** (Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing, Picture Span) are **high on artificiality and low on naturalism**: standardized, time-limited, single-modality tasks with minimal distraction, social demand, or task-switching. Their EV for predicting classroom behavior, homework completion, or peer functioning rests almost entirely on **criterion (predictive) validity studies** (Kofler, Rapport et al.).
- The **NEPSY-II's Inhibition (Naming/Switching), Animal Sorting, Response Set, and Auditory Attention subtests** are **more naturalistic in verisimilitude**: game-like materials, multi-step instructions, set-switching, and distractor conditions that more closely resemble real-world classroom demands.

**Reviews by pediatric neuropsychologists** (Matthews & Davis, 2010; Davis & Matthews, 2010; summarized in *Essentials of NEPSY-II Assessment*, Brooks, Sherman, & Strauss) characterize the NEPSY-II as offering **better cross-domain and cross-modality assessment within one normed battery**, which in principle supports stronger treatment planning and prediction of daily functioning, but the same reviews caution that the NEPSY-II's structure has not been independently factor-analyzed until recently and that **subtest-level interpretation should be cautious in the Social Perception domain** ([Sage 2010](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282909346716); [Springer 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8)).

**A core empirical finding:** Toplak, West, & Stanovich (2013, *JCPP* 54(2):131–143) showed that performance-based EF measures (including WISC-V-style) have weak correspondence with everyday functioning and informant ratings (r ≈ .30; ≈9% shared variance) ([Toplak et al. 2013](http://www.keithstanovich.com/Site/Research_on_Reasoning_files/ToplakWestStanovich_2013.pdf); [PMC7483691](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7483691/)). This limitation applies to *both* instruments.

**Direct head-to-head EV studies comparing WISC-V and NEPSY-II are absent from the peer-reviewed literature as of the present search.** The only comparative data (Newberry, 2025) examine concurrent, not ecological, validity.

**Verdict on ecological validity:** The NEPSY-II is, by expert consensus and by the Pinto et al. verisimilitude framework, the **more ecologically valid instrument in design**, but EV in the strict predictive sense has been under-studied for both instruments in pediatric ADHD. The WISC-V's strengths (standardization, large normative sample, broad cognitive coverage) make it a **better norm-referenced tool but not necessarily a better predictor of real-world functioning**.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Newberry (2025) | Cross-sectional archival; binary + multinomial logistic regression | 272 | 8–16 | Moderate (archival; diagnostic heterogeneity; range extends past 12) | Only direct WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II comparison; PsyD dissertation, not peer-reviewed |
| *BMC Psychology* (2026) | CFA + within-subject discrepancies | 241 ADHD | 6–17 | Low-moderate | Strong psychometric; cross-sectional |

| PubMed 42343738 (2026) | Case-control WISC-V | 188 | 6–16 | Low | Logistic regression with WMI/PSI/CPI as predictors |
| PubMed 38248904 (2024) | MGCFA WISC-V German | 91+91 | — | Low | Partial scalar invariance only |
| PubMed 42501447 (2024) | WISC-V classification | 133 | 6–16 | Low | Cross-validated accuracy = .32 (chance-level) |
| Dombrowski et al. (2021) | WISC-V invariance | 5,359 | 6.0–16.93 | Low | **Full scalar invariance** across ADHD/anxiety/encephalopathy |
| Iran J Psychiatry Behav Sci (2025) | Psychometric, Davis method | 250+250 | 7–9 | High (single-site; Iranian sample; non-random) | Only PSI significant |
| Maherpub JNDD (2025) | Sensitivity coefficient | 240 | — | Moderate (Iranian sample) | WM + PS subtests valid |
| Cardinal Scholar (2015) | Canonical correlation | Clinical | Pediatric | Moderate (mixed clinical sample) | WMI/PSI–Inhibition relationship supported |
| IRIS Sapienza (2024) | Cross-sectional WISC-IV + NEPSY-II | 48 | 8–15 | Moderate (small n) | Inhibition most discriminating |
| Wells et al. (2017) | Construct validity, WISC-IV Digit Span | 34 ADHD + criterion | 8–13 | Low | Digit Span scoring modifications needed |
| Kasper et al. (2012) | Meta-analysis | >100 studies | Children | Low | Established large WM deficits in ADHD |
| Pievsky & McGrath (2018) | Umbrella review | 37 meta-analyses | — | Low | WM SMD ≈ 0.54 |

**Common methodological concerns:** (a) most studies are cross-sectional; (b) many use clinic-referred samples with elevated base rates of comorbidity; (c) the Newberry dissertation is the only direct comparison and is unpublished in a peer-reviewed journal; (d) measurement invariance of the WISC-V in ADHD has been shown to be partial (PubMed 38248904) in some samples, though full scalar invariance was found in the larger Dombrowski et al. (2021) study.

## 10. Conflicting Evidence Requiring Synthesis

A clear contradiction runs through the literature:

- **Pro-WISC-V-WMI studies** (*Kindheit & Entwicklung* 2018; PubMed 42343738; MDPI *Sustainability* 2021; MDPI *Behavioral Sciences* 2025) report large or medium-to-large effects, advocating WMI as a sensitive ADHD marker.
- **Anti-WISC-V-WMI-diagnostic-validity studies** (BMC Psychology 2026; PubMed 42501447; Iran J Psychiatry Behav Sci 2025; Maherpub 2025) report that discrepancies and even the WMI itself lack diagnostic sensitivity/specificity for individual-level classification.
- **Population-level data** (PubMed 36780371) show that low WMI is neither necessary nor sufficient for ADHD.
- **Methodological work** (Wells et al. 2017) suggests that standard WISC administration under-detects WM deficits, biasing the literature toward inflated "no deficit" findings.

**The most defensible synthesis:** the WISC-V WMI reliably detects *group-level* ADHD–control differences, but its predictive accuracy at the individual child level is modest, and use of the WMI as a stand-alone diagnostic marker is not supported. The NEPSY-II's subtests contribute incremental diagnostic value in the one available head-to-head study (Newberry, 2025), but the independent NEPSY-II ADHD evidence base is smaller and the comparison is methodologically asymmetric (NEPSY-II has no WM composite).

## 11. Citation Analysis of Influential Works

Using a forward-citation lens on the most-cited sources:
- **Barkley (1997), Psychological Bulletin** — foundational, >5,000 citations; anchors the inhibition-deficit framework ([Barkley 1997](https://dconducta.es/assets/barkley1997.pdf)).
- **Willcutt, Doyle, Nigg, Faraone, & Pennington (2005), Biological Psychiatry** — 83 studies; confirmed EF deficits in ADHD; WM in medium effect-size range (.46–.69); "neither necessary nor sufficient" ([Biological Psychiatry 2005](https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract)).
- **Martinussen, Hayden, Hogg-Johnson, & Tannock (2005), JAACAP** — early meta-analysis; source of d ≈ 0.47 verbal and d ≈ 0.85 spatial WM effect sizes ([JAACAP](https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(09)61489-1/abstract); [PubMed 15782085](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15782085/)).
- **Kasper, Alderson, & Hudec (2012), Clinical Psychology Review** — most rigorous moderator analysis of WM deficits in ADHD ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979)).
- **Kofler, Rapport, Bolden, Sarver, Raiker, & Alderson (2010/2011)** — generated the digit-span-backward construct-validity concerns; central to the Kofler/Wells program ([PMC5743590](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/)).
- **Pievsky & McGrath (2018), Clinical Psychology Review** — umbrella review ranking WM as second-largest ADHD-related neurocognitive deficit (SMD ≈ 0.54) ([Pievsky & McGrath 2018](https://exa.ai/library/publication/bkyymp4jqzv)).
- **Toplak, West, & Stanovich (2013), JCPP** — established r ≈ .30 correspondence between performance-based EF measures and everyday functioning ([Toplak et al. 2013](http://www.keithstanovich.com/Site/Research_on_Reasoning_files/ToplakWestStanovich_2013.pdf)).
- **Korkman, Kirk, & Kemp (2007), NEPSY-II manual** — anchors NEPSY-II literature.
- **Matthews & Davis (2010); Davis & Matthews (2010), J Psychoeduc Assess** (74 citations) — most influential independent NEPSY-II review ([Davis & Matthews 2010](https://exa.ai/library/publication/1fs8mqkt0rv)).
- **Dombrowski, Watkins, McGill, Canivez, et al. (2021)** — established full scalar invariance of WISC-V across diagnostic groups in N = 5,359 ([Dombrowski et al., 2021](https://www.ux1.eiu.edu/~glcanivez/Adobe%20pdf/Publications-Papers/Dombrowski,%20Watkins,%20McGill,%20Canivez,%20et%20al.%20(2021)%20WISC-V%20Clinical%20Invariance.pdf)).
- **Newberry (2025)** — only direct WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II ADHD comparison; not peer-reviewed ([AURA Newberry 2025](https://aura.antioch.edu/etds/1127/)).

---

## 12. Research Gaps

1. **No peer-reviewed head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy study of WISC-V and NEPSY-II in 8–12-year-old ADHD samples.** Newberry (2025) is the only direct comparison and is unpublished.
2. **Insufficient ecological-validity data for either instrument in pediatric ADHD.** Both lack rigorous criterion-validity studies linking scores to classroom, homework, or peer functioning.
3. **Lack of measurement-invariance work for the NEPSY-II in ADHD** (the 2024 EFA examined the normative sample only, not ADHD-vs.-control invariance).
4. **Subtest-level reporting is inconsistent.** Many studies collapse to index scores, losing information about modality-specific deficits (auditory vs. visual) central to Baddeley's model.
5. **Cross-cultural validity is poorly characterized for both instruments.** The Iranian diagnostic-validity studies (Brieflands 2025; Maherpub 2025) raise questions about generalization beyond North American and Western European populations.
6. **Treatment-prediction validity is unstudied.** No identified study has compared whether WISC-V WMI or NEPSY-II Animal Sorting/Response Set scores predict response to behavioral, pharmacological, or cognitive-training interventions.
7. **Standardized administration undermines WM detection.** The Wells et al. (2017) finding that discontinue rules and trial-level scoring suppress sensitivity has not been incorporated into the WISC-V research base.
8. **No identified study has compared both instruments within a multi-method, multi-informant, DSM-5-TR-framework ADHD diagnostic protocol**—i.e., the kind of study that would most directly inform clinical practice.
9. **Comparative evaluation against gold-standard EV reference (BRIEF-2)** is absent from the literature reviewed.
10. **Architectural incommensurability is rarely disclosed.** No study explicitly addresses that WISC-V WMI is factor-analytically derived while NEPSY-II domains are theoretically (Lurian) derived—an incommensurable evidentiary standard.

---

## 13. Recommendations for Peer-Reviewed Publication

For clinical assessment of children aged 8–12 referred for suspected ADHD, the evidence supports **complementary use of both instruments** rather than either alone:

1. Treat the **WISC-V WMI as a cognitive-profile and exclusionary tool** rather than a diagnostic marker. Use it for characterizing cognitive ability and excluding intellectual disability.
2. Use **NEPSY-II Attention/Executive subtests** (especially Animal Sorting, Response Set, Inhibition-Switching) as the **primary executive-function screen**, with the WISC-V providing the cognitive-ability frame.
3. **Supplement with performance-based attention tests** (CPT-3, CATA) and **rating scales** (Conners 3, BRIEF-2) consistent with current best-practice multi-method, multi-informant ADHD assessment.
4. **Report subtest-level data**, not just index scores, to capture modality-specific deficits.
5. **Use modified Digit Span Backward scoring** (counting all digits correct, ignoring discontinue rule) per Wells et al. (2017) until publishers revise standard procedures.
6. **Define "ecological validity" operationally** (Pinto et al. 2023 framework) and report prediction of classroom/behavioral outcomes to address the EV gap.
7. **Explicitly disclose the architectural incommensurability** between WISC-V WMI (factor-analytically derived) and NEPSY-II WM-relevant subtests (theoretically/Lurian-derived).
8. **Treat Newberry (2025) as suggestive, not definitive**, given its unpublished PsyD dissertation status, sample age range (8–16) extending beyond the target 8–12 window, archival design, and absence of replication.

---

## 14. Uncertainty Statement

The principal limitation of this review is the **absence of multiple peer-reviewed direct comparison studies**. The only direct comparison (Newberry, 2025) is a PsyD dissertation, not yet published in a peer-reviewed journal. Most inferences are triangulated from adjacent literature. Conclusions about ecological validity in particular are based on test-design review and the 2024 JINS systematic review, not on head-to-head pediatric ADHD outcome data. Several key figures (notably from *Biological Psychiatry* 2005, *Clinical Psychology Review* 2012, and *Assessment* 2023) were extracted at the abstract/secondary-citation level and should be verified against full text before citation in a peer-reviewed manuscript.

# The Neoanalytic–Oralist Divide over the Iliad and the Epic Cycle: Cypria Motifs, Achilles' Death, and the Zeus–Thetis Scene

## 1. Framing the Divide

Since the Second World War, Homeric scholarship has been split between two methodological programs that map roughly onto geography as well as theory. Wolfgang Kullmann, the founding figure of post-war neoanalysis, described the situation bluntly: in America and England the Parry–Lord theory of oral poetry predominated, while "on the continent the approach which probably contributed most to Homeric research has been neoanalysis" ([Kullmann 1984 GRBS](https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/download/5411/5311/15193)).

**Neoanalysis** "employs analyst technique in pursuit of a unitarian interpretation of the Iliad" ([Burgess 2006, *Oral Tradition* 21/1](https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf)). Its founders were Kakridis (who coined the term in 1944) and Pestalozzi; its modern exponents include Schadewaldt, Kullmann, Dowden, Burgess, Currie, Tsagalis, and Danek. The Cycle poems are "essentially just… verse manifestations" of the wider oral mythological tradition, but Homer's poems engage with them through motif transference in a way that signals his unique reworking ([Burgess 2006](https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf)). Kullmann's **Faktenkanon** — the constraint that certain basic plot elements could not be altered — distinguished neoanalysts from the older Analysts while preserving the assumption of a single authorial intelligence ([BMCR review of Montanari–Rengakos](https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2013/2013.09.21/)).

**Oralism** (Nagy, Foley, Bakker) treats the Iliad, Odyssey, and the Cyclic poems as variants of a single fluid tradition. Jonthan Burgess summarizes: "instances of the epic stories surrounding the Trojan War… which once existed as malleable story-patterns that featured and fostered variation within limits" ([Foley & Arft in *Cambridge Companion to Homer*](https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/14397ED473238E742B12447115062E67/9780511998409c3_p78-95_CBO.pdf/epic_cycle_and_oral_tradition.pdf)). Under this view, correspondences between the Iliad and the Cycle are not allusions to precursor texts but manifestations of a shared traditional language: formula, type-scene, and "traditional referentiality" (Foley), or the deixis of performance (Bakker).

By 2011 Margalit Finkelberg could summarise the difference in a single formula in "Homer and His Peers": "in the Neoanalysts' eyes the intertextual relations between Homer and the Cycle mean that Homer enjoyed a special status which was due to the fact that his poems were composed with the help of writing, [while] from the standpoint of oral formulaic theory Homer and the Cycle should nevertheless be placed on the same plane as independent variants of a common tradition" ([Finkelberg 2011 PDF](http://old-eclass.uop.gr/modules/document/file.php/LITD328/Homer_and_His_Peers.pdf)). Both schools agree — and Finkelberg concedes — that the Iliad and Odyssey "frequently evoke episodes whose proper place is in the poems of the Epic Cycle" ([Nagy on CHS](https://chs.harvard.edu/curated-article/gregory-nagy-oral-traditions-written-texts-and-questions-of-authorship/)). They disagree on whether this constitutes textual allusion or traditional symmetry.

The methodological fault lines, as Burgess isolates them, are **texts**, **typology**, and **motif priority** ([Burgess 2006](https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf)). Early neoanalysis assumed Homer had written precursor poems ("*Achilleis*," "*Memnonis*") "before his eyes"; oralists object that motifs are freely adaptable and that no instance of a motif can be shown to have priority over another. Burgess's own resolution is to relocate the source not in Cyclic texts but in "oral mythological traditions (Level 1) as the primary or source material," with the Homeric poems as a "metacyclic" outgrowth of cyclic myth and epic.
