## 5. How Prior Experience Shapes Adoption

Five overlapping findings from the literature:

**1. Institutional trust is the primary precondition.** Using 2023 Latinobarómetro data (19,205 individuals, 17 countries), trust in financial institutions raises the probability of digital payment adoption by **62%** (logit estimate), with stronger effects among high-income individuals; youth, education, and mobile ownership also correlate positively [https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7099/13/5/140]. The authors explicitly tie this to informality: fostering financial trust is "key for tackling inequality and informality."

**2. Trust transfers from familiar institutions, not from the platform itself.** A Chilean SEM study found **trust in third-party assurances** (escrow, guarantees) — not trust in the individual vendor — was the strongest predictor of continued online purchase intent [https://eprints.qut.edu.au/48525/2/48525.pdf]. Design implication: borrow the visual and procedural authority of government IDs, central-bank payment rails, and known local brands.

**3. Interpersonal trust and social-media usage drive e-commerce app use.** A multilevel UTAUT model (12,309 internet users, 18 countries) found interpersonal trust and social-media usage have positive, significant effects on e-commerce application use, outweighing structural factors like market size and infrastructure [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43093-025-00626-3]. This predicts that **referral loops, WhatsApp-shareable trust signals, and community features will outperform generic security messaging** — the WhatsApp/peer-network effect on trust calibration is often the real first-tier trust mechanism in LAC.

**4. Knowledge-based trust and propensity-to-trust drive initial intention; perceived risk does not.** A Morocco study (with replicated patterns in Brazilian sources) found that knowledge-based trust (past experience) and propensity to trust drive initial trusting intention, while perceived risk showed no significant influence [http://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/teinso/v71y2022ics0160791x22002524.html]. The UX implication: design onboarding to **activate prior scripts** (the seller-rating thermometer, the "me calificó" mutuality, the WhatsApp purchase, the Pix receipt) — not to mitigate fear.

**5. Familiarity is itself a mediator.** The Brazilian SEM study shows platform familiarity positively influences adoption and partially mediates trust's effect [https://ojs.unifor.br/rca/article/download/17174/9490/79140]. Pix's success in Brazil is essentially a case study in this — the rails were low enough (free, instant, 24/7) that familiarity was achieved within a transaction or two [https://publications.iadb.org/publications/english/document/Digital-Transformation-and-Financial-Inclusion-The-Case-of-Instant-Payments-in-Brazil.pdf]. **Reduce onboarding friction aggressively, especially in markets with high informal-economy participation, because first-use experience is the dominant trust-building event for new users.**

### Why This Matters More in High-Informality Markets

Users in Argentina, Brazil, and Colombia have lived through repeated currency crises, inflation shocks, banking-system shocks, and the 2001 Argentine corralito, which produced generational distrust in formal institutions. LAC trust in financial institutions is "generally lower than in other regions", attributable to "historical experiences with past financial crises and high vulnerability to external shocks" [https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7099/13/5/140]. Users enter a gig platform with an *a priori* discount applied to whatever the platform says about safety, escrow, or dispute resolution — the platform has to **overperform** relative to the user's baseline institutional experience to clear that discount.

A concrete consequence: **instant, visible, deterministic outcomes matter disproportionately.** Pix, Mercado Pago, and Bre-B all converted skeptics precisely because the payment cleared within seconds and was *visible* as cleared in the user's account. Anything that introduces delay, ambiguity, or hidden state (e.g., a 3-day review window on a refund) gets read through the lens of "they're going to take my money and not give it back" — which is exactly the institutional trauma that produces the discount in the first place.

### Prior Negative Experience as a Suppressor

Workers who have been blocked without explanation develop defensive behaviours (screenshotting everything, avoiding platforms) and organize outside the platform via WhatsApp networks [https://exa.ai/library/publication/vmmw1m5gh41]. Conversely, visible trust signals measurably reduce friction: the Uber Brazil verification badge case shows verified users get "less wait from partners to accept trips" [https://www.uber.com/br/pt-br/newsroom/uber-lanca-novo-processo-de-checagem-de-usuarios-veja-como-conseguir-o-selo-de-verificacao/].

| **Brazil** | CPF + biometry via Serpro Datavalid; Pix device registration; tier-1 liveness; RG/CNH OCR across multiple legacy formats | Pix (instant, 0.33% merchant cost); Pix Cobrança for holds; consider Pix BNPL; build MED-style in-app refund flow with explicit deadlines | Mutual 1–5, rolling 500; explicit behavioural warnings tied to deactivation; suppress ratings outside user's control; replica (right of reply) for marketplace verticals; unrated = positive for allocation-based score (iFood model) | Centro de Ayuda with radicado; 72h review benchmark; photo evidence pre-collected; human review before irreversible penalties; LGPD Art. 20 automated-decision review rights |

## 7. Foundational UX Principles

- **Make every dispute outcome visible and instant.** Refund status, driver status, identity verification status — show, don't hide.
- **Default to a "platform-trust first" information architecture.** Trip details, route, identity surfaces, ETA, dispute receipt all visible before, during, and after the transaction. This is what the Brazilian literature finds actually moves the needle.
- **Tier verification by risk, not by rule.** Low-risk users get seconds, high-risk users get enhanced due diligence. Don't push everyone through the maximal-friction flow — that's how informal-economy workers churn.
- **Build a single pan-regional information architecture but localise the rails underneath.** Pix (BR) is essentially mandatory; Bre-B (CO) should be the strategic bet given EBANX's 83% first-year uptake; Argentina requires treating Mercado Pago as the de facto rail rather than designing for theoretical interoperability.
- **Recognise internal trust gradients within each country.** Colombia's rural 82.8% informality vs. urban 42.5% means a national launch cannot assume a single trust norm; Argentina's own-account 62.4% informality vs. dependent 36.1% means gig workers specifically sit in the high-informality segment where the platform becomes their first encounter with institutionalized reputation.
- **Treat Pix fraud reconciliation as a primary design constraint in Brazil** — Pix has normalised instant reversibility expectations for consumers, and your refund process must clear that bar or be read as institutional betrayal.

---

## 8. Anti-Patterns to Avoid

- **Releasing liability unilaterally in T&Cs** — every Argentine platform T&C Fairwork reviewed did this [https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/en/fw/blog/fairwork-argentina-scores-2022-new-report-about-gig-economies-in-latin-america/].
- **Gating dispute channels to high-rated users only.**
- **Hiding fee or commission mechanics.** Rely on user-side price negotiation (InDrive model) where users' trust calibration is price-driven, and on transparent fare computation where it is information-driven (Uber pattern).
- **Treating "no formal income" as fraud.** It excludes ~40% of Brazilian workers and similar shares in Argentina and Colombia [https://valorinternational.globo.com/economy/news/2024/07/22/tight-job-market-hides-high-informality.ghtml].
- **Building identity flows on top of a European stack.** False-positive rates of 15–25% will collapse the funnel and worker morale [https://blog.gu1.ai/es/kyc-latam-complete-guide/].
- **Cash-only settlement without robust reconciliation.** This is the structural phantom-account pattern that defeated rating-based incentives in historical Argentina-Uber [https://7c0h.com/blog/new/uber_in_argentina.html].
- **Generic "terms violation" deactivation messages.** These are the single most-cited grievance across Brazilian legal guides and the Colombian Constitutional Court case.
- **A captive ombudsman.** Rappi's Defensoría shows that a 70% rejection rate sustains distrust even with high case volume [https://restofworld.org/2024/rappi-mediator-service/, https://www.portafolio.co/economia/regiones/defensoria-del-repartidor-fortalece-atencion-tras-quejas-por-bloqueos-en-rappi-492510].

---

## 9. Blind Spots Worth Monitoring

- **Migrant, refugee, and Venezuelan-diaspora populations** (a major Colombian and increasingly Brazilian cohort) whose trust systems are formed by border-crossing and remittance patterns rather than national institutions.
- **The worker-as-customer-of-platform trust relationship.** The trust relationship runs both directions; algorithmic wage-setting and schedule volatility are underexplored.
- **WhatsApp/peer-network effect on trust calibration.** How a platform's signal is weighed against the user's WhatsApp group opinion is often the real first-tier trust mechanism in LAC.
- **Cross-border gig flows** (Colombian workers on Argentine platforms, Brazilian drivers crossing to Paraguay) with distinct identity and dispute complications.
- **Accessibility** (disability, low literacy, older users) — relevant in markets with significant elderly informal workers (Argentina especially).
- **Category-specific trust norms.** The Zolvers evidence (4.4× formalization multiplier for <6h domestic-work jobs; 4.1× for 6–23h [https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/52a1bdcd1edffe350388ebe298d72b86-0370012026/original/11-Digital-labor-platforms-domestic-service-and-formalization.pdf]) shows domestic work is fundamentally different from mobility, care is different from delivery, and so on — **paid intermediation plus verifiable references plus a substitution guarantee** outperforms star ratings in high-intimacy categories [https://zolvers.com/, https://www.ilo.org/media/85391/download].

final.content:
# DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Autism Diagnostic Criteria: A Comparative Analysis with Special Reference to Sensory Processing

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5, 2013; text-revised 2022) and the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11, endorsed May 2019; effective for global reporting January 1, 2022) were harmonized through a formal WHO–APA collaboration, but they differ substantively in how they weight and define sensory processing differences. DSM-5 lists "hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment" as one of four explicit, equally weighted (polythetic) subcriteria for Criterion B (restricted, repetitive patterns), requiring only 2 of 4 subcriteria. ICD-11 embeds atypical sensory responses within a broader free-text description of "restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities" while providing multiple "Required" features across which clinicians may combine manifestations — without mandating sensory items or setting any minimum count.

---

## (A) Side-by-Side Criteria Comparison

| Feature | **DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR (APA, 2013; 2022)** | **ICD-11 (WHO, 2019; CDDR 2024)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | 299.00 (ICD-10-CM crosswalk retained as F84.0) | 6A02 (single stem code) with linearization subtypes 6A02.0–6A02.5, 6A02.Y, 6A02.Z |
| **Core social-communication criteria** | **Criterion A — persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts**, specified *monothetically* via 3 subcriteria: (A1) social-emotional reciprocity; (A2) nonverbal communicative behaviors; (A3) developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. *All 3 must be met* (criteria may be met "currently or by history") (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | **Required feature 1** — "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and to sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication." No mandated subcriteria; 7 (or, per Kamp-Becker's count, 19) illustrative "manifestations may include" items are enumerated (e.g., limitations in understanding or interest in verbal/nonverbal social communication, integrating spoken language with nonverbal cues, social awareness, imagining/responding to others' feelings, mutual sharing of interest, making/sustaining peer relationships) — clinicians may select combinations without any fixed count (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf) |
| **Restricted/repetitive behaviors & sensory processing (weighting)** | **Criterion B** — at least *2 of 4* required: (B1) stereotyped/repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech; (B2) insistence on sameness / inflexible adherence to routines; (B3) highly restricted, fixated interests; (B4) **"Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement)."** Sensory processing is a *named, equally weighted, polythetic* sub-criterion (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | **Required feature 2** — "A range of restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities that are clearly atypical or excessive for the individual's age and sociocultural context." 16 possible manifestations listed; atypical sensory responses are listed ("…lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity and/or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, which may include actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures — especially clothing and food — odours and tastes, heat, cold or pain"), but *no minimum number of manifestations is mandated*. Sensory differences are therefore not formally weighted more than any other RRB manifestation (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/) |
| **Severity specifiers** | Three *required* levels tied to social-communication and RRB domains: **Level 1 — "Requiring support"; Level 2 — "Requiring substantial support"; Level 3 — "Requiring very substantial support,"** each with behavioral anchors (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | *No equivalent severity-level specifier.* Differentiation achieved through **six subtypes** (6A02.0–6A02.5) indexing intellectual development (with/without Disorder of Intellectual Development) and language function (mild/no impairment, impaired, absent); plus 6A02.Y and 6A02.Z (https://www.springermedizin.de/the-reclassification-of-neurodevelopmental-disorders-in-icd-11/51520996) |
| **Age / onset requirement** | **Criterion C** — "Symptoms must be present in the **early developmental period** (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life)." The DSM-IV "<3 years" requirement was removed (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | Onset occurs "during the developmental period, typically in early childhood, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." CDDR further acknowledges onset may be recognized only in retrospect; multiple passages allow "compensation" to mask features (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/) |
| **Functional impairment threshold** | **Criterion D** — "Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning" (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | Requirement 4 — "The symptoms result in significant impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning. Some individuals with ASD are able to function adequately in many contexts through exceptional effort, such that their deficits may not be apparent to others. A diagnosis is still appropriate in such cases" (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf) |
| **Co-occurring condition coding** | Specifiers: with/without intellectual impairment; with/without language impairment; associated known genetic/medical condition; associated neurodevelopmental/mental/behavioral problem; with catatonia (use additional F06.1). Also introduces a separate diagnosis, **Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder (SCD)**, for individuals with social-communication deficits who do not meet the RRB threshold | Intellectual development and language ability coded via the 6A02.x linearization subtypes themselves; catatonia retained as separate additional code. **No SCD analogue** — ICD-11 instead requires co-occurrence of both essential features |

**Key quantitative difference:** Kamp-Becker (2024) calculates that the ICD-11 ASD construct permits ~304 (19 × 16) distinct manifestation combinations meeting essential features (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/) — far wider than DSM-5's narrower 3-of-3 social and 2-of-4 RRB combinatoric space.

---

## (B) Peer-Reviewed Evidence Synthesis (2013–present)

Note that **no published head-to-head study** compares DSM-5 directly against ICD-11 ASD criteria in the same blinded clinical sample — the evidence below is necessarily a mix of (i) DSM-IV-TR vs DSM-5, (ii) ICD-10 vs DSM-5 clinic comparisons, (iii) ICD-10→ICD-11 textual reviews, and (iv) ICD-11 narrative analyses.

### Study 1 — Kulage, Smaldone & Cohn (2014), *Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders* [the only true systematic review/meta-analysis in this evidence base]
- **Design:** Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies from 418 records, comparing DSM-IV-TR vs DSM-5 ASD criteria applied to the same populations.
- **Sample:** Pooled across 14 studies using ADOS, ADI-R, DSM-IV-TR/ICD-10 checklists.
- **Key statistics:** Pooled decrease in ASD diagnosis under DSM-5 = **31% (95% CI 20–44%, p = 0.006)**; decrease for Autistic Disorder = **22% (95% CI 16–29%, p < 0.001)**; decrease for PDD-NOS = **70% (95% CI 55–82%, p = 0.01)**; decrease for Asperger's disorder = 70% (95% CI 26–94%, p = 0.38, not significant). (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/)
- **GRADE quality: Low-to-moderate** (heterogeneous reference standards; consistent direction of effect; risk of study-level bias; criteria comparison rather than outcome data).
- **Relevance:** Quantifies the under-diagnosis risk that ICD-11's prototype-based approach was designed to mitigate — though the meta-analysis compares DSM-5 to DSM-IV-TR, not to ICD-11 directly.

### Study 2 — McPartland, Reichow & Volkmar (2012), *JAACAP*
- **Design:** Re-analysis of DSM-IV field-trial data using proposed DSM-5 algorithm.
- **Sample:** N = 977 (657 clinical ASD; 276 non-autistic comparison; 125 clinicians across 21 international sites).
- **Key statistics (95% CIs):** Overall sensitivity 60.6% (57–64%); overall specificity 94.9% (92–97%). Subgroup sensitivities: Autistic Disorder = 0.76; Asperger's Disorder = 0.25; PDD-NOS = 0.28. By cognitive ability: IQ < 70 = 0.70; IQ ≥ 70 = 0.46 (χ²(1) = 34.9, p < .001) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/). **Caveat:** published in 2012, before the user's 2013-present window; included because it is the most rigorous quantitative DSM-5 evaluation available.
- **GRADE: Moderate** (large multi-site sample but re-coded historical field-trial data).
- **Relevance:** Demonstrates that the monothetic social-communication rubric excluded many cognitively able individuals and PDD-NOS cases — a direct precedent for ICD-11's intentional loosening.

### Study 3 — Wilson et al. (2013), King's College London Adult ASD Diagnostic Clinic study
- **Design:** Retrospective clinic comparison.
- **Sample:** N = 150 intellectually able adults evaluated for ASD.
- **Key statistics:** Of ICD-10R-diagnosed adults, **only 56% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**; a further 19% met DSM-5 Social Communication Disorder criteria. Of those with DSM-IV-TR Autistic Disorder/Asperger Syndrome, **78% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**. Reducing required RRB criteria or scoring "uncertain" as "present" raised sensitivity without sacrificing specificity. Authors warn: *"Reduced rates of ASD diagnosis may mean some ASD individuals will be unable to access clinical services"* (https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/).
- **GRADE: Low-to-moderate** (single-site, modest sample, intellectually able adults only).
- **Relevance:** Identifies the precise population (cognitively able adults) most likely to be protected by ICD-11's looser prototype structure.

### Study 4 — First et al. (2021), *World Psychiatry*
- **Design:** Systematic cross-walk comparing ICD-11 CDDG "Essential Features" with DSM-5 criteria across 103 diagnostic entities.
- **Sample:** 103 (or 104) diagnostic categories rated by expert panels.
- **Key statistics:** ASD-specific categorical rating was among **20 disorders (19.4%) rated "major differences,"** 42 (40.8%) "minor definitional differences," 10 (9.7%) "minor differences due to greater DSM-5 specification," 31 (30.1%) "essentially identical." Notes ICD-11 RRB examples are less dominated by features typical of ASD + intellectual disability (e.g., object flipping, smelling/touching) and include sensory and special-interest manifestations more characteristic of cognitively able individuals (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825; https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/).
- **GRADE: Moderate** (comprehensive but qualitative; no quantitative pooling).
- **Relevance:** Authoritative harmonization comparison authored by members of both WHO and APA work groups.

### Study 5 — Kamp-Becker (2024), *Molecular Psychiatry*
- **Design:** Perspective / critical-textual analysis.
- **Sample:** Not applicable (textual analysis).
- **Key statistics:** Calculates ~304 (19 × 16) symptom combinations satisfy ICD-11 essential features; notes ICD-11 explicitly **does not include** features typically observed in low-functioning/nonverbal autism (e.g., flipping objects, preoccupation with unusual objects, excessive smelling/touching, echolalia, visual fascination), while including sensory hyper/hyporeactivity. The author warns ICD-11 *"bears a large danger of false positive diagnoses, of further increased prevalence rates, limitations of access to ASD-specific services and of increasing the non-specificity of treatments"* (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).
- **GRADE: Low** for empirical effect estimates (perspective piece) but **High** for descriptive mapping of ICD-11 text. Panel 3 treated this source more cautiously as theoretical opinion.
- **Conflict note between panels:** Both sources agreed on the descriptive mapping (ICD-11 omits several low-IQ-typical items), but Panel 1 read this as warning of *exclusion* of low-IQ populations, while Panel 3 read First et al. as framing this *relatively* more positively as a balance shift.

**Aggregate confidence:** Low-to-moderate overall. The most rigorous quantitative evidence is Kulage 2014 and McPartland 2012; sensitivity estimates for DSM-5 alone range from ~46% to ~97% depending on cognitive ability and prior DSM-IV subtype. No large prospective head-to-head DSM-5 vs ICD-11 diagnostic-accuracy study exists. The closest ICD-11-specific reliability data are global kappas of 0.45–0.88 across mental disorders (n=1,806 adults, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5980511/) and a Mexico City pediatric field study (n=52, kappas 0.46–0.53 outside DBD, https://www.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.202000830), neither reporting ASD-specifically.

---

## (C) Clinical Guideline Positions

### World Health Organization (WHO)
WHO adopted ICD-11 at the 72nd World Health Assembly in May 2019, with global reporting effective January 1, 2022 (https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/classification-of-diseases). On March 8, 2024, WHO released the *Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements (CDDR)* — including chapter 6A02 ASD — explicitly positioning ICD-11 as the global diagnostic standard (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240077263; https://www.who.int/news/item/08-03-2024-new-manual-released-to-support-diagnosis-of-mental--behavioural-and-neurodevelopmental-disorders-added-in-icd-11). WHO explicitly states that *"atypical responses to sensory stimuli are included as part of the diagnostic requirements in ICD-11, in contrast to ICD-10, where unusual sensory processing was not yet considered a core (diagnostic) feature"* (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/). As of May 2024, 132 Member States are at various ICD-11 implementation phases; 72 have commenced implementation; 14 are collecting/reporting data using ICD-11 (https://www.who.int/news/item/08-02-2024-icd-11-2024-release).

### American Psychiatric Association (APA)
APA published DSM-5 (2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022), consolidating autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, and PDD-NOS into Autism Spectrum Disorder (https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/1f89fd09-aeb1-41f8-abe5-8009bf215e13/downloads/ca0faa99-2adc-4a73-b5fe-7aff6a5faaef/DSM%205%20TR%20English.pdf). DSM-5 was the first major system to formally include sensory processing (Criterion B4) as a polythetic, equally weighted ASD sub-criterion. APA has not announced any plan to adopt ICD-11 criteria in the US; DSM-5/DSM-5-TR remains the dominant psychiatric classification. However, APA's DSM-5 Steering Committee has explicitly tasked itself with "harmonizing as much as possible with ICD-11" and acknowledged that ICD-11 symptoms "are well aligned with the symptoms in DSM-5" (https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp.20250878).

### American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
The 2020 AAP Clinical Report ("Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder," *Pediatrics* 145(1):e20193447) references DSM-5 criteria explicitly: *"Symptoms of ASD are further shaped by deficits in imitation and of processing information across sensory modalities… Repetitive behaviors and perseveration may be primary compulsions but may also be related to atypical processing of sensory information"* (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/145/1/e20193447/36917/Identification-Evaluation-and-Management-of). The 2012 AAP policy statement recommends **against** a standalone Sensory Processing Disorder diagnosis, asserting *"sensory problems are likely to be symptoms of other recognized developmental disorders, such as autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and anxiety disorder"* (https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp-rj.2022.170405; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/is-sensory-processing-disorder-for-real/). AAP does **not** yet recommend ICD-11 adoption; clinical practice uses DSM-5 criteria cross-walked to ICD-10-CM codes for billing.

### National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, UK)
NICE CG128 (under-19s), CG142 (adults; last updated June 2021), and CG170 (under-19s management) explicitly accept **either DSM-5 or ICD-11** to assign an autism diagnosis, and use verbatim language: diagnosis should be based on *"ICD-11 or DSM-5 criteria"* (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg142/chapter/recommendations; https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/CG128/chapter/recommendations). NICE CG142 lists *"altered sensory sensitivity, sensory processing difficulties and emotional regulation difficulties"* among core features clinicians should be alert to (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg142/resources/autismspectrum-disorder-in-adults-diagnosis-and-managementpdf-35109567475909). NICE has not mandated ICD-11 over DSM-5.

---

## (D) Advocacy Organization Positions on Neurodiversity Alignment

### Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN, US) — most explicitly neurodiversity-affirming
ASAN embraces the neurodiversity paradigm: *"Neurodiversity means… there is no such thing as a 'normal' brain… people with brain-based disabilities… should be accepted and included… The neurodiversity movement also says that we shouldn't try to cure or get rid of autism"* (https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/). Per the published chapter "Lobbying Autism's Diagnostic Revision in the DSM-5" (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13), ASAN *"achieved significant partial successes in protecting access to diagnosis, addressing disparities in diagnosis for marginalized groups, and blocking harmful proposals. Nonetheless, the lack of formal autistic representation within the process limited ASAN's impact, leading to criteria that are likely still too narrow and a problematic severity scale."* ASAN's 2012 talking points specifically opposed the DSM-5 3-of-3 social communication requirement as "an overly restrictive standard" (https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/05/asan-talking-points-for-public-comment-on-dsm-5-autism-spectrum-disorder-criteria/) and opposed the two-part severity rating, arguing that severity based on "need for support" is preferable but still pathologizes autistic traits (https://www.thetransmitter.org/spectrum/will-new-dsm-5-autism-criteria-impact-services/). ASAN opposes splitting autism into "profound" or "severe" subcategories (https://autisticadvocacy.org/2023/02/asan-comments-for-january-18-2023/). While ASAN has not formally endorsed ICD-11 over DSM-5 in a dedicated position document, its structural preferences — no minimum item counts, recognition of masking, inclusion of the full spectrum, avoidance of deficit-based severity — align more naturally with ICD-11 than DSM-5.

### National Autistic Society (NAS, UK) — neutral/pluralistic
NAS states: *"An autism diagnosis should be based on criteria listed in the… DSM-5 or… ICD-11, according to the… NICE guidelines"* (https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment), and notes *"both reference the 'core characteristics' of autism… including sensory differences."* NAS reframes restricted/repetitive behaviors in non-pathological, neurodiversity-affirming terms as *"self-soothing or self-regulating behaviours, and focused and dedicated interests."* NAS treats the two manuals as functionally equivalent classification tools.

### Autism Speaks (US) — has not framed the choice as a neurodiversity question
Autism Speaks uses DSM-5 as its primary reference (https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5) and notes *"the DSM-5 revised the symptoms… adding sensory symptoms as a diagnostic criterion"* (https://www.autismspeaks.org/blog/expert-qa-dsm-5-and-asd). Its framing remains primarily medical/biomedical (treatment-seeking, severity levels, supports). Autism Speaks has historically been critiqued by neurodiversity advocates (including ASAN) for cure-oriented rhetoric.

**Synthesis:** ASAN's documented advocacy maps onto the structural differences distinguishing ICD-11 from DSM-5, making its position closest to viewing ICD-11 as more neurodiversity-affirming in principle. NAS's sensory-inclusive framing likewise aligns with ICD-11's more expansive sensory language. Autism Speaks has not taken a comparative position. **No major advocacy organization has issued a formal "ICD-11 is more neurodiversity-affirming than DSM-5" position document.**

---

## (E) Diagnostic Safety Risks

### Over-diagnosis / false-positive risk under ICD-11
Kamp-Becker (2024) warns that ICD-11's combinatoric structure *"bears a large danger of false positive diagnoses, of further increased prevalence rates, limitations of access to ASD-specific services and of increasing the non-specificity of treatments"* (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/). Differential-difficulty concern: ICD-11 features (e.g., "lack of adaptability to new experiences," "excessive adherence to rules when playing games") are difficult to distinguish from anxiety disorders, behavioral inhibition, or OCD. ICD-11's reference to "compensation" without operationalization compromises behavioral observation validity.

### Under-diagnosis / exclusion risk under DSM-5
McPartland et al. (2012) showed DSM-5 would have excluded **~39.4% of individuals with a clinical DSM-IV ASD diagnosis**, particularly cognitively able individuals (sensitivity IQ ≥ 70 = 0.46), prior-Asperger's (0.25) and prior-PDD-NOS (0.28) cases (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/). Wilson et al. showed **44% of ICD-10-diagnosed ASD adults failed DSM-5 criteria** (https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/). Kulage et al.'s meta-analysis confirmed pooled **31% decrease in ASD diagnosis under DSM-5 vs DSM-IV-TR (95% CI 20–44%)** (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/). Risk: *"reduced rates of ASD diagnosis may mean some ASD individuals will be unable to access clinical services"* (Kulage et al.).

### Gender / female-presentation under-diagnosis
A systematic review and meta-analysis on camouflaging (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11065-023-09630-2) confirms *"a bias in clinical procedures towards males"* and that females use significantly more compensation and masking strategies. Women are more likely to receive *prior* psychiatric diagnoses (anxiety, eating disorders, borderline personality) before ASD is recognized — i.e., misdiagnosis with subsequent inappropriate interventions (e.g., DBT for borderline when ASD is the underlying condition) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10926859/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12467426/). **Critically, in one Italian adult sample, females misdiagnosed with other conditions had *significantly higher* Hyper/Hyporeactivity to sensory input scores than males — sensory-focused presentations in women are particularly prone to misdiagnosis** (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3425/11/7/912).

### Sensory-focused presentation risks
Under either manual, a sensory-only presentation is **not sufficient for ASD diagnosis** and risks being missed entirely or misattributed. DSM-5 formally incorporates sensory differences as B4 only when accompanied by other ASD features, requiring it to be paired with another RRB. ICD-11 includes sensory atypicalities among 16 possible RRBs but does not require them. The 2012 AAP policy statement recommended against standalone SPD diagnosis. Occupational therapy interventions (sensory integration therapy) lack conclusive effectiveness evidence per AAP 2012 — creating a risk of *inappropriate intervention* for sensory-focused children who do not meet ASD criteria.

### Inappropriate intervention downstream
Delayed or missed ASD diagnosis in cognitively able adults can lead to years of misapplied interventions for anxiety, OCD, eating disorders, or BPD (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12467426/). Conversely, over-broad ICD-11 application risks labeling individuals with primary anxiety, OCD, or personality disorders as autistic, delaying access to evidence-based treatment for the actual primary condition (Kamp-Becker 2024).

### Safety summary
DSM-5's documented risk is *under-diagnosis* of cognitively able, sensory-focused, adult, and previously-PDD-NOS populations. ICD-11's hypothesized risk is *over-diagnosis* and non-specificity, with consequent service dilution. **Sensory differences drive both problems:** they are collapsed under DSM-5's 2-of-4 RRB threshold (causing exclusion), and amplified by ICD-11's no-minimum structure (risking inclusion of non-autistic sensory-anxious populations).

---

## (F) Reimbursement / Coding Summary

### United States
**HIPAA-mandated code set: ICD-10-CM.** Clinicians diagnose using DSM-5/DSM-5-TR (the APA's reference), but bill using ICD-10-CM codes — currently **F84.0 (Autistic Disorder)** for ASD, with DSM-5-TR severity specifiers (Levels 1–3) and accompanying intellectual/language/catatonia specifiers captured via additional ICD-10-CM codes (https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0; https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026). This creates a recognized coding–diagnosis mismatch: a DSM-5 ASD diagnosis is routinely billed as F84.0 regardless of severity level. WHO's ICD-10 → ICD-11 official mapping treats F84.0 as equivalent to **6A02.Z (Autism spectrum disorder, unspecified)** (https://autoicdapi.com/icd10-to-icd11/F84.0). US has **not adopted ICD-11 for morbidity/billing**. NCVHS recommended adoption research in 2019 (https://ncvhs.hhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Recommendation-Letter-Preparing-for-Adoption-of-ICD-11-as-a-Mandated-US-Health-Data-Standard-final.pdf); the CDC issued a 2023 RFI; AHA responded in January 2024 supporting transition but urging evaluation of need for a US Clinical Modification (https://www.aha.org/lettercomment/2024-01-12-aha-responds-cdc-rfi-icd-11-morbidity-coding-use). A 2023 strategy paper (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10531107/) proposes the US may adopt ICD-11 without a CM version. **Projected US morbidity/billing adoption: no earlier than 2027–2029.**

### European Union / United Kingdom
UK uses ICD-10 historically; NICE accepts **either DSM-5 or ICD-11** for clinical diagnosis. WHO reports 132 member states at various ICD-11 implementation phases; 14 actively collecting data using ICD-11 (https://www.who.int/news/item/08-02-2024-icd-11-2024-release). **France** is pursuing phased adoption led by the National Health Information Agency (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12208713/). Many EU clinicians continue to use ICD-10 (F84.0 etc.) for billing during the transition. The ICD-11 CDDR (March 2024) is intended as the clinical companion to the MMS linearization.

### Effect on coverage/reimbursement
**No payer — US or EU — has reported coverage changes specifically attributable to ICD-11 criteria vs DSM-5 criteria.** Reimbursement tracks the diagnostic code, not the underlying manual. The practical risk is administrative: during transition, dual coding, coder training, and EHR mapping (especially for ICD-11 postcoordination and stem/extension codes) create temporary billing-error risk. Indirect effects: (1) if ICD-11 criteria are more inclusive, more patients may receive ASD diagnoses and generate autism-related claims (ABA, speech, OT); (2) if ICD-11 is more restrictive for some populations (e.g., removal of "atypical autism"), some patients may lose diagnostic eligibility and thus lose coverage in systems requiring an autism diagnosis for service authorization; (3) WHO 6A02.x subcodes enable more precise intellectual/language case-mix coding than F84.x, potentially affecting future risk-adjustment. **For sensory-focused presentations specifically:** because neither DSM-5 nor ICD-11 requires sensory abnormalities for diagnosis, no sensory-specific reimbursement code exists in either ICD-10-CM or ICD-11, and insurance coverage for sensory integration therapy remains inconsistent.

---

## Bottom-Line Synthesis

DSM-5 and ICD-11 share the two-domain structure of autism and both formally include sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity. Their substantive divergence is **algorithmic strictness**: DSM-5 is monothetic (3 of 3 social + 2 of 4 RRB, mandated severity levels); ICD-11 is prototype-based (no minimum symptom counts, intellectual/language qualifiers). The empirical literature shows DSM-5 reduces ASD diagnoses by ~31% vs DSM-IV-TR (Kulage 2014 meta-analysis), with the greatest losses among cognitively able adults and PDD-NOS populations — precisely the groups ICD-11 was designed to protect. ICD-11's inverse risk (false-positive diagnoses, reduced specificity) is theoretically prominent but empirically unquantified (Kamp-Becker 2024). **For sensory-focused presentations specifically, ICD-11 is structurally more permissive**: sensory reactivity counts toward the RRB domain without requiring a second RRB feature, whereas DSM-5 requires another B-criterion symptom. Reimbursement is unaffected by criteria choice in the short term, since payers track codes (ICD-10-CM F84.0 in the US, ICD-10 nationally in EU), not manual. **The single largest evidence gap remains the absence of a large, blinded, head-to-head clinical validation study applying both DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria to the same population reporting sensitivity, specificity, and kappa — particularly across sensory-dominant presentations.**

# Comparative Analysis of Transitional Justice Mechanisms Following Mass Atrocities

## Framing the Question

Transitional justice (TJ) encompasses the judicial and non-judicial, domestic and international, retrospective and prospective measures a society uses to reckon with systematic human rights violations. Ruti Teitel's foundational framework characterizes the field as evolving through three "constitutional moments": post-war (Nuremberg), cold-war decolonization (truth commissions), and contemporary post-authoritarian/post-conflict transitions (ICC prosecutions) (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/89c5/7d341b721b9ae0f4222a0f5fea3012c69f35.pdf).

The empirical record is genuinely contested. A widely cited 2006 ETH survey concluded bluntly that "there is little evidence that TJ produces either beneficial or harmful effects," because rigorous cross-national analysis was scarce and the field was "driven by principles rather than data" (https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/103597/FullText.pdf). Later quantitative work is more optimistic but strongly conditional. The Transitional Justice Data Base (TJDB) found that TJ improves democracy and human rights scores only in specific combinations — trials plus amnesties, or trials plus amnesties plus truth commissions — and that truth commissions *alone* had a negative association with those goals (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:1875316a-4e73-436c-bf38-09c52943e66b/files/mb005fe06fd52177765574e6acba61df0). A synthesis of 25 individual-level studies concluded that "transitional justice matters," that justice is understood by victims as a *social-political* rather than purely legal category, that different victims need different measures, and that outcomes depend heavily on context and implementation (https://onlinelepvestry.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/pops.12395).

## 1. Truth and Reconciliation Commissions

### 1.1 South Africa (1996–1998; Final Report 2003)

**Design.** The TRC was created by the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34/1995 with three committees — Human Rights Violations, Amnesty, and Reparation and Rehabilitation — and operated under a **conditional amnesty** bargain: perpetrators could escape criminal and civil liability only by fully disclosing politically motivated gross violations. The Constitutional Court upheld this in *AZAPO v President* (1996), reasoning that amnesty was the "cornerstone" of the negotiated settlement *and* that the same Act mandated reparations — "reparation is essential to counterbalance amnesty" (https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume5/chapter5/subsection0.htm).

**Scale.** Approximately 21,676 individuals were designated as victims; 17,428 applied for and received the once-off grant; the TRC took statements describing violations affecting roughly 44,000 people and documenting 37,672 violations (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-165-171.pdf; https://atjhub.csvr.org.za/south-africa-truth-and-reconciliation-commission-1996-2002/). The TRC granted amnesty to roughly 700–849 perpetrators out of 7,112 applications (refusing ~5,392) and referred approximately 350 names for prosecution (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-172-202.pdf; https://www.justice.gov.za/Trc/amntrans/index.htm).

**Reparations — the chronic failure point.** The Reparation and Rehabilitation Committee recommended per-victim payments benchmarked to the 1997 median annual household income (R21,700), implying roughly **R130,200–R138,000 per victim** over six years (https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume5/chapter5/subsection8.htm). Parliament halved this and approved a one-off R30,000 grant instead (https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2020-11-08-the-unfinished-business-of-the-trc-is-killing-us-say-apartheids-victims/). Total disbursement: R497,798,781 in final grants plus R53,165,325 in interim grants, a combined R550,964,106 — averaging approximately R28,563 per recipient (about 22% of the R130,200 recommended) (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-172-202.pdf). As of 2018, over R1.43 billion sat unspent in the President's Fund; GroundUp reported that as of April 2016, ~R556 million had been disbursed with over R1 billion remaining, much redirected toward community programs rather than individual redress (https://groundup.news/article/apartheid-compensation-process-flawed-says-khulumani/; https://globalreparations.com/documents/Case_Study_-_South_Africa.pdf). A October 2025 Gauteng High Court ruling rejected government's attempt to delay a R167 million apartheid damages claim (https://pmg.org.za/committee-question/35410/).

**The broken prosecution bargain.** A 2003 moratorium and "high-level executive interference in the period from 2003 until about 2017" (per the 2019 *Rodrigues* judgment) effectively halted TRC-referred prosecutions (https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2019-06-04-npa-allowed-manipulation-of-criminal-justice-system-in-trc-cases/). The NPA-commissioned Ntsebeza Review (2023) recommended a commission of inquiry into political interference; that Khampepe Commission was still hearing testimony in 2026 (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/IAC-55-NPA-Opinion-TRC-matters-June2023-final.pdf; https://www.ewn.co.za/2026/04/30/npa-accused-of-failing-constitutional-duties-in-apartheid-era-crime-cases).

**Victim experience.** The Centre for the Study of Violence and Reconciliation found that hearings' "greatest achievement" lay in restoring victim dignity: "it feels like I got my sight back by coming here and telling my story" (https://sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/volume5_0.pdf). But a Khulumani Support Group survey of 20 survivors found most became disillusioned; eleven of twenty felt amnesty was unfair, with nine calling it "wrong" (https://csvr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2000/01/tellingitlikeitis-3.pdf). Rape victims were largely excluded from the "closed list" because sexual violence was not always defined as a political crime qualifying for amnesty (https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2020-11-08-the-unfinished-business-of-the-trc-is-killing-us-say-apartheids-victims/).

**Transition and recurrence.** Gibson's peer-reviewed assessment concludes the TRC "did indeed exert independent influence on the democratization process through its contributions toward creating a more reconciled society," and that it did not undermine rule-of-law institutions (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022002706287115). Perceptions were group-polarized: Afrikaner participants rated the TRC least effective, Xhosa participants most effective (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0021934703258988). A separate strand of Gibson's work notes that "it is doubtful that the truth and reconciliation process was a cause of peace," since 1990–94 violence had largely abated by 1996 (same source).

### 1.2 Canada (2008–2015)

**Design.** Canada's TRC arose from the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSA, implemented 19 September 2007) — the largest class-action settlement in Canadian history — covering ~150,000 children forced into 140 federally funded schools between 1879 and 1997 (https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100015576/1571581687074). The TRC was *one component* of a broader package that included the Common Experience Payment (CEP), the Independent Assessment Process (IAP) for abuse claims, healing programs, and commemoration. Over six years, **6,500 Survivors and witnesses testified** (https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1524494530110/1557511412801).

**Compensation — the model worked.** The CEP distributed a C$1.9 billion designated amount ($10,000 plus $3,000 per additional school year) to roughly 86,000 former students; total paid reached $1,622,422,106, averaging ~$20,457 per recipient, with about 98% of eligible former students paid by December 2012 (https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1315320539682/1571590489978). The IAP awarded $5,000–$275,000 per person for proven sexual or serious physical abuse (https://www.residentialschoolsettlement.ca/detailed_notice.pdf). Additional funds: $125 million to the Aboriginal Healing Foundation, $60 million for the TRC, $20 million for commemoration.

**Calls to Action — the implementation failure.** The Final Report (December 2015) included 94 Calls to Action. A decade on, Indigenous-led monitors consistently find:
- **Yellowhead Institute (2023):** zero Calls completed; 81 of 94 unfulfilled (https://yellowheadinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/YI-TRC-C2A-2023-Special-Report-compressed.pdf).
- **Assembly of First Nations (September 2025):** approximately **13 of 94 completed**, only two in the prior five years, and zero in 2024–25 (https://afn.bynder.com/m/21a223c344077b7/original/Progress-on-Realizing-the-Truth-and-Reconciliation-Commission-s-Calls-to-Action-September-2025.pdf).
- **Academic Cody Groat / Global News (2025):** fewer than 20 of 94 fully implemented, with one tally showing 14 completed, 42 in progress, 16 not started, 22 stalled (https://globalnews.ca/news/11579370/under-20-truth-and-reconciliation-calls-implemented-decade-later/).

Government framing — "more than 85% of the 76 calls requiring the federal government's sole or shared leadership have been completed or are well underway" — counts items "well underway" as progress (https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1524494530110/1557511412801). Concrete wins exist: the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (Call to Action 80, achieved 2021), the Indigenous Languages Act (Calls 13/14, 2019), child-welfare legislation (2020), and the National Council for Reconciliation Act (Bill C-29, 2024).

## 2. Prosecutorial Tribunals

### 2.1 ICTY (Former Yugoslavia, 1993–2017)

**Output.** The ICTY indicted **161 individuals** over 24 years: 90 sentenced, 19 acquitted, 13 referred to national jurisdictions, 37 proceedings terminated (often due to accused deaths), and 2 awaiting retrial before the MICT (https://www.icty.org/en/cases/key-figures-figs-cases; https://www.icty.org/sites/icty.org/files/images/content/Infographic_facts_figures_en.pdf). The Tribunal heard testimony from approximately **4,650 live witnesses**, with court transcripts documenting testimony of more than **10,800 individuals** (same source). By ethnicity, indictees were overwhelmingly Serb (94), followed by Croat (29), Albanian (9), and Bosniak (9) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_indicted_in_the_ICTY).

**Sexual violence jurisprudence.** 78 indictees (48%) had sexual-violence charges; 32 were convicted for such crimes (https://www.icty.org/sid/10586). The Čelebići case (1998) established rape as torture under customary international law.

**Cost.** Cumulative cost approximately **$2.2 billion** over 24 years, with annual budgets exceeding $100 million; one comparative law study computes roughly $18 million per concluded trial (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-journal-of-international-law/article/abs/costs-of-international-justice/C72C5059E6BF5F3ECDA217F1621777D1). Arithmetic: $2.2B ÷ 161 ≈ **$13.7 million per accused**; $2.2B ÷ ~90 sentenced ≈ **$24 million per conviction**.

**Contested legacy.** The 2012–13 acquittals of Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač (Operation Storm) and Momčilo Perišić produced a crisis of confidence — a sitting ICTY judge, Frederik Harhoff, circulated an email questioning the dilution of joint criminal enterprise doctrine (https://www.toaep.org/pbs-pdf/49-slydal; https://www.cips-cepi.ca/2013/07/17/oversell-but-underperform-the-increasingly-troubled-legacy-of-the-icty/). Surveys found publics viewed the ICTY as a foreign body rather than "their" tribunal (https://www.ictj.org/sites/default/files/ICTJ-FormerYugoslavia-Justice-Facts-2009-English.pdf). Milanović concluded that the ICTY "failed to persuade target audiences" — judgments establishing facts did not translate into local acceptance (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-journal-of-international-law/article/abs/impact-of-the-icty-on-the-former-yugoslavia-an-anticipatory-postmortem/CD016D8E8B971AF1F361456AA85EC3AF). An empirical study of Tribunal staff and 65 Bosnian victims found the ICTY "has not realized" its objectives of delivering justice and restoring peace, and that trials are "most effective when combined with restorative justice" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/g7vhzmhjqhc).

The EU made ICTY cooperation "a sine qua non in accession negotiations"; Croatia's accession depended on such cooperation (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14683850701565973). Cross-national data from post-conflict societies 1982–2010 found international tribunals "do not appear to contribute to reducing the recurrence of civil war or improvements in human rights practices" — though neither did they exercise negative effects (https://sah.borca.ai/papers/146401203).

### 2.2 ICC — Kenya (2007–08 Post-Election Violence)

**Context.** The Waki Commission recorded **1,133 deaths, 3,561 injuries, 117,216 instances of property destruction, and mass displacement** (350,000–600,000), with police responsible for all 405 recorded gunshot deaths (https://www.ictj.org/sites/default/files/ICTJ-Kenya-Dialogue-Inquiry-2008-English.pdf). Parliament defeated a domestic tribunal bill in February 2009; the ICC Prosecutor opened a *proprio motu* investigation on 31 March 2010. Charges were confirmed on 23 January 2012 against four suspects.

**Case 1: Kenyatta.** The Prosecution withdrew charges on 5 December 2014 because "the evidence has not improved to such an extent that Mr Kenyatta's alleged criminal responsibility can be proven beyond reasonable doubt" — key witnesses died, "others were too terrified to testify," and the government refused records requests (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2014_09939.PDF; https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-withdrawal-charges-against-mr). Trial Chamber V(B) terminated proceedings on 13 March 2015. The BBC called it "the most high-profile collapse of a case in the ICC's history" (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-30353311).

**Case 2: Ruto and Sang.** On 5 April 2016 Trial Chamber V(A) vacated charges — 17 prosecution witnesses had withdrawn cooperation due to intimidation and political interference — while explicitly declining to acquit "without prejudice" to future re-prosecution (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/ruto-and-sang-case-icc-trial-chamber-va-terminates-case-without-prejudice-re-prosecution). One judge declared a mistrial over "intolerable political meddling" (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-35974172).

**Victims got nothing.** Because there was no conviction, the Trial Chamber majority held it had no power under Article 75 to order reparations (https://repozytorium.uni.wroc.pl/Content/131195/PDF/112_Musial_Budnicka_J_ICC_court_decision_on_reparation_for_victims_of_the_post_election_violence_no_reparation.pdf); the Trust Fund for Victims confirmed it "is not permitted to award reparations... where no conviction by the court exists" (https://capitalfm.africa/no-reparations-without-conviction-icc-tells-kenya-victims/). The Victims' Legal Representative described the withdrawal as a "betrayal" of thousands whose "lives had been torn asunder" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2014_09983.PDF). Politically, the indicted Kenyatta and Ruto formed an alliance and won the 2013 election.

**Domestic complement — also failed.** Kenya's Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission delivered a 4-volume, 2,210-page report in May 2013 based on ~40,000 statements, but the National Assembly never adopted it or created the recommended implementation committee (https://www.justiceinfo.net/en/44424-how-kenya-s-truth-commission-report-became-a-political-ghost.html).

### 2.3 ICC — Sudan / Darfur (2005–)

**Design.** UNSC Resolution 1593 (2005) referred the Darfur situation to the ICC — the first Chapter VII referral against a non-state party. The first Al-Bashir arrest warrant issued on 4 March 2009 for war crimes and crimes against humanity; a second warrant on 12 July 2010 added three counts of genocide, the first ICC indictment of a sitting head of state (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2010_04825.PDF).

**Implementation failure.** Al-Bashir was never arrested and traveled freely to non-cooperating and even state-party jurisdictions including South Africa, China, and India. The African Union directed member states in 2009 to "withhold cooperation" with the ICC regarding Al-Bashir's arrest (https://exa.ai/library/publication/pzccxhpd5gx). Quantitative analysis indicated the indictment "accelerated patterns of obstruction and intimidation of peacekeeping actors," complicating UNAMID's mandate (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01436597.2019.1579640). Darfuri victim groups formally withdrew from the case in frustration; "no official from the ICC has ever stepped foot on the Sudanese region" (https://justiceinconflict.org/2015/11/05/tired-of-waiting-darfur-victims-withdraw-from-icc-case-against-bashir/).

**Partial redemption.** The one advance is *The Prosecutor v. Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman* ("Ali Kushayb"), a Janjaweed leader who was surrendered to the Court and **convicted** — reparations proceedings were actively underway in 2025–26, with victims' counsel and IDP camp coordination committees participating, and "the authorities of the Government of Sudan have not submitted any written observations" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/0902ebd180f0061b.pdf). The Cassese Commission's 2005 recommendation of a Darfur Compensation Commission was never established (https://www.ictj.org/sites/default/files/ICTJ-Sudan-Darfur-Reparations-2007-English_0.pdf).

## 3. Reparations Programs

### 3.1 Germany's Holocaust Reparations

**Architecture.** Established by the 1952 Luxembourg Agreements between the FRG, Israel, and the Claims Conference: DM 3 billion (~$714 million) to Israel in goods and services; DM 450 million (~$107 million) to the Claims Conference for individual indemnification; the Federal Compensation Act (BEG, 1956) for personal injury, liberty, professional advancement, and property; the Federal Restitution Law (BRüG, 1957) for movable property (https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany/).

**Scale.** Germany's Federal Ministry of Finance reports total public-sector compensation payments of **€85.361 billion by 31 December 2024** (€83.616 billion through 2023 plus €1.745 billion in 2024), with BEG alone accounting for €48.952 billion and the Luxembourg Agreement €1.764 billion (https://www.bundesfinanzministerium.de/Content/DE/Downloads/Oeffentliche-Finanzen/Wiedergutmachung/leistungen-oeffentliche-hand-wiedergutmachung-en.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=5). The Claims Conference states that since 1952 Germany has paid more than **$95 billion** in indemnification to individuals (https://www.jns.org/antisemitism/germany-to-pay-over-1-billion-holocaust-survivors).

**Ongoing, needs-adaptive payments.** Annual payments have grown sharply: from ~€510 million ($557 million) in 2015 to a record $1.4 billion (€1.29 billion) for 2024 — the largest single-year figure since reparations began (https://apnews.com/article/german-jews-holocaust-survivors-claims-conference-compensation-6e50867ada8a79d32d192c99020ee1cc). October 2025 negotiations produced €923.9 million ($1.08 billion) for survivor home care in 2026 — the largest home-care budget in the organization's history, up from €34 million in 2009 (a ~27-fold nominal increase) — plus €175 million ($205 million) for Shoah education through 2029 and hardship-fund supplemental payments of €1,450 each to more than **127,000 survivors** (https://www.claimscon.org/2025/10/negotiations-25/). Composition of 2024 figures: $535 million direct to survivors (monthly pensions; hardship payments); $888.9 million for home care and social welfare services delivered through ~300 agencies in 83 countries; increased funding for Holocaust education (https://www.jta.org/2023/06/14/global/germany-agrees-to-record-1-4-billion-in-annual-holocaust-reparations-as-survivors-age). As of mid-2019, approximately 25,000 survivors worldwide still received monthly BEG pensions (https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany/).

**Distinctive features.** A perpetrator-state payment sustained across 70+ years, adapting to beneficiaries' aging (median age 87); negotiated representation through the Claims Conference (founded 1951); explicit prevention investment justified by "a troubling decline in public understanding of key Holocaust facts" amid rising antisemitism.

### 3.2 United States — Japanese American Redress

**Design.** The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (Pub. L. 100-383), sponsored by Rep. Norman Mineta (an internee) and Sen. Alan Simpson, signed by President Reagan on 10 August 1988. The Act conceded that WWII relocation was based on "race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership" rather than security (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Liberties_Act_of_1988; https://www.congress.gov/bill/100th-congress/house-bill/442/text).

**Execution — complete and on time.** The Justice Department's Office of Redress Administration paid **$20,000 plus a formal presidential apology to 82,219 eligible claimants**, totaling **$1,644,380,000** ($1.6 billion+), and **closed on schedule on 5 February 1999** (https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/1999/February/059cr.htm). The statute authorized a $1.25–1.65 billion fund (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2011-title50/html/USCODE-2011-title50-app-restituti.htm). Eligibility required being alive on 10 August 1988 — an inherent limit that excluded the deceased majority of internees; an additional $5,000 paid to 145 Japanese Latin Americans settled in *Mochizuki* litigation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Liberties_Act_of_1988). The Act also created the **Civil Liberties Public Education Fund** with $5 million annually, explicitly to "discourage the occurrence of similar injustices and violations of civil liberties in the future" (https://uscode.ecfr.io/statutes/pl/100-383.pdf).

**Symbolic-legitimizing contagion.** A controlled experiment demonstrated that informational exposure to the Japanese American redress experience increased Asian American respondents' support for Black reparations (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11332238/).

### 3.3 Reparations Critique

Critical scholarship cautions that reparations can be "palliative" — offering limited material or symbolic redress without addressing structural injustices (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17502977.2022.2042650). The South African case exemplifies this: the President's Fund remains partially disbursed after 25+ years, while perpetrators obtained amnesty. The "transformative reparations" literature suggests reparations are most effective when linked to non-temporary structural changes and meaningful victim participation (https://www.elgaronline.com/view/journals/cilj/8/1/article-p39.xml). Symbolic reparations (memorialization, official apology, commemoration) play a recognized restorative role — Carlos Martín Beristain argues symbolic measures aim at "recognizing the dignity of the victims, fostering the memory of relevant historical facts" (https://www.brandeis.edu/creativity-arts-social-transformation/news-events/pdfs/repairing_symbolic_reparations_greeley.pdf) — though poorly designed monuments can be "ineffective, even detrimental."

## 4. Lustration Policies (Post-Communist Eastern Europe)

**Typology.** Three archetypes (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/662648):
- **Dismissal** (Albania, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, unified Germany): barring collaborators from public positions;
- **Exposure** (Hungary, Poland, Romania): making secret-police collaboration records public without categorical bans;
- **Confession** (Poland's 1997 Act): allowing tainted officials to retain positions if they voluntarily disclosed collaboration.

**Czech Republic (1991 Act No. 451/1991).** The earliest and "semi-retributive" regime banned former StB collaborators, agents, and communist party functionaries from specified public posts. The Constitutional Court reviewed and moderated the law's most extreme provisions; extensions in 1995 and 2000 raised rule-of-law concerns (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-social-inquiry/article/abs/lustration-laws-in-action-the-motives-and-evaluation-of-lustration-policy-in-the-czech-republic-and-poland-19892001/A54F46A5C8E41697959589830750116C).

**Poland (1997 and 2006/07).** The 1997 Act combined exposure with a confession pathway. Late 2006/07 "late lustration" expanded vetting to journalists, academics, business leaders, and others in "positions of public trust," and would have required up to **700,000 people** to file collaboration declarations. On **11 May 2007 the Constitutional Tribunal (K 2/07) struck down most of it**, including provisions covering journalists, teachers, and academics, warning that "the state must respect human rights and not have recourse to vengeance" (http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/6648435.stm; https://trybunal.gov.pl/fileadmin/content/omowienia/K_2_07_GB.pdf).

**Germany (Unification).** The 1990 Unification Treaty allowed dismissal of senior GDR party functionaries and Stasi collaborators; the 1991 Stasi Records Act established the Federal Commissioner for Stasi Records, enabling vetting of judges, professors, and teachers. This produced "thousands" of discharges (https://files.core.ac.uk/download/pdf/41100396.pdf). Germany benefited from absorption into the FRG, providing institutional capacity others lacked.

**Empirical assessment.** David's cross-national typology of 12 postcommunist countries finds "a robust relationship between lustration policies and democracy": extensive programs are **associated with ~30% higher levels of democracy over time**, controlling for macroeconomic and political factors; compulsory, mildly punitive employment-change programs outperform purely symbolic "moral cleansing" programs (https://www.academia.edu/106110356/The_Impact_of_Lustration_on_Democratization_in_Postcommunist_Countries). Horne's nine-country study finds lustration "consistently and positively contributes to citizen trust in public institutions" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0010414011421766). Survey experiments in Czechia, Hungary, and Poland show **dismissal and confession increase trust in government and in tainted officials, while exposure reduces trust in tainted officials** (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/662648).

**Limits.** The 1995 ECtHR case of *Vogt v. Germany* (21 Eur. H.R. Rep. 205) held that some lustration approaches may violate freedom of expression under Article 10 ECHR. European Court of Human Rights jurisprudence has been "unsettled" on whether lustration laws survive contemporary scrutiny (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/D0651FBE5434D968F2F397C9F1754938/S1574019608004604a.pdf/lustration_and_lapse_of_time.pdf). Lustration was "unique to post-communist states and was not seen in any other transitional context" (https://https-sage-cnpereading-com-443.webvpn1.xju.edu.cn/doi/10.1177/08883254231163183).
