## 5. Comparative Synthesis Against the Three Criteria

### 5.1 Serving Victims

| Mechanism | Strengths | Limitations |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| **TRCs** | Restore dignity via public testimony; produce official recognition (https://sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/volume5_0.pdf) | Monetary reparations chronically underfunded (South Africa: R30,000 vs. R130,200+ recommended; Canada: 13–20 of 94 Calls implemented); conditional amnesty frustrates victims seeking punishment (https://csvr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2000/01/tellingitlikeitis-3.pdf) |
| **Tribunals** | Provide voice; establish facts; deliver named-perpetrator accountability | Trials average 5+ years; victim participation rights inadequate (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2014_09983.PDF); few mid/low-level perpetrators reached (ICTY: ~90 sentenced of 161; remainder transferred/withdrawn) |
| **Reparations** | Material acknowledgement; survivor support (Germany: $1.4B+ annually; US: $1.6B fully disbursed) | Cannot heal trauma; coverage narrow (only ~25,000 BEG pensions remain; deceased excluded by US eligibility rule); $5K Japanese Latin American settlement |
| **Lustration** | Signals state rejection of complicity; restores integrity of public institutions | Categorical bans harm individual tainted officials disproportionately; rule-of-law risks; *Vogt v. Germany* |

### 5.2 Enabling Democratic Transitions

**TRCs** stabilize transitions by domesticating conflict through ritualized truth-telling. South Africa's TRC served as "an instrument of national myth-making" integrating restorative language into post-apartheid constitutionalism; Gibson's evidence shows it independently strengthened democratization, though it did not "cause" peace (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022002706287115). Canada's experience shows that a TRC alone does not automatically produce structural change — political will and resources matter decisively.

**Prosecutorial tribunals** have inconsistent effects: the ICTY's most important external pressure came via EU accession conditionality (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14683850701565973). ICC interventions against sitting officials can destabilize democracy by prolonging conflict or provoking backlash (Sudan, Kenya).

**Reparations** materially support democratic legitimacy by acknowledging state responsibility; ongoing recognition undergirds Germany's postwar stabilization. The U.S. Civil Liberties Act's apology constitutes Greiff's "recognition function" essential to democratic reconciliation.

**Lustration** was most effective in the German and Czech cases, where strong democratic institutions and bounded scope coupled with international human rights frameworks (https://files.core.ac.uk/download/pdf/41100396.pdf). Late or expanded lustration programs risk "party-political instrumentalization" rather than democratic consolidation (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13510340902732581). David's quantitative work shows extensive lustration associated with ~30% higher democracy levels over time.

### 5.3 Preventing Recurrence

**Statistical evidence:**
- 2025 cross-national study: implementing any combination of trials, truth commissions, exile, or purge within five years of a mass atrocity extends the wait time to the next such atrocity by **approximately 4×** (https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/cjhr/2025/00000024/00000002/art00007).
- World Bank-UN analysis: only prosecutions of **low- and mid-level** violators are associated with decreased conflict recurrence; new constitutions and truth commissions are also positively associated with peace durability (https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/dev4peace/transitional-justice-rule-law-and-conflict-recurrence).
- *International Studies Quarterly* (2017) — the **motivation-addressing vs. opportunity-addressing** distinction: motivation-addressing mechanisms (truth commissions, comprehensive trials, reparations, amnesties) significantly reduce conflict recurrence by mitigating grievances; opportunity-addressing mechanisms (purges, exiles, selective trials of opposition) have little systematic effect (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/61/3/690/4643613).
- Truth commissions specifically show significant reductions in targeted mass killings (TMKs) following implementation, though issuance of final reports and recommendations for reforms *alone* is not associated with TMK reduction (https://researchconnect.suny.edu/en/publications/truth-commissions-and-the-prevention-of-targeted-mass-killings/).
- The 2006 ETH survey notes the evidence base remained thin: "there is little evidence that TJ produces either beneficial or harmful effects" (https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/103597/FullText.pdf).

---

## 6. Mechanism-by-Mechanism Verdict

**Truth and Reconciliation Commissions.** Best serve victim dignification and historical reconciliation when paired with comprehensive reparations; moderately serve democratic consolidation; credibly reduce recurrence when final reports and reform recommendations materialize (SUNY mass-killing study). South Africa shows partial implementation and conditional amnesty can erode victim trust. Canada exemplifies how implementation gaps can transform TRCs from transformation into performance. Critical caveat: TJDB found truth commissions *alone* had a negative association with democracy and human rights — positive effects require combination with trials and/or amnesties.

**International Prosecutorial Tribunals.** Strongest at establishing historical fact and breaking denial (ICTY: 161 indictments; ~10,800 witnesses; documented Srebrenica facts beyond dispute). Weakest at delivering timely justice: ICC Kenya trials collapsed due to witness interference; ICC Sudan produced no arrest despite multiple warrants until the Kushayb conviction in 2025+. The finding that international tribunals "do not appear to contribute to reducing the recurrence of civil war" (https://sah.borca.ai/papers/146401203) coexists with the norm-building legacy. Most credible recent work suggests comprehensive (motivation-addressing) trials reduce recurrence, while selective opportunity-addressing prosecutions do not.

**Reparations Programs.** Most effective at the symbolic-acknowledgment function: Germany's €85.4 billion+ total and $1.4B annual payments, the U.S.'s $1.6B for Japanese Americans, converted state wrongdoing into officially accepted responsibility. The Japanese American case shows measurable "contagion" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11332238/). Limitations: cannot heal psychological or structural harm alone; South African case demonstrates how chronic implementation gaps transform reparations from remedy into renewed grievance.

**Lustration Policies.** Distinctive strength: cheap, administratively feasible, and — as survey experiments demonstrate — dismissal and confession variants increase trust in both government and tainted officials (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/662648). Strongest quantitative association with democratic consolidation (~30% higher democracy levels). Distinctive weakness: post-1989 European experience is unique to post-communist settings; cross-regional generalization limited. Long-running lustration raises ECHR concerns (*Vogt v. Germany*); the Polish Constitutional Tribunal's K 2/07 ruling demonstrated how late expansive vetting can be struck down as unconstitutional.

---

## 7. Cross-Modal Conclusions

**First**, no mechanism is sufficient in isolation. The empirical record consistently shows that combined approaches — truth commissions plus trials plus reparations, embedded within constitutional reform and human rights institutions — outperform single-mechanism strategies (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/61/3/690/4643613; https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/cjhr/2025/00000024/00000002/art00007). The TJDB finding that truth commissions alone show *negative* associations with democracy and rights is sobering — combination with trials and/or amnesties is empirically necessary.

**Second**, the *ranking* of officials prosecuted matters: low- and mid-level prosecutions correlate with reduced recurrence; top-elite prosecutions show weaker and more conditional effects (https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/dev4peace/transitional-justice-rule-law-and-conflict-recurrence). This suggests a paradox: the ICTY/ICC's symbolic power coexists with limited instrumental deterrent effect.

**Third**, mechanism effectiveness is highly context-dependent. International prosecution fails when states refuse cooperation (Sudan; ICC's enforcement gap, https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2013/3/25/the-enforcement-gap-how-the-international-criminal-court-failed-in-darfur). TRCs underperform when reparations are underfunded or excluded populations are large (South Africa's "closed list"). Lustration depends on the existence of a viable democratic core to absorb tainted personnel (Germany with FRG; Czech with civic dissidents; Poland with Solidarity networks).

**Fourth**, **victim-centering is the field's most underdeveloped operational dimension.** Kenya victims described the prosecution's withdrawal as a "betrayal"; CSVR research found South African victims felt the TRC "failed" them on amnesty and reparations despite public testimony's emotional power (https://csvr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2000/01/tellingitlikeitis-3.pdf). Reparations struggles in Canada and South Africa indicate that recommendations and resources must travel together.

**Fifth**, prevention of recurrence is best served by mechanisms that build enduring institutional counterweights — constitutional protections, independent judiciaries, human rights commissions — rather than one-off moments of accountability. The cross-national evidence indicates that the *motivation-addressing* purpose of mechanisms drives the durability effect, not their punitive content alone (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/61/3/690/4643613).

**Verdict on the three criteria:**
- **For serving victims:** comprehensive, prompt, administratively simple reparations — decoupled from criminal conviction — are the strongest mechanism (Germany, U.S. Japanese American redress), ideally paired with truth-telling that provides official recognition; the TRC-plus-package model (Canada) is the most promising architecture when material compensation is delivered upfront.
- **For enabling democratic transitions:** conditional-amnesty truth commissions (South Africa's model, despite implementation failures) and early, bounded, judicially reviewable lustration (Czech 1991, German unification-era Stasi vetting) show the strongest evidence; international tribunals' transition value is largely indirect via EU accession conditionality or norm entrepreneurship, not direct reconciliation.
- **For preventing recurrence:** motivation-addressing mechanisms (grievance-mitigating truth-telling, comprehensive reparations, structural reform) outperform opportunity-addressing ones (selective elite trials, exposure-only lustration), with truth commissions showing significant reductions in targeted mass killings per the SUNY study — but only when final reports and reform recommendations are actually implemented.

The single most important cross-cutting variable is **political will and implementation**. The German, U.S., Czech, and Canadian compensation successes share sustained, adequately funded execution; the South African, Kenyan, and Sudanese failures share the inverse. A TRC without funded reparations becomes a second victimization; a tribunal without state cooperation becomes symbolic theater; a reparations program without structural reform becomes palliative. The strongest lesson across all cases is that attention to victim-centered design, comprehensive reparations, and follow-through on recommended reforms is the indispensable variable distinguishing mechanisms that consolidate democratic transitions from those that, despite extensive documentation and costly processes, leave underlying structural causes of violence largely intact.

# Farm Management & Traceability Platform Selection for a 5,000-Farmer Coffee Cooperative (Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia)

## Headline Finding

Neither **Olam's AtSource** nor **Fairtrace** is a farm-management platform your cooperative can independently procure. They are **buyer-side or certification-system tools** that your cooperative must *integrate with*, not buy. For your actual farm-management needs, the defensible commercial choices are **Farmforce**, **KoltiTrace (Koltiva)**, **SourceTrace/DataGreen**, **Sirio (Nuup)**, **TerraTrac (TechnoServe)**, or **AgUnity**, layered with free Fairtrade infrastructure (Fairtrace + Plot Insights).

The consensus architecture across all sources is **two-layered**:
1. **Free certification/EUDR spine** — Fairtrace + Plot Insights (if Fairtrade-certified), fed by your farm platform.
2. **Paid operational farm-management platform** for farmer registry, GPS polygons, harvest/payment data, ICS forms.

---

## 1. What AtSource and Fairtrace Actually Are

### AtSource (ofi/Olam) — buyer-side, not procurable by cooperatives

AtSource is Olam Group's sustainability-intelligence platform launched in 2018, designed to give commercial buyers an "ESG view" of supply chains they source from (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-launches-atsource.html; https://www.atsource.io/atsource.html). Critically: it is **"open to ofi and Olam Group product supply chains"** — a cooperative cannot subscribe to it independently (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html). First-mile data is collected by **ofi's own enumerators** using the internal **OFIS Android app**, not by farmers (https://www.atsource.io/impact/does-your-sustainability-reporting-start-at-the-source.html; https://dvi-ke.fao.org/digital_solutions_details.php?id=120). Traceability runs "back to farmer-group level" in AtSourceV and to "individual farms/farmers" in AtSource+ when possible. AtSource is co-designed with Rainforest Alliance (e.g., the Sui River Forest Reserve project; the Living Income metric originated by RA) and tracks Fairtrade/4C premiums (https://www.atsource.io/dashboard.html; https://www.atsource.io/impact/revitalising-coffee-production.html). Pricing: "custom enterprise pricing model… public pricing is not disclosed" (https://netzerocompare.com/software/atsource).

**Verdict:** Do not budget for AtSource. It costs nothing to your cooperative but gives you no operational tool. If you sell through ofi/Olam, ask buyers what data they need and whether their enumerators will collect it — you still need your own platform for internal management, your other buyers, and certifications.

### Fairtrace + Plot Insights — mandatory Fairtrade infrastructure, not farm management

**Fairtrace** is FLOCERT's web-based transaction platform used by **~6,000 organisations reporting ~500,000 transactions/year**, recording volumes, Fairtrade Price, and Premium paid in a "report and verify" mutual-assurance model (https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/; https://flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf). It has **no farmer-facing component and no GPS mapping capability**.

**Plot Insights** is Fairtrade's companion geolocation/EUDR tool launched 2024, hosted in the Fairtrade Unify portal (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/Press-centre/fairtrade-digital-system-plot-insights-gives-fairtrade-cooperatives-an-eudr-readiness-edge.html). It accepts plot data as points (<4 ha) or polygons (≥4 ha) in .kml, GeoJSON, Shapefile, Excel, CSV at six decimal places, validates against **Satelligence satellite monitoring (Sentinel-1/2 + Landsat, 10 m, 81–93% accuracy)** (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf), and outputs EUDR-ready GeoJSON for the EU TRACES platform. **GeoLink API** now exchanges data with Fairtrace (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf). Fairtrade explicitly warns that trader-held geolocation is often inaccurate and cooperatives should own their plot data (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/news/heres-how-fairtrade-is-supporting-farmers-and-businesses-eudr).

**Languages:** English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, Vietnamese per Plot Insights guidance documents (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf).

**Cost:** **Free** for certified cocoa and coffee producer organisations (SPOs) (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf).

**Verdict:** If you are Fairtrade-certified, Fairtrace reporting is **mandatory**; Plot Insights is the cheapest path to EUDR-grade geolocation for Fairtrade members. Neither replaces your farm-management platform — your farm tool must produce clean geolocation that uploads into Plot Insights.

---

## 2. Real Candidates: Platform-by-Platform Comparison

### 2.1 Farmforce (Norway; ex-Syngenta Foundation) — strongest single-vendor certification fit

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Basic-phone usability | **Farmforce Connect** designed for "farmers new to smartphones, with limited digital skills, varying degrees of literacy," apps that "require little storage space… function on low-spec phones… synchronise only once a day" (https://www.klimaantropologen.no/farmforceconnect; https://farmforce.com/products/farmer-app/). Standard model: cooperative field staff run Android app; farmers receive SMS receipts and price/agronomy alerts (https://measict.weebly.com/uploads/3/2/4/3/3243215/farmforce-agextension-smartphonesms_computer-global.pdf). |
| GPS polygon mapping | Built-in polygon drawing linked to farmer ID; integrates Global Forest Watch; mapped **~4,550 ha of forest coffee and 4,500+ Ethiopian smallholders** in the Farm Africa / Norwegian Embassy / ECOM pilot (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/; https://farmforce.com/articles/brewing-sustainable-agtech-for-the-coffee-supply-chain/). |
| Certification modules | Explicitly supports **Organic, Fairtrade, Rainforest Alliance, GlobalGAP, FSMA** plus CLMRS and EUDR deforestation compliance (https://farmforce.com/; https://farmforce.com/solutions/deforestation-monitoring/certification-process/; https://agtecher.com/en/software/farmforce-digital-agricultural-supply-chain-solution/). Includes a "Certification Registry" tracking mapping status required for RA. |
| Multi-language | **English, Spanish, French, Portuguese** on the staff app (https://solevant.com/software/farmforce). Capterra lists 15 languages including Indonesian, French, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Portuguese, Thai, Vietnamese (https://www.capterra.ie/software/189458/farmforce). Amharic and Oromo are not in the published list, although deployments exist in 17+ countries including Indonesia and East Africa. |
| Offline | **"Bush-proof… works offline in most remote areas of the world"** — proven offline-first in Ethiopian forest-coffee zones with patchy 2G/3G (https://farmforce.com/articles/from-the-syngenta-foundation-to-the-world-the-story-of-farmforce/; https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/). |
| Cost | **NOK 330/year (~USD 31) per farmer** + implementation fee **NOK 55,000–220,000 (~USD 5,200–20,800)** (https://softwarefinder.com/facility-management-software/farmforce; https://www.getapp.ie/software/2071368/farmforce). For 5,000 farmers: **~USD 155,000/year + USD 5–21k implementation**. |

Scale: 1.4M farmers, 1.1M mapped fields, 32 countries, 27 crops (https://agritechobservatory.review.fao.org/en/farmforce).

### 2.2 KoltiTrace / Koltiva (Swiss-Indonesian) — lowest recurring cost, native in all three geographies

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Basic-phone usability | Field-agent model: FarmGate/FarmXension apps for trained cooperative staff; **$1/farmer/yr FarmCloud** gives farmers data access/notifications via mobile; chatbot for agronomic advice (https://www.koltiva.com/koltitrace; https://www.sustainable-supply-chains.org/fileadmin/INA/Erfolgsgeschichten/Kaffeeinnovationsfonds/Recipe_Books/Handbook_Origin_centered%20coffee_traceability.pdf). |
| GPS polygon mapping | Polygon mapping is core; validated **25,274 coffee farmer plots across Latin America including Colombia** (https://www.koltiva.com/post/koltiva-empowers-traceability-over-25000-coffee-farmers-across-americas); Adena Coffee case covers 1,900+ smallholders across 30 villages and 240 t/year with EUDR-aligned data (https://www.koltiva.com/post/deforestation-free-coffee-supply-chains-adena-coffee-koltiva-eudr-compliance-transparency). Gayo/Toraja highland case: 143.5 ha surveyed. |
| Certification modules | Explicitly positions KoltiTrace as complementary to "certifications such as Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade" plus EUDR; incorporates Cool Farm Tool for GHG (https://www.koltiva.com/post/koltiva-empowers-475-000-coffee-producers-worldwide-and-strengthens-indonesias-leadership-in-sustai). |
| Multi-language | Implied via 15 customer-success offices across Indonesia, Colombia, Ethiopia; **no published explicit language list** — confirm in writing (Bahasa Indonesia, Spanish, English/French expected). |
| Offline | "Digitizing producers and plot-level data collection, even in remote areas" implies offline capture, though offline sync is not explicitly documented in published materials (https://www.koltiva.com/post/deforestation-free-coffee-supply-chains-adena-coffee-koltiva-eudr-compliance-transparency). |
| Cost | **CoffeeTrace platform: $1,200/country/yr; FarmGate/FarmXension/FarmRetail apps: $120/user/yr; FarmCloud: $1/user/yr** (https://www.sustainable-supply-chains.org/...Handbook_Origin_centered_coffee_traceability.pdf). Field-agent scenario (50 staff users / 5,000 farmers across 3 countries): platform $3,600 + FarmGate $6,000 + FarmCloud $5,000 = **~$14,600/yr ≈ $2.92/farmer/yr**. Note: pricing source is a 2020 GIZ/INA Indonesian pilot handbook — current quotes may differ. |

Scale: 440K+ farmers, 17 countries, coffee in 22 countries (https://www.koltiva.com/post/koltiva-empowers-475-000-coffee-producers-worldwide-and-strengthens-indonesias-leadership-in-sustai).

### 2.3 SourceTrace / DataGreen (India; 26–37 countries)

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Basic-phone usability | Android-first app plus PDAs and POS; field-agent-facing; offers SMS and audio advisory ("advisory audio and text messages") (https://sourcetrace.com/main/). |
| GPS polygon mapping | Captures GPS coordinates at farmer registration; "farm perimeter plotting and area calculation using phone built-in GPS"; Coffee Board of India / Karnataka deployments (https://sourcetrace.com/farm-management/; https://sourcetrace.com/agricultural-value-chain/). |
| Certification modules | Built-in certification module for **Fair Trade and Organic**, plus internal certifications on Android; Coffee Innovation Fund reference pricing shows $1,200/country/yr + $120/user/yr + $1/farmer/yr (https://www.sustainable-supply-chains.org/...Handbook_Origin_centered_coffee_traceability.pdf; http://measict.weebly.com/uploads/3/2/4/3/3243215/sourcetrace-valuechain-smartphone-global.pdf). |
| Multi-language | Multi-country deployments; configurable per deployment; **no explicit published list**. |
| Offline | Both online and offline capture modes. |
| Cost | SaaS subscription **from USD 99/month** (Standard); field-agent scenario (50 users / 3 countries): ~$3,600 country fees + $6,000 user licences + $5,000 FarmCloud ≈ **$14,600/yr** (same structure as Koltiva per Coffee Innovation Fund handbook). |

### 2.4 Sirio (Nuup, Mexico/Central America) — strongest Latin-American coffee co-op option, IDB-funded

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Basic-phone usability | Co-designed with three coffee co-ops; "saves us time, and we no longer have to carry paper forms around" (Yochin Cooperative) (https://nuup.org/en/sirio-english/). |
| GPS polygon mapping | Full ICS module with plot geolocation, polygon and point capture, EUDR-ready (https://nuup.org/en/sirio-english/; https://www.ensambles.coffee/post/sirio-empowering-mexican-coffee-farmers). |
| Certification modules | Digital forms for **Organic, Fairtrade, and Rainforest Alliance** within the Internal Control System (https://nuup.org/en/sirio-english/). |
| Multi-language | Spanish primary; IDB-funded expansion to Mexico/Guatemala/Honduras. |
| Offline | **"Does not even require an internet connection to work"** — offline mobile app + cloud web console (https://www.ensambles.coffee/post/sirio-empowering-mexican-coffee-farmers). |
| Cost | Funded as a non-profit by IDB: **USD 960,000 grant, 41 organisations, ~14,392 producers as of 2025**; pricing for non-partner organisations not disclosed (https://www.iadb.org/en/project/RG-G1066). Likely very low cost for partner co-ops; not a primary fit for Ethiopian/Indonesian operations without expansion. |

### 2.5 TerraTrac (TechnoServe Labs) — free open-source Android capture app

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Basic-phone usability | Android-only; aimed at field buyers/factory managers, not farmers (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.technoserve.farmcollector). |
| GPS polygon mapping | Captures point (plots <4 ha) or polygon (≥4 ha); **partners with EUSPA for authenticated Galileo signals** — a spoof-proof GNSS differentiator for EU exposure (https://www.technoserve.org/tns-labs/terratrac-eudr-compliance/; https://www.technoserve.org/blog/eu-deforestation-regulation-mobile-app/). |
| Certification modules | EUDR-focused; designed to *feed* certification systems, not replace them. |
| Multi-language | Currently **French, Spanish, Amharic, Oromo**; Swahili coming soon — strong fit for Ethiopia and Latin America, weaker for Indonesia (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/paul-stewart-1165826_terratrac-activity-7214208074289475584-iPA8). Indonesian can be added via the open-source codebase. |
| Offline | **"Works offline and allows the user to download the list of plots in csv and geojson formats"** (https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile). |
| Cost | **Free, open-source (Apache-2.0 GitHub repo)** (https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile). |

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Basic-phone usability | Strongest design for low-literacy farmers — large distinct colorful icons, tested with illiterate farmers; offline peer-to-peer transactions via QR codes; each farmer holds a low-cost Android (~$54–75 Redmi 7A class) permanently identity-locked; **"replaces" feature phones with cheap Androids** (https://solve.mit.edu/solutions/32293; https://www.agunity.com/blog/experience-ethiopia-first-deployment). |
| GPS polygon mapping | Collects GPS data for EUDR; maps farmers — public material emphasises transactions over polygon QA tooling. |

| Multi-language | Local-language deployments (Amharic context in Ethiopia; Tok Pisin in PNG); no full language list. |
| Offline | **Fully offline transactions via QR; syncs when signal returns.** |

### 2.7 Other specialised platforms

- **Coffee Trace (Rwenzori Model)** — QR traceability + SCA grading + EUDR; 500+ verified farmers (https://coffeetrace.online/).
- **OriginTrace (Sysmera / CIRAD)** — offline-first Android, multilingual, published **99.9% valid GPS across 11,348 plots in East African deployments** (8,105 farmers, 9 co-ops); Ethiopia KMU deployment covers 12,700+ farmers, 15,300+ plots (https://origintrace.app/; https://www.sysmera.com/origintrace/).
- **AGnimble Trace** — purpose-built for coffee, GPS polygons + offline, GeoJSON-ready; 316+ farmers across 23 countries (https://agnimble.com/traceability/).
- **Beyco (Progreso / Solidaridad pilot)** — blockchain-backed, 7 Colombian coffee co-operatives for climate insetting, Scope 3, EUDR (https://www.solidaridadnetwork.org/news/from-bean-to-claim-how-farmer-owned-data-builds-trust-in-supply-chains/).
- **Chekkit (TRACE / IFAD Rwanda)** — Cardano-blockchain, GS1 QR codes, in-browser scanner (no install), used with Kopakaki Dutegure cooperative (https://chekkitapp.com/customers/ifad-rwanda-coffee-traceability).
- **Fairfood Trace** — blockchain-based, "easily accessible, even for smallholder farmers in low tech environments"; collectors **"can use the application without the internet"** with NFC-based farmer cards; first coffee user was Trabocca (https://fairfood.org/solutions-for-a-fair-supply-chain/trace-3/; https://fairfood.mintlify.app/introduction). Not a GIS mapping tool.

---

## 3. GPS Accuracy in Mountainous / Forested Coffee Terrain

The single most consistent finding: **standard smartphone GPS is the limiting factor, not the platform**. Consumer-grade phone GPS delivers **3–10 m horizontal accuracy** in clear sky; under shade and on slopes, accuracy degrades. A 2026 academic benchmark of mobile GNSS apps found a best-performing app at **~3.0 m RMSE** (acceptable fit-for-purpose ≤5 m in rural areas) (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12518-026-00785-0). Unassisted tablet GPS under tree canopy shows ~11–12% area error on average — acceptable for compliance but relevant if you use area data for yield or premium calculations (https://www.50x2030.org/sites/default/files/resources/documents/2026-05/IDU-cd6fedd9-8358-44d8-a677-06eb2dba3cb6.pdf).

**Practical field techniques** that apply to any platform: waypoint averaging (stand still 20–30 sec per vertex), mid-morning capture for better satellite geometry, wait for accuracy readout to stabilise, avoid tall shade canopy (Ethiopian forest coffee is the extreme case) (https://www.indonesia-coffee.com/en/articles/indonesian-coffee-eudr-compliance-2025-complete-guide-G5j8W_; https://plotvera.com/guides/eudr-smallholder-geolocation).

**Differentiation across platforms:**
- **TerraTrac** partners with the **EUSPA Galileo** programme for authenticated, spoof-proof geolocation — meaningful if your cooperative has any EU exposure (https://www.technoserve.org/blog/eu-deforestation-regulation-mobile-app/).
- **Plot Insights** adds a satellite-validation backstop (**Satelligence, 81–93% accuracy across South America, Africa, Asia, 10 m Sentinel resolution**) so imperfect farmer-collected GPS can be risk-checked after the fact (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf).
- **OriginTrace** publishes its own quality metric: **99.9% valid GPS across 11,348 East African plots** (https://www.sysmera.com/origintrace/).
- **Farmforce** has the strongest mountain-track-record: the Farm Africa / ECOM Ethiopia pilot mapped 4,550 ha of forest coffee — the EUDR-hard end of the spectrum (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/).

**Mandatory thresholds to encode in your choice:** EUDR accepts a single geolocation point for plots ≤4 ha; polygons are mandatory for plots >4 ha; six decimal places for both (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex-v12). RA goes further: group-certified small farms must have **35% of farms as polygons at the first certification audit and 100% by the second audit cycle**. Your platform must therefore support polygon capture from day one.

---

## 4. Certification Integration: What You Must Report Into

### Fairtrade
- **Fairtrace** is mandatory for all Fairtrade-certified organisations; it is the system in which volumes, Fairtrade Price, and Premium are recorded (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/07/SAM-FairtraceUserGuide-TR-19-en.pdf).
- **Plot Insights** satisfies Fairtrade Coffee Standard 3.1.6 and Cocoa 3.4.5 on geolocation (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf).
- ~900+ Fairtrade-certified cocoa and coffee cooperatives representing ~1M farmers; ~70% of Fairtrade coffee ends up in Europe, making EUDR readiness central (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/news/heres-how-fairtrade-is-supporting-farmers-and-businesses-eudr).

### Rainforest Alliance
- Certificate holders must upload geolocation (points and polygons, 6 decimals) to the **RA Certification Platform (RACP)** and report certified-volume transactions in **MultiTrace** (now migrating to a new RA traceability platform accessed via "MyRA") (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/multitrace-traceability-user-manual-guidance; https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/new-traceability-platform-everything-you-need-to-know).
- Since **16 June 2025**, **EUDR-aligned requirements (EUDR1 polygons ≥4 ha, EUDR2 six-decimal geolocation, corruption/fraud measures, fee/tax evidence) are integrated assessments for all coffee/cocoa farm certificate holders**, and an EUDR Data Sharing Policy governs sharing geolocation with buyers (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/eudr-data-sharing-policy).
- All RA buying/selling of certified volumes must be recorded in MultiTrace at the latest two weeks after quarter-end; first buyers must record the **Sustainability Differential (SD)** and **Sustainability Investments (SI)** separately (https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Full-Mutual-Recognition-and-Traceability-for-Coffee-February-2022.pdf). Traceability types: **Identity Preserved, Segregation, Mass Balance** (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/traceability-annex).
- **No gathered evidence shows native MultiTrace integrations with any third-party farm platform** — your cooperative will need to report into MultiTrace separately regardless of which farm tool you use.

### Platform certification matrix

| Platform | Fairtrade | Rainforest Alliance | Organic | EUDR / Geo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AtSource | Yes (4C/Fairtrade premiums tracked) | Yes (co-designed with RA on Sui River; Living Income metric from RA) | Yes | Yes — but buyer-side only |
| Fairtrace + Plot Insights | **Native** | No | No | **Native** (Feeds EU TRACES via GeoJSON) |
| Farmforce | Yes (explicit module) | Yes | Yes | Yes (GFW overlay) |
| KoltiTrace | Yes (complementary) | Yes (complementary) | Configurable | Yes |
| SourceTrace | Yes | Configurable | Yes | Yes |
| Sirio (Nuup) | Yes (ICS form) | Yes (ICS form) | Yes | Yes |
| TerraTrac | Indirect | Indirect | Indirect | **Primary purpose** |
| Cropin | Configurable | Configurable | Configurable | Yes (enterprise-tier; ~USD 50–250k/yr, likely beyond budget) |

---

## 5. Multi-Language Support — Evidence Quality

Best-documented: **Plot Insights** (EN, ES, PT, FR, **Indonesian**, VI — all three cooperative languages covered); **Farmforce** (15 languages per Capterra, including Spanish, Indonesian, French, Chinese, Hindi, Portuguese, Thai, Vietnamese — but no published Amharic/Oromo); **TerraTrac** (French, Spanish, **Amharic, Oromo**, Swahili coming).

**Confirmed gaps in evidence:** Koltiva, SourceTrace, AgUnity, Fairfood Trace have no published explicit language lists despite operational presence in your geographies. Obtain **written confirmation** of interface and support languages — including Amharic/Oromo for Ethiopia, Spanish for Colombia, Bahasa Indonesia for Indonesia — before contracting.

---

## 6. Offline Functionality

- **TerraTrac, Farmforce, Sirio, AgUnity, Fairfood Trace** — explicit offline-first architectures documented (https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile; https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/; https://www.ensambles.coffee/post/sirio-empowering-mexican-coffee-farmers; https://solve.mit.edu/solutions/32293; https://fairfood.mintlify.app/introduction).
- **Koltiva** — implied via "even in remote areas"; offline sync not explicitly documented.
- **Plot Insights / Fairtrace** — web-platform; not designed for offline capture. Cooperatives prepare shape files offline in tools like SW Maps, QField, or KoboCollect and upload.
- **AtSource** — cloud buyer dashboard; field enumeration offline through ofi-managed OFIS — outside your control.

---

## 7. Cost Analysis for 5,000 Farmers

| Platform | Per-farmer/user cost | Setup cost | **Annual cost for 5,000 farmers** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plot Insights + Fairtrace** | Free for certified SPOs | EUR 0 | **USD 0/yr** (mandatory if Fairtrade-certified) |
| **TerraTrac** | Free open-source | ~USD 5–10k Android devices/training | **USD 0 licence + ~USD 5–10k devices/training** |
| **Sirio (Nuup)** | Free for IDB-partner co-ops; undisclosed otherwise | TBD | Likely <USD 1/farmer/yr for partners (Latin American co-ops only) |
| **Farmforce** | NOK 330/yr (~USD 31) per farmer | NOK 55,000–220,000 (~USD 5.2k–20.8k) | **~USD 155,000/yr + USD 5–21k setup** |
| **Koltiva / KoltiTrace (field-agent)** | $1,200/country + $120/user + $1/farmer | One-time registration/training unquantified | ~$3,600 platform + $6,000 FarmGate (50 staff users) + $5,000 FarmCloud = **~$14,600/yr ≈ $2.92/farmer/yr** |
| **SourceTrace (field-agent)** | Same Koltiva pricing structure per Coffee Innovation Fund handbook | TBD | **~$14,600/yr** (same structure) |
| **Cropin** | Enterprise SaaS, six-figure USD | Per-deployment | **Likely USD 50k–250k+/yr** — beyond limited-budget reach |
| **AtSource** | Not for sale to co-ops | — | Not applicable |

**Caveat:** Koltiva/SourceTrace pricing is from a 2020 GIZ/INA Indonesian pilot handbook; current quotes may differ. Add device, SIM/data, training, and field-staff cost (1 officer per 300–700 farmers per Farmforce design assumption = roughly 7–17 staff per 5,000 farmers in cooperative in-house; ~50 staff if you include all extension workers across three countries) to any of the above.

---

## 8. Recommended Architecture for Your Cooperative

Given budget constraint, three-country footprint, basic-phone farmer base, mountainous terrain, and certification requirements:

1. **Adopt Plot Insights + Fairtrace immediately** if Fairtrade-certified (which is effectively a precondition to use them). Free, mandatory, covers geolocation and EUDR, multilingual including Indonesian/Spanish/French, with Amharic-/Oromo-friendly workflows when paired with TerraTrac.

2. **Use TerraTrac as the Android capture app** for enumerators. Free, open-source, EUSPA Galileo authentication, offline-first, Amharic/Oromo/Spanish already available; Indonesian can be added via the open-source codebase. Pairs with Plot Insights for EUDR submission.

3. **For operational farm management** (harvest collection, payments, ICS, certification forms), choose:
   - **Farmforce** (~USD 155k/yr for 5,000 farmers) — the only mature, off-the-shelf commercial option covering every required standard across all three countries, with the strongest Ethiopian mountain-track-record.
   - **KoltiTrace/Koltiva** (~$2.92/farmer/yr field-agent model) — if current prices hold, the lowest-cost commercial alternative with native presence in all three geographies; verify current pricing and offline sync in writing.
   - **Sirio (Nuup)** — preferable for the Colombian operations if the cooperative can join the Nuup/IDB ecosystem.

4. **Reserve AtSource for buyers** — not a tool you deploy independently. If a significant share of your volume flows through ofi/Olam, request access and accept that first-mile data is enumerated by ofi's own staff.

5. **Layer AgUnity** if low-literacy inclusion is a binding constraint and the cooperative can subsidise ~$54–75 Android handsets per farmer.

6. **Plan for dual RA reporting** — Rainforest Alliance transactions must be recorded in RA's MultiTrace regardless of which farm tool you use; budget staff time for this.

---

## 9. Critical Actions Before Contracting

1. **Field-validate GPS accuracy** on representative plots in each of the three countries with the actual Android model to be deployed.
2. **Obtain written confirmation** of interface and support languages including Amharic/Oromo, Bahasa Indonesia, Spanish.
3. **Confirm current-year pricing** for KoltiTrace (2020 handbook is dated), Farmforce (subscription still NOK 330/yr?), and Koltiva offline-sync architecture.
4. **Verify integration or manual export paths** into Rainforest Alliance's traceability platform (MultiTrace via RACP/MyRA) — no documented native third-party integration exists.
5. **Clarify the cooperative's Fairtrade certification status** — if not certified, Plot Insights/Fairtrace economics change materially (Plot Insights is currently free only for Fairtrade-certified SPOs).
6. **Budget separately** for devices (ruggedized Android ~$150–300 each), SIM/data plans, training, change management, and a field-staff layer of roughly **50–100 people** across three countries (1 agent per 50–100 farmers per the Coffee Innovation Fund field-agent model; 1:300–700 per Farmforce assumption).
7. **Clarify data sovereignty** under Indonesia's PDP law, Ethiopia's data protection regime, and Colombian Habeas Data rules, and confirm contractual terms on data sharing with buyers — Fairtrade's stance is that cooperative-owned plot data is preferable because trader-held data "may not be very accurate" (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/news/heres-how-fairtrade-is-supporting-farmers-and-businesses-eudr).
8. **Check national traceability integrations** (Ethiopia ECX traceability, Federación Nacional de Cafeteros platforms in Colombia, Indonesia e-STDB) — not surfaced in any panel evidence but materially relevant.

---

## Headline Cost Summary

For a 5,000-farmer cooperative on a limited budget: **license cost can be close to zero** by combining Plot Insights + Fairtrace (free, mandatory if Fairtrade-certified) with TerraTrac (free open-source) as the Android capture layer, plus Farmforce (~USD 155k/yr) or KoltiTrace field-agent deployment (~$15k/yr) as the operational backbone. Add ~USD 50k–100k/yr realistic budget for devices, SIM/data, training, and a field-staff layer, and the cooperative has a defensible, multi-country, EUDR- and certification-ready stack.

task.problem: Our cooperative of 5,000 smallholder coffee farmers in Colombia, Ethiopia, and Indonesia needs to select a farm management and traceability platform.
