- Premium Resources Ltd. 10-Q for Q1 2025 (period ended Mar 31, 2025): [SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/795800/000164117225010011/form10-q.htm).
- NexMetals Mining Corp. 10-Q for Q2 2025 (period ended Jun 30, 2025): [SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/795800/000149315225011913/form10-q.htm); [issuer Q2 MDA/PDF](https://nexmetalsmining.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/q2_2025_report_nexm_fs_mda.pdf).

- Share-consolidation news release, June 18, 2025: [SEC ex99-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/795800/000164117225016471/ex99-1.htm).
- 8-K and press release, December 2, 2025 (US$25M BCL milestone paid): [SEC 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/795800/000149315225025663/form8-k.htm); [Newsfile](https://www.newsfilecorp.com/release/276535/NexMetals-Secures-Title-to-Selebi-and-Selkirk-Assets-in-Botswana-Following-Completion-of-Milestone-Payment).

# Industrial Automation Market in Saudi Arabia (2015–2025): Market, Vision 2030 Drivers, Siemens/ABB Awards, and Practical Sales Implications

---

## Executive Summary

Saudi Arabia's industrial automation market sits at approximately **USD 2 billion in 2024–2025** (consensus across Data Bridge, Reports & Insights, IMARC), with forecast **CAGR of 7–10%** and the pure industrial-robotics sub-segment accelerating fastest at ~11.9% CAGR (IMARC). Robotics penetration is comparatively low — Saudi Arabia is **not formally tabulated in the IFR World Robotics country dataset**, with the best IFR-derived estimate at **~37.9 robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers** (Visual Capitalist citing IFR), versus a 2024 global average of 132–177 depending on methodology revision. Vision 2030 has converted into measurable vendor demand: ABB's Q4 2023 country orders rose **+171% YoY** ([ABB Q4 2023 Group presentation](https://library.e.abb.com/public/0834f841fe5a4829bd9ce21ad23d8f70/ABB-Q4-2023_Group%20presentation.pdf)). Siemens has visible named awards at NEOM (Port of NEOM crane automation; ENOWA water pipeline DCS); ABB's most visible flagship contracts are with **Red Sea Global** rather than NEOM.

---

## 1. Market Size, CAGR, and Robotics Penetration

### 1.1 Market Size (USD)

No single official Saudi government statistic exists for the industrial automation market; figures are reconstructed from commercial research houses. The consensus range for 2024–2025 is approximately **USD 1.99 B – 2.3 B**, depending on whether the taxonomy includes only core automation components or extends to smart-factory software and services:

| Source | Segment | Base value | Forecast | CAGR | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Data Bridge | Industrial automation (overall) | USD 1.99 B (2024) | USD 3.72 B (2032) | **10.40%** stated (recomputed endpoint ≈ 8.1%) | [source](https://www.databridgemarketresearch.com/nucleus/saudi-arabia-industrial-automation-market) |
| Reports & Insights | Manufacturing automation | USD 1.99 B (2025) | USD 4.41 B (2034) | **9.26%** | [source](https://www.reportsinsights.com/quants/research/manufacturing-automation-market/saudi-arabia) |
| IMARC | Industrial automation components | USD 2.3 B (2025) | USD 4.7 B (2034) | **8.18%** | [source](https://www.imarcgroup.com/saudi-arabia-industrial-automation-components-market) |
| IMARC | Smart factory automation | USD 1.005 B (2025) | USD 1.99 B (2034) | **7.89%** | [source](https://www.imarcgroup.com/saudi-arabia-smart-factory-automation-market) |
| IMARC | Industrial robotics only | USD 199.2 M (2025) | USD 548.8 M (2034) | **11.92%** | [source](https://www.imarcgroup.com/saudi-arabia-industrial-robotics-market) |
| Grand View Research | Industry 4.0 (incl. robotics, IIoT, AI) | USD 1.247 B (2023) | USD 4.663 B (2030) | **20.7%** | [source](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/horizon/outlook/industry-4-0-market/saudi-arabia) |
| Grand View Research | Process automation & instrumentation | USD 355.9 M (2024) | USD 630.5 M (2030) | **9.7%** | [source](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/horizon/outlook/process-automation-and-instrumentation-market/saudi-arabia) |
| 6Wresearch | Industrial automation (pre-2021 baseline) | n/a | n/a | **4.1%** (2020–26) | [source](https://www.6wresearch.com/industry-report/saudi-arabia-industrial-automation-market-2020-2026) |
| Mordor Intelligence | MEA industrial automation (Saudi = largest) | USD 5.28 B (2025) | USD 7.44 B (2030) | **7.10%** | [source](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/middle-east-and-africa-industrial-automation-market) |

**Internal-inconsistency note:** Data Bridge's stated 10.40% CAGR does not reconcile with its own endpoint values (recomputed CAGR from USD 1.99 B to USD 3.72 B over 8 years is ≈8.1%). Treat the 10.4% headline with caution.

**Quantitative reconciliation:** A conservative sales-rep takeaway is the Saudi industrial automation market is **USD 1.99–2.3 B in 2024/2025, growing at 7–10% CAGR, with industrial robotics as the fastest sub-segment (~11.9% CAGR)**. The 6Wresearch pre-2021 figure of 4.1% CAGR has been superseded by post-2022 acceleration tied to Vision 2030 program execution.

### 1.2 Robotics Penetration Rate (robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers)

**Key finding:** Saudi Arabia is **not formally included** in the IFR World Robotics country-level robot density dataset ([Roboradar24](https://roboradar24.com/country/saudi-arabia); [IFR WR 2024 data availability](https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Database_-_data_availability__WR_2023.pdf); [IFR WR 2026 data availability](https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Database_-_data_availability_WR2026.pdf)). Saudi data is reported inside an aggregated **Gulf Cooperation Council chapter** in IFR World Robotics 2026 ([WR 2026 Contents](https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Contents_WR_2026_-_Industrial_Robots.pdf)), which is paywalled.

**Best available estimates (third-party modeled, not IFR-measured):**
- **~37.9 robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers** (rank #42 globally) per [Visual Capitalist](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/the-growth-of-industrial-robots-by-country/), citing IFR + the 2025 AI Index
- **68 per 10,000 workers** per [Roboradar24](https://roboradar24.com/country/saudi-arabia) — flagged explicitly as a modeled estimate
- **120 per 10,000** cited via SDAIA by [worldmetrics.org](https://worldmetrics.org/saudi-arabia-industry-statistics/) — outlier, single-source

**Comparative benchmarks ([IFR WR 2025 Foreword](https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Foreword_WR_2025_Industrial_Robots.pdf); [IFR Press Release](https://ifr.org/ifr-press-releases/news/global-robot-demand-in-factories-doubles-over-10-years)):**
- Global average: **177 robots per 10,000 (2024, pre-revision methodology)**; revised methodology drops world average to 132
- Korea: 1,220; Singapore: 818; China: 567; Germany: 449; Japan: 446
- UAE peer: 142 (Roboradar24 ranking — [source](https://roboradar24.com/rankings/robot-density))

**Industrial robot trade flow ([IndexBox](https://www.indexbox.io/search/industrial-robot-price-saudi-arabia/); [IndexBox MENA overview](https://www.indexbox.io/blog/industrial-robot-middle-east-market-overview-2024-5/)):**
- Saudi Arabia imported approximately **1,300 industrial robot units in 2023** (~USD 33 million), +13% YoY; import CAGR 2010–2023 ≈ 49%
- MENA industrial robot imports totaled **USD 262 million in 2024**; Saudi Arabia accounts for ~75% of MENA robot consumption (~29K units) and ~88% of regional production (~25K units)

**Manufacturing employment scale:** GASTAT reported the Saudi manufacturing workforce at **1,341,920 in Q2 2024** ([Gulf Migration reproduction of GASTAT](https://gulfmigration.grc.net/saudi-arabia-employed-population-aged-15-and-above-by-nationality-saudi-non-saudi-sex-and-main-group-of-economic-activities-q2-2024/?print=pdf)). The Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources (MIM) reported **9,991 operating factories employing ~980,000 workers** with ~SAR 966 B invested by Q4 2024 ([Argaam, Dec 2024](https://www.argaam.com/en/article/articledetail/id/1827405)). At 37.9 robots per 10,000 workers × 1,341,920 manufacturing employees, implied operational stock is on the order of **~5,090 robots** — order-of-magnitude only.

**Implied stock estimate** from actual Saudi robot imports (~1,300 units/year from 2023, growing) and a 10–15 year installation history suggests the operational stock is plausibly in the **low-to-mid five figures**, consistent with the 37.9/10K figure.

## 2. How Saudi Vision 2030 Has Driven Demand for Robotics

### 2.1 National Industrial Development and Logistics Program (NIDLP)

Launched in 2019 as one of Vision 2030's executive "Realization Programs," NIDLP covers Industry, Mining, Energy, and Logistics and designates the **Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR)** and **Local Content** as its two enabling focus areas ([NIDLP Delivery Plan 2021–2025, p. 7](https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/bsan2azp/2021-2025-national-industrial-development-and-logistics-program-delivery-plan-en.pdf)).

- **Investment target:** NIDLP seeks approximately **USD 427 billion in cumulative investment by 2030** across the four sectors ([6Wresearch citing NIDLP](https://www.6wresearch.com/industry-report/saudi-arabia-industrial-automation-market-2020-2026); [Research and Markets](https://www.researchandmarkets.com/reports/5017942/saudi-arabia-industrial-automation-market-2020))
- **Industry 4.0 target:** "5 [4IR] Centers launched by 2025" ([Vision 2030 NIDLP page](https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/en/explore/programs/national-industrial-development-and-logistics-program))
- **Execution track record:**
  - 2022 Annual Report: SAR 435 B (+38% YoY) non-oil sector exports, 266,000 new jobs ([NIDLP 2022 Report](https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/ol2ngw4q/ndlp-report-2022-en.pdf))
  - 2023 Annual Report: **87% execution rate** ([NIDLP 2023 Report](https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/2o1mbfnn/nidlp-2023-annual-report-eng.pdf))
  - 2024 Annual Report: **163 of 284 initiatives completed (57%)** ([NIDLP 2024 Annual Report](https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/uvknp4di/nidlp_annual_report-2024_-en.pdf))
  - 2025 Annual Report: **91.9% execution rate** against 2021–2025 targets; 93% of initiatives completed or progressing ([NIDLP 2025 Annual Report](https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/yomoyk4o/nidlp-annualreport-2025-en.pdf))
  - Q3 2024: SAR 433 B (USD 115.3 B) NIDLP-sector GDP, +2.4% YoY; 13 of 23 targets met ([Arab News, Oct 2024](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2584658/%7B%7B))

### 2.2 National Industrial Strategy (NIS) — October 2022

Launched by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in October 2022. Headline targets ([The National, Oct 2022](https://www.thenationalnews.com/business/economy/2022/10/19/saudi-arabia-launches-national-industry-strategy-that-aims-to-triple-output-to-149bn/); [NIS document PDF mirror](https://engine.strategicgears.com/files/Saudi_Arabias_National_Strategy_for_Industry_EN.pdf); [Aawsat, MIM minister statement](https://english.aawsat.com/home/article/3953836/saudi-arabia-seeks-double-exports-raise-number-factories-36000-2035)):

- **Triple industrial output** by 2030
- Industrial exports target: **~SAR 557 B (USD 148.5 B)** by 2030
- **800 investment opportunities worth ~SAR 1 trillion (USD 266.6 B)** for sustainable economic returns by 2030
- Factory count: increase to **36,000 by 2035** (baseline ~9,991–12,000)
- **SAR 1.3 trillion (~USD 345.9 B)** of total additional industrial investment
- Industrial GDP nearly tripled; high-tech exports sextupled, focused on 12 sub-sectors
- In May 2023, MIM identified the **first 50 priority industrial opportunities worth USD 25.6 billion** ([The National, May 2023](https://www.thenationalnews.com/business/economy/2023/05/02/saudi-arabia-identifies-50-industrial-opportunities-worth-256bn/)). Minister AlKhorayef specifically referenced the **Future Factories Programme** as the automation lever.

### 2.3 Future Factories Initiative (Tanafusiya) — Flagship Automation Policy

Operated jointly by the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources (MIM) and the Saudi Industrial Development Fund (SIDF):

- **Goal:** Transform **4,000 traditional factories into smart (Industry 4.0) factories** ([my.gov.sa service page](https://my.gov.sa/en/services/251928); [ARRC report](https://arrc-sa.com/media-center/reports/6a6000d505aa2fec2f431c5c))
- **Tanafusiya Accelerator financial incentives:** up to **25% of project cost in non-dilutive incentives** ([SIDF Tanafusiya page](https://sidf.gov.sa/en/ServicesforInvestors/ISSI/Pages/Tanafusiya-Accelerator.aspx))
- **SIDF loan terms:** financing up to **75% of project cost**, grace period up to **24 months**, minimum **7-year tenor**, fast-track approval within **8 weeks**
- **Future Factories Main Digitization Track** subsidizes digitization of procedures, planning, communications, production line control, material handling ([MIM Future Factories page](https://www.mim.gov.sa/en/initiatives-programs/industrial-sector-initiatives/industrial-sector-support-initiative/Future-Factories-Initiative-The-Main-Digitization-Track))
- **SIRI Framework:** the program uses the global **Smart Industry Readiness Index** to assess factory readiness ([ARRC report](https://arrc-sa.com/media-center/reports/6a6000d505aa2fec2f431c5c))
- **Promising Factories Initiative:** soft loans up to **50% of project cost, 10-year tenor, 24-month grace, 20% advance disbursement** ([SIDF ISSI announcement](https://www.sidf.gov.sa/News/SIDF-Announces-Its-Financing-Incentives-as-Part-of-ISSI))

### 2.4 Localization, RHQ, and NEOM Future Factories

- **Regional Headquarters (RHQ) Program:** joint initiative of the Ministry of Investment and the Royal Commission for Riyadh City; ABB licensed its Saudi RHQ in August 2023 ([Logistics Middle East](https://www.logisticsmiddleeast.com/logistics/abb-rhq-program))
- **Special Economic Zones:** four SEZs inaugurated May 2023 (Jazan, Ras Al-Khair, KACST Cloud Computing, KAEC) create localization requirements for multinationals
- **NEOM Future Factories:** in December 2022, MIM, Modon, and NEOM signed an agreement supporting NEOM's **Future Factories** advanced-manufacturing program — a direct policy hook for robotics vendors
- **Demand evidence:** ABB's Q4 2023 Group presentation showed **Saudi Arabia orders +171% YoY** ([ABB Q4 2023 Group presentation](https://library.e.abb.com/public/0834f841fe5a4829bd9ce21ad23d8f70/ABB-Q4-2023_Group%20presentation.pdf))

### 2.5 Giga-Project Demand Pull

- **NEOM-Oxagon:** industrial city launched November 2021 ([Vision 2030 Oxagon](https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/en/explore/projects/oxagon); [Data Center Dynamics, Nov 2021](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/neom-announces-oxagon-floating-industrial-district-that-will-house-data-center/))
- **Red Sea Global:** 28,000 km² tourism development, opening 2030; ACWA-led consortium financial close Feb 2022 at **USD 1.302 billion** for utilities PPP ([Aawsat, Feb 2022](https://english.aawsat.com/home/article/3494076/acwa-power-led-consortium-reaches-financial-close-1302-billion-red-sea-project))
- **Qiddiya, AMAALA, ROSHN, KAEC** each generate greenfield automation demand
- Local content / IKTVA requirements push manufacturers to install domestic automation to qualify for government and PIF procurement

## 4. Three Practical Implications for a Sales Rep Targeting Manufacturing in Saudi Arabia

### Implication 1 — Lead with Future Factories / Tanafusiya Funding Mechanics, Not Just Product Specs

The buyer's **capex hurdle is being directly subsidized**. With **Tanafusiya covering up to 25% of project cost** in non-dilutive incentives ([SIDF Tanafusiya](https://sidf.gov.sa/en/ServicesforInvestors/ISSI/Pages/Tanafusiya-Accelerator.aspx)), SIDF loans of **up to 75% of project cost at 7+ year tenor and 24-month grace**, and the **Main Digitization Track** subsidizing baseline digital control ([MIM Future Factories](https://www.mim.gov.sa/en/initiatives-programs/industrial-sector-initiatives/industrial-sector-support-initiative/Future-Factories-Initiative-The-Main-Digitization-Track)), the effective net cost to a qualifying buyer is materially lower than list price.

**Action:** Open every manufacturing account conversation with a **1-page Tanafusiya eligibility pre-check** (Industry 4.0 / energy efficiency technologies only; SIRI maturity assessment; SAR 100 M cap on Promising Factories path). Partner with a SIDF-registered consultant for joint account planning. Target the **~9,991 existing factories** ([Argaam, Dec 2024](https://www.argaam.com/en/article/articledetail/id/1827405)) earmarked for modernization, and the **~26,000 new factories planned by 2035** to reach the 36,000 target. Reframe the offer around **"net-cost-to-buyer"** rather than list price.

### Implication 2 — Bundle Around the Giga-Project Industrial Anchors (Oxagon, NEOM, Red Sea Global)

NEOM-Oxagon is being built as a fully automated industrial port-and-logistics hub; Siemens has already secured **PCS 7 automation on the NEOM water transmission pipelines** ([Arab News, Sep 14, 2023](https://www.arabnews.com/business/siemens-inks-deals-with-several-saudi-companies-to-boost-industrial-digitalization-2373471)) and **crane-automation components with Mevea at Port of NEOM** ([Mevea, Jul 2024](https://www.mevea.com/news-events/news/siemens-integrates-meveas-digital-twin-technology-in-automated-cranes-for-port-of-neom-saudi-arabia/)). ABB has **Red Sea Global** smart-energy + EVCI ([ABB News, Dec 2021](https://new.abb.com/news/detail/85573/abb-powers-red-sea-tourism-project-with-smart-energy-technology); [ABB EVCI](https://new.abb.com/news/detail/123357/sustainable-tourism-and-emobility-abbs-evci-at-the-red-sea-amaala-destinations-in-saudi-arabia)).

**Action:** **Tier-1 opportunity** — position as a **Tier-2 automation supplier** into the OEM/EPC ecosystem already on site: **ZPMC** (cranes at Port of NEOM); **Mutlaq Al Ghowairi Co.** (civil/ME on NEOM water pipelines); **Air Products + thyssenkrupp** (NEOM green hydrogen EPC, USD 6.7 B + 2 GW electrolysis); **ACWA Power** (Red Sea utilities PPP, USD 1.302 B financial close); **Hitachi Energy** (NEOM HVDC transmission). Track MEED / Arab News / TradeArabia project-tracking feeds weekly; pre-qualify via local EPC partners (SSEM, Rawafid Industrial, Advanced Water Technology, SETE, Al Fatah). The fact that **9 bidders** competed for the NEOM Gayal water transmission contract in 2022 ([Arab News, Oct 14, 2022](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2181086/%7B%7B)) confirms the funnel is competitive.

### Implication 3 — Differentiate on Service Localization (IKTVA) and Digital-Twin Capabilities

Vision 2030 mandates local content (IKTVA) and in some cases in-Kingdom manufacturing. ABB's Red Sea EVCI explicitly includes **locally manufacturing EV charging pedestals** ([ABB EVCI](https://new.abb.com/news/detail/123357/sustainable-tourism-and-emobility-abbs-evci-at-the-red-sea-amaala-destinations-in-saudi-arabia)). ABB has documented milestones in Saudi Arabia since 1986 (Riyadh factory), 1993 (first local mobile substation), 2015 (Dammam HV GIS factory), and the **2022 Process Automation Dammam factory inaugurated with Saudi Aramco** ([ABB Saudi Arabia timeline](https://new.abb.com/news/detail/47127/how-abb-technology-leadership-provides-solutions-for-saudia-arabias-developing-economy); [ABB Story](https://www.abb.com/global/en/company/stories/saudi-arabia-energy-industries)). ABB licensed its Saudi RHQ in August 2023 ([Logistics Middle East](https://www.logisticsmiddleeast.com/logistics/abb-rhq-program)). Siemens has parallel local depth (Dammam Hub expansion; SIBS subsidiary).

**Action:** Lead the value proposition with: **(a) local service hubs** (Dammam, Riyadh, Jeddah, NEOM site offices); **(b) local-content / IKTVA scoring** (Saudi-employed engineers, locally assembled cabinets, in-KSA training programs); and **(c) digital-twin and simulation capabilities** (Siemens-Mevea at Port of NEOM is a proof point — [Mevea, Jul 2024](https://www.mevea.com/news-events/news/siemens-integrates-meveas-digital-twin-technology-in-automated-cranes-for-port-of-neom-saudi-arabia/)). For a sales rep without an incumbent NEOM/Red Sea contract, the most defensible niche is **brownfield Industry 4.0 retrofits of the existing ~9,991-factory base**, where local presence matters more than Giga-Project references and where Tanafusiya funding lowers the capex hurdle.

---

## 5. Caveats and Source Uncertainty

1. **Robot density is not IFR-measured** for Saudi Arabia. The 37.9, 68, and 120 figures are derived/third-party estimates, not primary IFR country tables ([IFR WR 2024 data availability](https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Database_-_data_availability__WR_2023.pdf)). The 2024 IFR methodology revision makes historical Saudi density comparisons non-comparable ([manufacturing-metrics.org](https://manufacturing-metrics.org/en/robot-density-digital-adoption-by-country/))
2. **Market sizing varies by 6–7×** across research firms depending on taxonomy. Conservative rep should cite **USD 1.0–2.3 B (2024–2025) growing at 7–12% CAGR**
3. **ABB NEOM-specific contracts were not identified** in publicly available sources; ABB's giga-project visibility is concentrated at Red Sea Global
4. **Contract values for most Saudi Vision-2030-flagship automation awards are not publicly disclosed** by Siemens, ABB, or NEOM; the ~€53.4 M Siemens B2S attribution (Panel 2) is not independently verified
5. **Data Bridge's stated 10.4% CAGR** does not reconcile with its endpoint values (recomputed ≈ 8.1%); treat with caution

---

# New Zealand Construction Metalworks (Structural Steel Fabrication) Market – 2024

**Structural scope note:** This report covers structural/construction steel fabrication only. Reinforcing steel (rebar) is noted where relevant but is largely separate from the structural-steel industry statistics cited. Manufacturing of raw steel by New Zealand Steel / Pacific Steel (the only local producers) is referenced as a supply input but is not itself the "fabrication" market.

---

## (a) Market Size and Growth, 2018–2024

### Official statistics – Stats NZ / MBIE
The closest official classifications available are:
- **ANZSIC C22 – Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing** (GDP contribution)
- **Combined C21 + C22 – Metal Product Manufacturing** (sales from the Economic Survey of Manufacturing)

**Sales of Metal Product Manufacturing (C21+C22), quarterly, current prices (NZD millions), Stats NZ / Figure.NZ**

| Year | Annual aggregate (sum of 4 quarters, NZD millions) |
|---|---|
| 2018 | ~11,141 (Q1 2,520 + Q2 2,832 + Q3 2,928 + Q4 2,861) |
| 2019 | ~11,472 |
| 2020 | ~11,930 |
| 2021 | ~13,579 |
| 2022 | ~14,968 (peak quarter Q3 2022 = $3,937m) |
| 2023 | ~14,511 |
| 2024 | ~13,333 (Q1 3,166 + Q2 3,545 + Q3 3,398 + Q4 3,225) |

Source: Stats NZ, Economic Survey of Manufacturing, retrieved via Figure.NZ (https://figure.nz/chart/hbDmsIotoa3duUzT-Dwlp00904TYKse2n). These figures include primary metal forming plus all fabricated metal, so they over-state the structural steel fabrication subset.

**GDP(I) contribution of Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing (C22) – chained/nominal, Stats NZ national accounts 1992–2024**, available at https://figure.nz/chart/Ca2YJ0fZPUM3k0NR-sadrd3NXQ6Ox6wTk. The series shows a recovered trajectory after the 2008–09 GFC dip, with growth resuming into 2024.

### Industry analyst estimates – IBISWorld
IBISWorld (most recent release January 2026, see https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/industry/structural-steel-fabricating/235/) reports the **Structural Steel Fabricating in New Zealand** market at **NZ$1.8 billion in 2026**, with a 2021–2026 CAGR of **+2.1%**. The parent sector "Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing in New Zealand" was estimated at **NZ$1.5 billion in 2024, down 7.4% year-on-year** (https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/market-size/fabricated-metal-product-manufacturing/247/).

Note: IBISWorld's $1.8bn and Stats NZ's C22 figures use substantially different scopes; treat as separate series rather than reconciling them directly.

Steel Construction New Zealand's quarterly "Industry Updates" (https://scnz.org/) consistently report (figures are rolling 12-month/quarterly snapshots, repeated across the March, June and September 2023 updates):

- **Employment**: ~5,000 workers in the structural steel sector
- **Market share of structural steel in multi-storey construction**: ~50% nationally; >80% in Christchurch (versus near-zero pre-2010 Canterbury earthquakes)
- **SFC (Steel Fabrication Certification) participation**: 57 fabricators representing 92.5% of annual output (mid-2023); 65 fabricators in the September 2023 update

Sources:
- SCNZ Industry Update March 2023 (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/SCNZ-IU-Mar-23.pdf)
- SCNZ Industry Update June 2023 (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/SCNZ_IU_JUN2023-Web.pdf)

### Distributor volumes – Steel & Tube Holdings (NZX:STU)
Steel & Tube is NZ's largest steel distributor (not a fabricator, but indicative of total market volume):
- FY23 revenue NZ$589.1m (FY22 NZ$599.1m, -1.7%); volumes **146,409 tonnes** (-12.4% YoY)

- Total Metal Product Mfg (C21+C22) sales rose from **~$11.1bn (2018)** to a peak of **~$15.0bn (2022)**, then eased to **~$13.3bn (2024)** – a 2024-on-2018 CAGR of **roughly +3.1%** by my calculation using the Stats NZ quarterly aggregate above.
- Structural steel sector (sub-sector only): effective per-tonne revenue implied from ~100,000 t output at estimated sector revenue of NZ$1.5–1.8bn → **roughly $15,000–18,000 per tonne** including value-added fabrication margin on top of raw steel cost.
- Tonnage output has been **roughly flat at ~100,000 t/yr** through 2018–2024 per SCNZ, while capacity was expanded from ~100,000 t to ~150,000 t installed (driving the spare-capacity headage visible in the SCNZ surveys).
- Employment in the structural steel sector is reported by SCNZ at **~5,000 workers** and has not materially shifted in this window.

Caveat: SCNZ publishes quarterly tonnage updates only from 2022 onward in the publicly available Industry Updates I could retrieve; the 2018–2021 tonnage is implied from the stable ~100,000 t/yr descriptor carried across multiple later issues.

---

## (c) NZ Import Tariffs on Raw Steel (HS 7207–7216) and Margin Impact

The applicable duties on the Working Tariff Document of New Zealand (NZ Customs, https://www.customs.govt.nz/) for representative sub-headings used by the structural-steel sector (most-favoured-nation rates are reported by WCO-aligned NZ Customs; FTAs override these for qualifying origins):

| HS Code | Description (excerpt) | NZ MFN General Duty (2024–2026 reprint) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7208.10 | Flat-rolled, in coils, hot-rolled with patterns in relief | **5%** | https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7208-10/ (verified against NZ Customs Working Tariff Document Chapter 72, https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/it3lql10/introduction.pdf) |
| 7216.10–7216.22 | Angles, shapes and sections, hot-rolled L/T/I/H | **0%** on 7216.22 (T sections <80 mm), **2.5%** on 7216.21 (L sections <80 mm) | https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7216-22/ ; https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7216-21/ |
| 7216.31-7216.40 | U/I/H sections and other shapes | Generally **0–5%** depending on item | NZ Customs Working Tariff, Chapter 72 (current reprint) |

**Effective duty exposure**
- NZ has eliminated or reduced MFN duties through FTAs with most major steel-supplying countries (CPTPP – including Japan, Korea, Canada, Mexico, Vietnam; AANZFTA – including ASEAN; NZ-China FTA; NZ-Korea FTA; NZ-UK FTA; NZ-EU FTA – EU duties on structural steel and inputs largely duty-free per https://www.mfat.govt.nz/assets/Trade-agreements/EU-NZ-FTA/Annexes/Appendix-2-A-2-Tariff-Schedule-of-New-Zealand.pdf).
- For many of the largest origins (China, Korea, Japan) sections entering under HS 7216 attract **0%** MFN/ FTA duty.
- Flat-rolled feedstock (HS 7208) remains the most exposed line at 5% MFN where FTA preference is not claimed, but volumes from FTA partners and the only local producer (NZ Steel / Pacific Steel) significantly reduce the realised rate.
- A 5% MFN duty on imported plate/coil equates to roughly NZ$75–110/t on a ~$1,500–2,200/t landed raw steel price – a **3–5%** effective cost wedge over domestic supply, easily absorbed in fabrication margin when fabrication adds another $4,000–8,000/t of value-add at multi-storey prices.

### Customs import data – HS 7208, 7211, 7216 (2020–2024)
NZ Customs, in response to an OIA request (https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf, data extracted 2 September 2025), reported cleared import entries 2020–2024. Top origins of HS 7208 (flat-rolled, hot-rolled) include Australia, China, Indonesia, Japan and Korea. Combined HS 7208 + 7211 + 7216 imports are a multi-hundred-thousand-tonne flow annually, dwarfing NZ Steel's ~700,000 t/yr raw output and confirming NZ's reliance on imported feedstock and finished sections.

### Margin impact conclusion
For fabricators, **raw steel tariffs are a low-impact variable** of margin: (i) FTA preference eliminates most headline duties; (ii) raw steel is 35–55% of project cost and is contractually passed through to the client in most NZ construction contracts; and (iii) the much larger margin driver is fabrication labour, capacity utilisation, and steel-mill pricing volatility (e.g., Steel & Tube's FY23 commentary that "elevated pricing from steel mills almost offset[ting] softer volumes" – FY23 annual report). Greater risk lies in **non-tariff barriers** (Greenstar/EPD requirements, decarbonisation credentials) than in tariffs.

---

## (d) Three Major Infrastructure Projects with Steel Demand

### 1. City Rail Link (CRL), Auckland
- **Scope:** 3.45 km twin-bore underground rail tunnels linking Waitematā (Britomart) and Maungawhau (Mt Eden), with new Te Waihorotiu (Aotea) and Karanga-a-Hape stations (FDG NZ case study, 13 Jan 2026, https://www.linkedin.com/posts/fasteners-direct-global-ltd_fdg-project-case-study-city-rail-link-activity-7416916978277347328-SqND).
- **Steel tonnage:** **29,595 tonnes** of steel across the CRL structures (per SESOC 2023 conference paper, https://www.sesoc.org.nz/static/Documents/Conference/2023/SESOC2023-0043-Page-43-98-Page-Ethan-43-98-Page-Ethan.pdf).
- **Reinforcing steel:** **~25,000 tonnes** of locally manufactured reinforcing bar over a 3–4 year period, supplied by Pacific Steel / NZ Steel in Otahuhu (https://www.nzsteel.co.nz/news-and-media/local-steel-for-aucklands-city-rail-link/) – plus 1,500 tonnes of epoxy-coated reinforcing bar supplied by Steel & Tube (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/steel-and-tube_city-rail-link-crl-official-site-activity-6597992154012979200-PjhH, 6 Nov 2019).
- **Concrete:** 185,000 m³
- **Completion:** **2026** per FDG NZ's case study.
- **Total cost:** NZ$5.5 bn+ (project context; multiple public sources).

### 2. Te Ara o Te Ata – Mt Messenger Bypass, Taranaki (SH3)
- **Scope:** 6 km bypass of the steep Mt Messenger section of SH3 in North Taranaki; **two bridges (~30 m and ~125 m) plus a 235 m tunnel** (ConsultANZ, 16 April 2024, https://www.consultanz.com.au/list-major-infrastructure-projects-new-zealand-2021/).
- **Estimated value:** **NZ$280 million**.
- **Construction period:** under way; expected completion **2027**.
- **Mt Messenger Alliance:** Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency, Downer, **HEB Construction** (which has in-house fabrication via HEB Structures), Tonkin & Taylor, WSP.
- **Steel demand:** not officially tonnage-disclosed but the two bridges alone (125 m main span × ~30 m deck × typical 250–400 kg/m²) imply **roughly 1,500–2,500 tonnes of structural steel** for the bridge superstructures (bridge fabricators include Eastbridge-style heavy-steel specialists; the Karapiro Viaduct of comparable size on the Waikato Expressway used 1,300 t supplied by Eastbridge alone, per https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU1403/S00881/napier-firm-wins-waikato-expressway-steel-bridge-contract.htm, 26 March 2014).

### 3. National Infrastructure Pipeline – Context for Forward Steel Demand
Te Waihanga / NZ Infrastructure Commission National Infrastructure Pipeline (March 2024 snapshot, https://media.umbraco.io/te-waihanga-30-year-strategy/1oukkaqh/pipeline-snapshot-march-2024.pdf; December 2024 snapshot https://media.umbraco.io/te-waihanga-30-year-strategy/bysgbmlz/pipeline-snapshot-december-2024.pdf):

- **Total project value (March 2024):** **NZ$121.2 billion** (up 11.7% from NZ$108.5bn at Dec 2023).
- **$44 billion under construction** at March 2024.
- **Dec 2024 update:** funded/confirmed projects alone **NZ$107.9 bn**; combined (funded + unfunded) **NZ$204 bn** across **over 7,600 projects** from **147 providers**.
- **Forecast spend:** NZ$12.1 bn in 2024; NZ$11.6 bn in 2025.
- **Composition (March 2024 snapshot):** Transport NZ$61.9 bn; Energy NZ$20.6 bn; Community facilities NZ$7.5 bn; Housing NZ$5.6 bn; Health NZ$6.3 bn; Water NZ$6.6 bn.

Major named "Roads of National Significance" and major projects within this pipeline (NZTA SHIP 2024–34, https://nzta.govt.nz/assets/resources/state-highway-investment-proposal-2024-34/state-highway-investment-proposal-2024-34.pdf) include Whangārei–Port Marsden, Alternative to Brynderwyns, Warkworth–Wellsford, SH1 Ōtaki to North of Levin, and a second Waitematā Harbour Connection. Each harbours significant bridge work. The single-largest structural steel-intensive urban item is the East West Link (Auckland, ~NZ$1.85bn) per ConsultANZ (16 April 2024).

---

## (e) Top 3 Strategic Risks and Opportunities for Fabricators

### RISK 1 – Tariff exposure and raw-steel import dependency
- NZ has a single integrated flat-steel producer (NZ Steel / BlueScope at Glenbrook) and a single rebar producer (Pacific Steel). All other sections, plate and structural feed are imported.
- The Customs OIA release (https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf) shows significant import flows of HS 7208, 7211 and 7216 across 2020–2024 from China, Indonesia, Japan, Korea and Australia.
- Headline MFN duties are 5% (HS 7208) and 0–2.5% (HS 7216) – generally low, but **FTA preference erosion risk** is real: ongoing CPTPP/EU FTA reviews and any future NZ-US bilateral negotiations could shift the matrix. A 5% duty increase would translate to NZ$75–100/t on imported feedstock, with pass-through risk to fabricators if contract structures do not allow.

### RISK 2 – Demand-cycle volatility and structural over-capacity
- SCNZ's September 2023 update recorded **41% spare capacity** at 150,000 t installed potential vs. ~100,000 t actual output (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf).
- Steel & Tube's FY23 result – volumes down 12.4% and NPAT -43.7% YoY (https://www.nzx.com/announcements/416642) – confirms softness in the broader steel demand cycle into 2023.
- 2024 Q1–Q4 metal-product-manufacturing sales averaged $3,333m vs. $3,659m in 2023, a ~9% decline (Stats NZ/Figure.NZ), indicating the contraction extended into 2024.

### RISK 3 – Decarbonisation, embodied-carbon and procurement-quality regulation
- Construction-sector embodied-carbon disclosure (ESR / MfE whole-of-life carbon rules) is tightening. The SESOC 2023 paper on CRL explicitly attributes **40,234 tCO₂e** of embodied carbon to the CRL's 29,595 t of steel – a metric now used in tender evaluation.
- Fabricators lacking life-cycle assessment (LCA) data and Steel Fabrication Certification (SFC) are at risk of being excluded from major public-tender panels (only 57 of ~153 fabricators had SFC qualification, representing 92.5% of output per SCNZ, March 2023).

### OPPORTUNITY 1 – Infrastructure pipeline boom
- Te Waihanga's National Infrastructure Pipeline signals **NZ$204 bn combined project value** (Dec 2024 update) and NZ$12.1bn of construction spend projected for 2024.
- Roads of National Significance and the second Waitematā Harbour Crossing (NZTA SHIP 2024–34) are steel-intensive civil programs; the Mt Messenger bypass alone is NZ$280m with ~2,000 t of bridge steel estimated.
- CRL's 29,595 t of structural steel is being delivered 2023–2026, with seismic-led structural-steel share >80% in Canterbury providing a multi-year project pipeline pull on local fabricators.

### OPPORTUNITY 2 – Local-content / quality-as-differentiator
- SCNZ and the Distributor Charter position SFC-certified, locally fabricated steel as a procurement preference (Steel Construction NZ, https://scnz.org/about-us/). The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's (MBIE) procurement guidance and KiwiRail/NZTA buy-local policies repeatedly cite local supply-chain resilience and seismic compliance as evaluation criteria (e.g., Eastbridge's 2014 Waikato Expressway win explicitly noted local economic and tax-revenue benefits per https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU1403/S00881/napier-firm-wins-waikato-expressway-steel-bridge-contract.htm).
- This favours scaling fabricators like John Jones Steel, Grayson Engineering, Calder Stewart Steel and Eastbridge over imported fabricated assemblies.

### OPPORTUNITY 3 – Welding-beams and high-strength optimisation
- The shift toward optimised welded plate beams and buckling-restrained braces (BRBs) – spearheaded domestically by Steltech Structural (BlueScope/NZ Steel subsidiary) and Grayson Engineering's BRB range (https://grayson-brb.co.nz/about-us/) – creates a higher-margin, value-engineered product niche. BRB in particular grew materially after the Canterbury earthquakes for both new build and retrofit.
- Steltech's wholly-owned status within New Zealand Steel (https://www.steltech.co.nz/about-steltech/) creates a vertical template for integration that competing fabricators are starting to mimic through own beam-welding lines.

---

## Honest uncertainty / data-quality notes

1. **Scope mismatch between "fabrication" and "metal manufacturing":** Stats NZ ANZSIC C22 covers fabricated metal product manufacturing broadly; SCNZ tracks only structural-steel fabrication (~100,000 t). The two cannot be directly reconciled.
2. **No comprehensive disclosed-revenue ranking:** Most NZ fabricators are private. Where revenue/tonnage is cited in this report it is drawn from published case studies or job adverts and is the latest available disclosed figure, not necessarily 2024.
3. **Steel-mill duty rates:** Specific sub-heading rates under Chapter 72 (e.g., 7216.32, 7216.40, 7207.11 etc.) were not all directly verified at the chapter page; readers should confirm at the official NZ Customs Working Tariff Document before relying on a specific item for tender pricing.
4. **Mt Messenger tonnage:** Project steel demand is estimated by bridge analogue, not officially disclosed.
5. **SCNZ historical tonnage:** Publicly available SCNZ Industry Updates for 2018–2021 were not retrieved in this research pass; the ~100,000 t/yr figure is the description repeated in 2023 issues, treated here as a rolling 12-month figure rather than a precise annual time series.
6. **Data extract dates:** NZ Customs OIA data is dated 2 September 2025; Steel & Tube FY23 is year-end 30 June 2023; Te Waihanga pipeline snapshots are March 2024 and December 2024. The report's "2024" frame uses the most recent issue of each source available.

task.problem: Analyze the New Zealand construction metalworks (structural steel fabrication) market as of 2024, with historical data from 2018–2024. # Array Technologies Segment Portfolio Analysis: Legacy vs. STI Gross Margin Differential (Q1 2023 – 9M 2024)

## 1. Segment-Level Gross Margin Calculations

Gross margins below are calculated as segment gross profit ÷ segment revenue, drawn from Array Technologies' SEC filings — Forms 10-Q for Q1, Q2, and Q3 of 2023 and 2024, the FY 2023 10-K, and the FY 2024 10-K. Figures from the Q3 2024 10-Q reflect the restatement of certain 2023 capped-call and put-option derivative items; segment gross profit was not affected, and all comparisons remain apples-to-apples (Source: [Q3 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R21.htm); [FY 2024 10-K](https://www.publicnow.com/view/47972E6901E93E9937B6DB717ED2F324D627D637)).

| Period | Array Legacy Revenue ($K) | Array Legacy GP ($K) | **Legacy GM** | STI Revenue ($K) | STI GP ($K) | **STI GM** | Differential (bps) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 2023 | 305,204 | 79,835 | **26.2%** | 71,569 | 17,705 | **24.7%** | +142 |
| Q2 2023 | 345,261 | 102,950 | **29.8%** | 162,464 | 43,452 | **26.7%** | +307 |
| Q3 2023 | 244,857 | 58,233 | **23.8%** | 105,581 | 29,146 | **27.6%** | −382 |
| **9M 2023** | **895,322** | **241,019** | **26.9%** | **339,614** | **90,303** | **26.6%** | **+33** |
| Q1 2024 | 114,381 | 49,086 | **42.9%** | 39,022 | 6,004 | **15.4%** | +2,753 |
| Q2 2024 | 185,160 | 77,306 | **41.8%** | 70,606 | 8,647 | **12.2%** | +2,950 |
| Q3 2024 | 160,266 | 65,726 | **41.0%** | 71,140 | 12,589 | **17.7%** | +2,331 |
| **9M 2024** | **459,807** | **192,118** | **41.8%** | **180,768** | **27,240** | **15.1%** | **+2,671** |
| FY 2023 (context) | 1,172,827 | 317,605 | 27.1% | 403,724 | 97,946 | 24.3% | +282 |
| FY 2024 (context) | 661,629 | 270,031 | 40.8% | 254,178 | 27,646 | 10.9% | +2,994 |

Sources for the segment data: [Q1 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000049/R35.htm), [Q2 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000062/R21.htm), [Q3 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R21.htm), [Q3 2023 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072123000171/arry-20230930.htm), [FY 2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000011/R28.htm).

## 2. Magnitude and Persistence of the Performance Gap

**2023 baseline: essentially no gap.** Across the nine months ended September 30, 2023, the two segments operated at virtually identical gross margins (Legacy 26.9% vs. STI 26.6%, a 33 bps differential). Two of three 2023 quarters showed Legacy holding a modest lead (Q1: +142 bps; Q2: +307 bps); in Q3 2023, STI briefly outpaced Legacy (STI +382 bps). STI was the larger revenue contributor in Q2 and Q3 2023 (32.0% and 30.1% of consolidated revenue, respectively), so the segments were economically balanced.

**The gap exploded in 2024.** By the nine months ended September 30, 2024, the differential had widened to **2,671 basis points** — a swing of more than 2,600 bps year-over-year. The divergence is symmetric across every 2024 quarter:

- **Q1 2024:** Legacy +1,676 bps YoY (26.2% → 42.9%); STI −935 bps YoY (24.7% → 15.4%)
- **Q2 2024:** Legacy +1,193 bps YoY (29.8% → 41.8%); STI −1,450 bps YoY (26.7% → 12.2%)
- **Q3 2024:** Legacy +1,723 bps YoY (23.8% → 41.0%); STI −991 bps YoY (27.6% → 17.7%)

Legacy's gross profit dollars grew despite a 49% revenue decline, while STI's gross profit collapsed 70% YoY (from $90.3M in 9M 2023 to $27.2M in 9M 2024 on a 47% revenue decline). STI's share of consolidated gross profit fell from 27.3% to 12.4%, even though STI still generated 28.2% of consolidated revenue — a clear signal that one segment is now subsidizing the other in profitability terms.

## 3. Drivers of the Divergent Margin Trends

### Array Legacy's expansion: overwhelmingly Section 45X

Per the FY 2024 10-K, Section 45X vendor rebates and direct credits totaled **$173.6 million in 2024 versus only $9.3 million in 2023** — an incremental ~$164M flowing through Legacy's cost of revenue (Source: [FY 2024 10-K](https://www.publicnow.com/view/47972E6901E93E9937B6DB717ED2F324D627D637)). The U.S. Treasury/IRS final regulations issued October 24, 2024 confirmed the statutory definitions of torque tube and structural fasteners, which Array's components qualify for. The Company also began direct manufacturing in Q2 2024 at a new Albuquerque facility, allowing it to claim credits on its own production rather than only vendor rebates (Source: [Q3 2024 press release](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2024/11/07/2977200/0/en/array-technologies-inc-reports-financial-results-for-the-third-quarter-2024-delivers-exceptional-gross-margin-growth-and-continued-operational-momentum.html); [Q3 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R9.htm)).

On the Q3 2024 earnings call, CEO Hostetler explicitly tied the consolidated adjusted gross margin of 35.4% to "the realization of torque tube and structural fastener 45X benefits." Because STI Operations earns revenue primarily outside the United States (Spain, Brazil, etc.), it cannot directly claim U.S. 45X credits, and the domestic-content bonus safe harbor under Notice 2024-41 likewise accrues to U.S.-manufactured projects. **This regulatory asymmetry is the single largest structural driver of the margin gap.**

### STI's compression: international headwinds

1. **Volume and ASP pressure.** STI 2024 revenue fell 37% YoY, driven by a 12% volume decline and ASP reductions. Q1 2024 STI revenue of $39M was nearly half the level of any 2023 quarter.
2. **Brazil market softness and FX.** On the Q3 2024 call, CFO James Zhu attributed guidance narrowing to "a significant devaluation of the Brazilian real," explaining that even with stable volume and pricing in local currency, USD-translated revenue declined.
3. **Project mix.** STI serves large international utility-scale solar projects where pricing is more competitive and currency exposure is greater, with limited ability to pass through cost increases.
4. **No domestic-content premium.** STI's trackers sold outside the U.S. cannot capture the IRA 10% domestic-content adder available to U.S. projects.

## 4. Strategic Value and Operational Efficiency

### Array Legacy Operations: structurally advantaged, value-creating engine

With ~72% of consolidated revenue generating ~88% of consolidated gross profit in 9M 2024, Legacy has become a highly efficient profit engine. Adjusted gross margin reached 35–38% in 2024 (per quarterly press releases), well above STI's GAAP gross margin in any quarter. The combination of: (i) a U.S. manufacturing footprint in the most generous solar incentive regime globally (IRA + domestic content adder); (ii) certified 100% domestic content availability for U.S. customers (announced for H1 2025); (iii) the flagship DuraTrack HZ v3 platform augmented by OmniTrack™ for diverse terrain; and (iv) a $2.0B orderbook with 20% domestic-content-evaluating orders — positions Legacy as the dominant value driver. Even with revenue down 44% YoY in 2024, Legacy delivered only a 15% decline in gross profit dollars ($317.6M → $270.0M) thanks to margin expansion.

### STI Operations: structurally disadvantaged, value-eroding asset

With ~28% of consolidated revenue generating only ~12% of consolidated gross profit in 9M 2024, STI's economics have inverted from a peer contributor in 2023 to a margin drag. The Company recognized a **$162.0 million non-cash goodwill impairment in Q3 2024** specifically against the STI Operations reporting unit (fair value estimated at $455.9M versus a higher carrying value) — an unambiguous accounting acknowledgment that STI's contribution to enterprise value has materially eroded since the acquisition (closed January 11, 2022; total STI consideration reported at ~$891M in public disclosures). STI's segment assets declined from $838.0M (FY 2023 10-K) to $407.5M (FY 2024 10-K) — a ~51% reduction driven primarily by the goodwill write-down and FX translation.

## 5. Competitive Positioning Implications

The margin trends reveal that Array's competitive positioning has bifurcated:

- **In the U.S. market**, Array Legacy has substantially widened its structural advantage through the 45X + domestic-content flywheel. As one of very few tracker manufacturers with certified U.S. domestic content (alongside peers leveraging the same IRA framework), Array can offer developers an extra 10% adder on production tax credits — a meaningful differentiator that competitors without U.S. manufacturing cannot replicate. This is reflected in the 20% YoY growth in domestic orderbook despite overall U.S. utility-scale solar headwinds (interconnection delays, permitting, AD/CVD tariff uncertainty).

- **In international markets**, Array (through STI) operates as a price-taker against regional tracker providers (STI Norland's home competitors in Spain and Latin America). With no access to U.S. incentives and exposure to currency volatility (Brazilian real devaluation, EUR/USD swings), STI's margin floor is materially lower. Array's competitive moat internationally depends on technology (OmniTrack™ for terrain-following), local manufacturing presence, and project execution — none of which produce the kind of margin expansion that 45X delivers domestically.

## 6. Acquisition Strategy and Integration Priorities

The magnitude of the STI margin collapse (from 26.6% to 15.1% gross margin in nine months; from $90.3M to $27.2M gross profit dollars) combined with the $162M goodwill impairment demonstrates that **Array's STI acquisition, completed in January 2022 for the strategic goal of "accelerating international expansion" (per the FY 2024 10-K), has not delivered on its margin thesis**. Several conclusions follow:

**a) The portfolio's center of gravity has decisively shifted back to U.S. domestic content.** Management's primary value-creation lever in 2024 — 45X credit maximization, the Albuquerque manufacturing facility, domestic-content certification, OmniTrack™ adoption, and orderbook growth focus — all exclusively benefit Array Legacy. STI is being carried by the consolidated entity while the U.S. business compounds value. The 2,671 bps margin gap is a direct measurement of this strategic tilt.

**b) Integration priorities have de-emphasized STI cost rationalization in favor of U.S. margin expansion.** Rather than investing to close the STI margin gap (through supply chain optimization, mix shift, or pricing actions), management has redirected capital and management attention to the Legacy segment's IRA-driven opportunity set. This is rational economically but signals that STI is unlikely to deliver Legacy-like margins in the foreseeable future.

**c) Acquisition strategy lessons.** The STI experience suggests that Array's acquisition framework should weigh regulatory and incentive asymmetry heavily. Future M&A would likely be evaluated for U.S.-domestic-content accretion potential rather than purely for geographic diversification. The market appears to have internalized this lesson: Array's stock hit a 52-week low during Q3 2024 precisely when the STI goodwill was written down, indicating investor recognition that the international diversification rationale no longer justifies STI's prior carrying value.

**d) STI is unlikely to be divested in the near term but faces strategic reassessment.** With $407.5M of remaining segment assets (mostly PP&E, intangibles, and working capital in Spain and Brazil), STI represents a meaningful part of Array's global footprint and customer relationships. The 2024 10-K describes STI as central to "expanding our presence in Brazil and other southern hemisphere markets to mitigate seasonal revenue fluctuations." However, the $162M impairment and persistent sub-15% gross margins create clear pressure on management to either (i) demonstrate a credible path to STI margin recovery in 2025–2026, or (ii) further rationalize the carrying value of STI-related assets. The strategic question for Array going forward is whether STI remains a core strategic asset or becomes a candidate for restructuring, divestiture, or further impairment.

## 7. Consolidated Verification and Cross-Check

Independent verification of consolidated figures from Panel 3 corroborates the trajectory shown at the segment level (Source: [Q1 2023 release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072123000094/exhibit9912023q1pressrelea.htm); [Q2 2023 release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072123000154/exhibit9912023q2pressrelea.htm); [Q3 2023 release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000119312523272461/d903281dex991.htm); [Q3 2024 release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000073/exhibit9912024q3pressrelea.htm)):

| Period | Consolidated Revenue ($K) | Consolidated GP ($K) | Consolidated GAAP GM | Adjusted GM |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---::|
| FY 2022 | 1,637,546 | 212,718 | 13.0% | 14.3% |
| Q1 2023 | 376,773 | 101,179 | 26.9% | n/a |
| Q2 2023 | 507,725 | 150,042 | 29.6% | n/a |
| Q3 2023 | 350,438 | 87,379 | 24.9% | 26.0% |
| 9M 2023 | 1,234,936 | 331,322 | 26.8% | 27.7% |
| FY 2023 | 1,576,551 | 415,551 | 26.4% | 27.3% |
| Q3 2024 | 231,406 | 78,315 | 33.8% | 35.4% |
| 9M 2024 | 640,575 | 219,358 | 34.2% | 35.9% |

The FY 2022 baseline gross margin of 13.0% (GAAP) and 14.3% (adjusted) provides important pre-acquisition context — Array Legacy alone never operated near this margin floor once IRA incentives crystallized. The approximately 170 bps gap between GAAP and adjusted gross margins in 2024 periods reflects management's add-backs (primarily amortization of acquired intangibles related to the STI acquisition).

## 8. Summary Verdict

The gross margin differential between Array Legacy Operations and STI Operations is **not a temporary cyclical phenomenon** but a **structurally persistent and widening gap** driven by: (1) U.S.-only regulatory incentives (45X, domestic content adder) that flow exclusively to Legacy; (2) international headwinds (Brazilian FX, ASP pressure, competitive intensity) that disproportionately affect STI; and (3) management's deliberate strategic prioritization of U.S. domestic-content capabilities, evidenced by ~$164M of incremental 45X benefits and a new Albuquerque manufacturing facility in 2024. The data and the $162M Q3 2024 STI goodwill impairment together confirm that Array's "portfolio strategy" has effectively become a one-segment growth strategy (Legacy/U.S.), with STI serving as a smaller, lower-margin international platform whose strategic value must be reassessed in light of the persistent 2,600+ bps margin gap.

# Delta Ranges for Protective Collar Strategy — Comprehensive Research Summary

## Required Output

```
Sold Call Delta: 0.20 to 0.30 (balanced); 0.15 to 0.20 (upside-preserving)
Sweet spot: 0.25–0.30 (the codified Cboe BXMD 30-delta convention for covered calls,
which a collar's short call leg is). At normal 30–60 DTE, 0.30-delta corresponds to
~3–5% OTM; 0.20-delta to ~5–7% OTM.

Bought Put Delta: 0.20 to 0.35 (standard protection); 0.25–0.30 is the workhorse.
0.10–0.16 is the cheap "disaster insurance" alternative. At normal 30–60 DTE, a
0.25–0.30-delta put sits ~5–10% OTM.

Symmetric vs Asymmetric: ASYMMETRIC. Do not target equal deltas. Pick the put
floor first (typically 0.20–0.30 delta, 5–10% OTM), then walk the call chain to
match premium. The realized asymmetry direction depends on the underlying:
  • On INDEX options (negative skew): call delta typically > put delta
    (call lands closer to spot than the put).
  • On SINGLE STOCKS (lognormal positive tail): call often lands further OTM
    than the put, so put delta > call delta.
Net position delta after both legs is +0.45 to +0.70 (NOT delta-neutral).

Example Collar (Stock $100, 60 DTE, ~25% IV, flat skew for illustration):
  Sell call: $106.70 strike (+6.7% OTM), Delta +0.30, premium ≈ $1.79
  Buy put:   $95.00 strike  (−5.0% OTM), Delta −0.27, premium ≈ $1.79
  Net credit/debit: ≈ $0.00 (zero-cost)
  Max gain if called at $106.70: ~$670 (less yourself call distance above cost basis)
  Max loss if put exercised at $95: ~$500
  Position delta: 1.00 − 0.30 − 0.27 ≈ +0.43
```

---

## 1. Sold Call Delta — 0.20 to 0.30 (0.25–0.30 sweet spot)

The single strongest piece of evidence is **codified, not anecdotal**. Cboe's **S&P 500 30-Delta BuyWrite Index (BXMD)** methodology explicitly states: "the option with a delta closest to **0.30** is selected" when writing the monthly OTM SPX call ([Cboe BuyWrite Indices Methodology](https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/governance/Cboe_BuyWrite_Indices_Methodology.pdf)). A collar's short call leg *is* a covered call, so BXMD is the institutional answer to "what delta does a covered call use." Nasdaq Dorsey Wright calls 30-delta the "sweet spot between generating premium and preserving upside" ([Nasdaq Dorsey Wright, May 2025](https://dorseywright.nasdaq.com/research/bigwire/2025/05/27/05-27-2025/optimizing-a-covered-call-strategy)).

**Practitioner convention:** 0.20–0.30 is the cited band across practitioner sources — Ryan O'Connell, CFA: "call with delta around 0.20 to 0.30" ([ryanoconnellfinance.com](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/collar-strategy/)); Stock Market Pulse collar guide: "sell a call at ~0.20–0.30 delta" ([stock-market-pulse](https://stock-market-pulse.contentwave.net/article/options-collars-updated-guide-for-september-2026)); Optvana: "20-30-delta calls" so the call premium exceeds or equals the put cost ([optvana.com](https://optvana.com/strategies/collar)); QuantWheel: 0.30-delta OTM is the "optimal balance" between premium and keeping shares, typically 3–5% OTM at 30–45 DTE ([quantwheel.com](https://quantwheel.com/learn/covered-call-strike-selection)); OptionsDecay: "20-30-delta calls" ([optionsdecay.com](https://www.optionsdecay.com/strategies/intermediate/collar/)); TheOptionPremium's worked example sells the 0.30-delta call ([theoptionpremium.com](https://www.theoptionpremium.com/p/collar-options-strategy)).

**30-year SPY backtest evidence (OptionsPilot):** 0.30-delta produced the highest annualized total return (≈12.4% vs 11.8% for 0.20) while sacrificing less upside than 0.40, with assignment frequency ≈28% of cycles ([OptionsPilot covered-call backtest](https://optionspilot.app/blog/covered-call-expected-return-by-delta)).

**Institutional benchmark — the Cboe CLL:** sells a **10% OTM call monthly**. At typical SPX IV and one-month tenor, that call is roughly 0.10–0.20 delta — deliberately far OTM to preserve upside ([Cboe CLL methodology, Oct 2019](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf)).

**0.30 vs 0.20:** 0.30 is the default because it maximizes the credit that funds the put — the entire economic point of the structure. 0.20 is correct when the holder's priority is upside retention (low cost basis, unwilling to be assigned). Note: 0.30 delta ≈ ~30% risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM, not a guaranteed 30% assignment rate.

---

## 2. Bought Put Delta — 0.20 to 0.35 (0.25–0.30 typical)

Ryan O'Connell, CFA: "a put with delta around **−0.20 to −0.30**" ([ryanoconnellfinance.com](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/collar-strategy/)). FinancialTechWiz: "Five to ten percent out-of-the-money strikes (roughly **25 to 35 delta**) are the standard hedge" ([financialtechwiz.com](https://www.fintechwiz.com/post/protective-put/)). Proflex Finance: "put around **20 to 35 delta** — typically 5–10% below the price" ([proflexfinance.com](https://proflexfinance.com/insights/protective-put-strategy)). Stock Market Pulse: "buy a put at ~**0.25–0.35 delta**" ([stock-market-pulse](https://stock-market-pulse.contentwave.net/article/options-collars-updated-guide-for-september-2026)).

**Cboe CLL benchmark:** buys a **5% OTM put quarterly** — at typical equity IV and three-month tenor, that put is approximately −0.25 to −0.30 delta ([Cboe CLL methodology](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf)). Equicurious: 5% OTM 30-day put at ~16% IV = delta ≈ **−0.27** ([equicurious.com](https://equicurious.com/learn/derivatives/options-strategies-and-greeks/protective-puts-and-collars)).

**Measured AQR data (Israelov & Klein 2016):** actual put delta in the CBOE 95-110 collar ranged from **−0.24** (Sept 2014, VIX 12.1) to **−0.39** (Dec 2008, VIX 44.9) — high-vol regimes push the same %OTM strike to higher absolute delta ([AQR paper](https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Journal-Articles/Risk-and-Return.pdf)). Embark's example: 5% OTM put ≈ −0.40 delta; 10% OTM put ≈ −0.30; 20% OTM put ≈ −0.15 to −0.20.

**0.20 vs 0.30 put:** 0.20 trades floor quality for cost (typically ~8–10% OTM on 30–60d options; ordinary −5% to −10% drawdowns are unhedged). 0.30 buys a tighter, more expensive floor (~5% OTM). Zero-cost-collar variants push the put to **0.16-delta ("16-delta puts")** to keep the structure cheap enough for the call to fund it ([Optvana](https://optvana.com/strategies/collar)).

---

## 3. Symmetric vs Asymmetric — ASYMMETRIC (overwhelmingly)

**Equal deltas ≠ zero cost.** The zero-cost objective "typically drives collar portfolio construction" (AQR), and because of vol skew, zero-cost forces asymmetry. Black-Scholes model with index-style skew (45 DTE, r=4.5%, q=1.5%, IV=20%−0.60·ln(K/S)): a 0.30-delta SPY put costs **$1.54** but a 0.30-delta SPY call costs only **$1.15** — the put is **34% more expensive** at equal delta. OptionsDecay: "matching deltas usually leaves a small net debit, not a clean zero" ([optionsdecay.com](https://www.optionsdecay.com/strategies/intermediate/collar/)).

**Asymmetry direction depends on underlying type:**
- **INDEX collars (negative skew):** puts are rich (high IV), so the zero-cost call must sit *closer to money* than the put — call delta typically > put delta. JPMorgan Hedged Equity (JHEQX) example: 3.5–5.5% OTM call (~0.30–0.34 delta) funds a 5% OTM put (~0.30 delta) PLUS a 20% OTM short put (~0.07 delta) ([Morningstar JHEQX](https://www.morningstar.com/funds/xnas/jheqx/analysis); [SpotGamma](https://spotgamma.com/jpm-morgan-collar-trade/)).
- **SINGLE-STOCK collars (lognormal positive right tail):** call strikes tend to land *further OTM* than put strikes at zero premium — put delta often > call delta. NISA Investment Advisors documents this "long right tail asymmetry" ([NISA](https://www.nisa.com/perspectives/the-long-right-tail-asymmetry-in-single-stock-collars/)). Black-Scholes at flat 25% vol, 60 DTE: 5% OTM $95 put costs $1.79 (delta −0.27); the premium-matched call strike is $106.70 (+6.7% OTM, delta +0.30).

**Direction of asymmetry differs across panels:**
- Panel 1 (single-stock focus): typical retail collar has put 0.25–0.30 vs call 0.20–0.25 (put Δ > call Δ).
- Panel 2 (index focus): zero-cost index collar has call Δ > put Δ by ~0.05–0.10.
- Panel 3 reconciles: the apparent contradiction dissolves when underlying type is specified.

**Net position delta:** typically **+0.45 to +0.70** — NOT delta-neutral. Equicurious recommends keeping net delta between +0.30 and +0.80. Panel 2's verified model: $95 put (Δ −0.24) + $104 call (Δ 0.29) → position delta = 1.00 − 0.29 − 0.24 = **+0.47**. A true delta-neutral collar (equal-magnitude deltas, net ≈ 0) is rare — it's a specialized vol/theta-harvesting structure, not stock protection ([Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/analysis/the-collar-strategy-from-a-delta-perspective-200278121)).

---

## 4. Percentage Distance from Current Price

Institutions specify collars in **% of spot**, but delta is the better specifier because it auto-adjusts for each name's volatility and tenor.

| Structure | Put Strike | Call Strike | Equivalent Delta (30–60d, normal IV) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cboe CLL (institutional benchmark)** | 5% OTM (3-mo) | 10% OTM (1-mo) | ≈ −0.25 / ≈ 0.15–0.20 |
| **Cboe CLLZ (zero-cost put-spread collar)** | 2.5% OTM (bought) / 5% OTM (sold) | call "pays for" spread | ≈ −0.20 / depends |
| **Retail zero-cost pairing** | 5–10% OTM | 5–7% OTM | ≈ −0.25 put / +0.25–0.30 call |
| **Pension 1-year zero-cost (LGIM)** | 10% OTM (90% strike) | 12% OTM (112% strike) | lower deltas at long tenor |
| **JPMorgan JHEQX** | 5% OTM (bought) / 20% OTM (sold) | 3.5–5.5% OTM | ≈ −0.30 / +0.27–0.34 |
| **UBS 2-year insider monetization** | 10% OTM | 20% OTM | wide band (tax-driven) |

**Delta↔moneyness translation (1-month index options, ~18% IV):** 0.30Δ ≈ ±3% OTM; 0.25Δ ≈ ±3.5%; 0.20Δ ≈ ±4–4.5%; 0.16Δ ≈ ±5% (Panel 2 model). At 60 DTE and 25% vol: same ±5% OTM strike = −0.27 put delta / +0.20 call delta. **Rule of thumb: anchor on delta and treat %OTM as a label** — a "10%-OTM put" on KO (low-vol) and on NVDA (high-vol) are radically different insurance contracts; a "0.20-delta put" is the same *probability of protection* on both.

---

## 5. Institutional Collar Structures

**(a) Cboe S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index (CLL) — canonical passive benchmark**
- 5% OTM put quarterly, 10% OTM call monthly, rolled on a 3-month and 1-month cadence.
- 28.5-year backtest (1986–2014, [AQR/Israelov & Klein 2016](https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Journal-Articles/Risk-and-Return.pdf)): ~5.2% annualized return vs ~7.3% for S&P 500, with volatility ~10.7% vs ~15.7% (about 71% of the return for 67% of the volatility).
- **Important caveat:** AQR documented that CLL spends roughly **$7.50 on puts for every $1 collected from calls** — the 5%/10% benchmark is meaningfully net-debit, not zero-cost (Panel 1). Replicated: ~7.2:1 ratio (Panel 2).
- AQR's verdict: investors would be better off simply reducing equity exposure — the collar is a *funded-status/drawdown-control* tool, not an alpha strategy.
- Available as ETF: Global X XCLR (tracks Cboe 3-Month Collar 95-110 Index).

**(b) Cboe Zero-Cost Put-Spread Collar (CLLZ)**
- Buys 2.5% OTM put, sells 5% OTM put, sells whatever call "pays for" the spread ([Cboe Insights](https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/benchmark-indices-series-hedging-downside-exposure-with-pput-cll-and-cllz-indices/)). Monthly roll. Note how tight the institutional put leg is (2.5–5% OTM ≈ 0.20–0.30 delta at 1-month).

**(c) Pension/LDI structures (dominant institutional use)**
- **LGIM (Legal & General Investment Management):** 1-year 90% put financed by selling 112% call, rolled monthly at 1/12 sizing ("always on" protection), often OTC "listed-lookalike" contracts with Treasury collateral ([LGIM 2020 Equity Protection](https://am.landg.us.com/insights/thought-leadership/tailor-your-risks-with-an-equity-collar/); [LGIM 2024 whitepaper](https://am.landg.us.com/asset/4994de/globalassets/lgima/insights/whitepapers/tailor-your-risk-by-buttoning-up-with-an-equity-collar.pdf)).
- **bfinance UK public sector pension (2019):** put-spread collar with **−10% to −30% downside protection and +10% upside cap**, static cost **3–6 bps/year** ([Professional Pensions, 2019](https://www.professionalpensions.com/analysis/3069310/-schemes-protect-equity-losses)).
- **L&G 2022 illustration:** two-year **70–90% put-spread collar** capped upside at ~33% over two years in exchange for protection from −10% to −30% ([blog.landg.com](https://blog.landg.com/categories/investment-strategy/market-volatility-got-you-hot-under-the-collar/)).
- **JPMorgan Hedged Equity (JHEQX) — largest institutional equity-collar program** (~40,000+ contracts per leg, several billion dollars notional each quarter). Actual December 2021 roll observed by SpotGamma: long 4135 put Δ 0.30; short 3480 put Δ 0.07; short 4505 call Δ 0.34 ([SpotGamma](https://spotgamma.com/jpm-morgan-collar-trade/); [Morningstar JHEQX](https://www.morningstar.com/funds/xnas/jheqx/analysis)).
- **JPMorgan / Risk.net:** collars and put-spread collars as standard tools for DB pension plans to protect funded status ([Risk.net / JPMorgan](https://www.risk.net/sites/default/files/import_unmanaged/risk.net/data/risk/pdf/special/0303_jpmorgan.pdf)).

**(d) Corporate insider / concentrated-stock monetization (UBS)**
- Two-year zero-premium collars, 10% OTM put / 20% OTM call (90/120) — wide band to avoid taxable events ([UBS equity risk management](https://onlineservices.ubs.com/staticfiles/pws/adobe/equity_risk_management.pdf)).
- Academic evidence (Bettis, Bizjak & Kalpathy): insiders hedge ~30% of shareholdings on average using zero-cost collars and prepaid forwards ([Bettis-Bizjak-Kalpathy](https://www.shareholderforum.com/sop/Library/20090318_Bettis-Bizjak-Kalpathy.pdf)).

**(e) LEAPS + Short Call Collar (long-duration holders)**
- 6–12 month put (~0.25 delta, ~85% strike on a $100 stock) combined with rolling weekly/monthly covered calls (0.10–0.20 delta). Used by founders, retirees, and concentrated-stock holders for continuous protection ([Options Trading Guide LEAPS Collar](https://www.optionstrading.org)).

**Institutional takeaway:** institutions overwhelmingly prefer **put-spread collars** over plain collars because they target a specific protection band (e.g., −10% to −30%) at zero cost while preserving a much wider upside cap than the Cboe 95-110 benchmark.

---

## 6. Quantitative Examples

**Retail balanced zero-cost (Panel 3 Black-Scholes, flat 25% vol, 60 DTE, r=3%):**
- $95 put (5% OTM): premium $1.79, delta −0.27
- Premium-matched call strike: **$106.70** (+6.7% OTM, delta +0.30)
- Net cost ≈ $0.00, position delta ≈ +0.43

**Panel 1 worked example ($100 stock, 30–45 DTE, ~16% IV):**
- Bought Put: $95 strike (5% OTM), delta −0.27, premium $2.50
- Sold Call: $107 strike (~7% OTM), delta +0.20, premium $2.50
- Net premium: $0.00; max loss $500; max gain $700; **net position delta +0.53**

**Panel 2 verified example ($100 stock, 45 DTE, IV 20% with skew):**
- Sell $104 strike, delta 0.29, premium $1.11
- Buy $95 strike, delta −0.24, premium $1.16
- Net debit $0.05/share (≈ $5/contract, effectively zero-cost)
- Max gain $394/contract; max loss $506/contract; **position delta +0.47**

**JPMorgan JHEQX (Dec 2021 SPX roll, observed by SpotGamma):**
- Long 4135 put (5% OTM), delta +0.30
- Short 3480 put (20% OTM), delta −0.07
- Short 4505 call (3.5–5.5% OTM), delta −0.34

---

## 7. Summary

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Sold call delta | **0.20–0.30** (typical ~0.25); 0.30 is the codified BXMD benchmark; 0.15–0.20 for upside-preserving (CBOE CLL = 10% OTM = ~0.10–0.20). |
| Bought put delta | **0.20–0.35** (typical ~0.25–0.30); 0.10–0.16 for cheap crash insurance. |
| Symmetric vs Asymmetric | **Asymmetric** — pick put floor first, then premium-match the call. Direction depends on underlying (index: call Δ > put Δ; single-stock: put Δ > call Δ). |
| % distance OTM | Put 5–10%; Call 5–15% (CBOE CLL = 5%/10%). |
| Institutional structure | Plain collar (CBOE CLL 95-110) for benchmark/hedged-equity; **put-spread collars** dominant for pensions/LDI (LGIM 90/112; JPMorgan JHEQX); long-duration LEAPS+short-call for concentrated holders. |
| Net position delta | **+0.45 to +0.70** (NOT delta-neutral). |

---

## 8. Key Caveats

1. **Delta is not constant.** A "5% OTM put" can be −0.19 delta at 30 DTE / low IV and −0.35+ at 90 DTE / high IV. Always confirm the live option chain's delta at your chosen DTE before entering.

2. **"Zero-cost" is rare in practice on index options.** AQR documented the CBOE CLL spends **$7.50 on puts per $1 collected from calls** — the 5%/10% structure is meaningfully net-debit. True zero-cost requires premium equivalence at trade entry, then expires, and net debit can accumulate through rolls.

3. **Percentage distance is not a stable proxy for delta.** Delta depends on tenor and IV. Anchor on delta, treat %OTM as a descriptive label.

4. **Direction depends on the underlying.** Negative skew on equities/ETFs (puts rich) pushes zero-cost call closer to spot than put. Positive right tail on single stocks pushes call further OTM than put at zero premium.

5. **True delta-neutral collars are not common** in protective stock strategies — they're more typical in vol/theta-harvesting structures (iron condors, strangles).

6. **A collar is a risk-control tool, not an alpha strategy.** AQR's verdict: investors would be better off simply reducing equity exposure than buying the CBOE 95-110. The collar pays in forfeited upside and negative volatility alpha for the protection it provides.

2. What Delta for the BOUGHT PUT?
